Social networks research in educational contexts is highly interdisciplinary and simultaneously addresses theoretical, statistical, and research design challenges.  Members of the lab combine research approaches from the social sciences, statistics, and computer science. They address empirical research questions with modern ways of data collection (often combining data from digital behavioral traces with surveys) and advance the development of statistical methods, algorithms, and scientific software. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Pore-Scale Modelling of Multiphase Flow and Reactive Transport Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Pore-Scale Modelling of Multiphase Flow and Reactive Transport 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a highly motivated doctoral student to develop advanced numerical models for investigating multiphase flow and reactive transport processes in porous materials. We are offering a doctoral position in the Durability of Engineering Materials research group at ETH Zurich. The group, led by Prof. Ueli Angst, addresses research challenges related to the durability of engineered materials, combining experimental and computational approaches in corrosion science, materials science, porous media, and reactive mass transport. One important research challenge in this field is understanding multiphase transport in porous materials and its role in natural and engineered systems. As liquids move through porous materials, gas can become trapped within the pore space, forming bubbles or irregular gas clusters. These trapped gases can subsequently dissolve, grow, or change in composition, with their evolution closely linked to fluid distribution, mass transport, and chemical reactions. Understanding these processes is important for a wide range of applications, including the durability of construction materials, geological waste containment, CO2 sequestration, and underground energy storage. Job description This doctoral project aims to advance the understanding of multiphase flow and reactive transport in porous media through the development and application of advanced numerical models The research will focus on the evolution of gas and liquid phases in complex pore geometries, considering processes such as gas compressibility, gas–liquid interfacial mass transfer, and (electro-)chemical reactions The successful candidate will develop and apply numerical methods for pore-scale simulations of multiphase flow, coupling fluid dynamics with gas dissolution, diffusion, and reactive transport The research will investigate how gas–liquid interface dynamics and pore geometry influence gas entrapment and evolution The project will build on ongoing research in pore-scale modelling and offer opportunities for collaboration with experimental researchers Profile MSc degree in Mechanical Engineering, Civil Engineering, Computational Science and Engineering, Applied jobs.title: Doctoral position in robotic spraying for biocementation
jobs.description:
Doctoral position in robotic spraying for biocementation Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral position in robotic spraying for biocementation 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair for Digital Building Technologies invites applications for a PhD position on robotic spraying as an additive manufacturing process for biocementation. The research brings together two closely coupled lines of work: the development of an additive robotic fabrication system based on material deposition and microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP), with a focus on applying MICP to the fabrication of architectural elements. This PhD is part of the SNSF-funded project “DFabuLis: Digital Fabrication Using Living Systems”, conducted in collaboration with Dr. Dimitrios Terzis, Senior Scientist in the Laloui group at EPFL. Project background Conventional cement-based construction binds aggregates through an energy-intensive process. Bio-binders offer a different fabrication logic. In biocementation, certain bacteria precipitate calcium carbonate between particles, allowing binding to form under ambient conditions. This project treats the bio-binder as a fabrication parameter. Through robotic deposition of bacterial and cementation solutions, mineral binding can be spatially controlled across a printed structure, producing architectural elements with locally differentiated density, strength, porosity, and surface properties within a single component. The research will investigate how robotic deposition of biocement can be translated into architectural production strategies, from material placement and component geometry to surface formation and assembly. In collaboration with the Soil Mechanics Laboratory at EPFL, the project connects robotic fabrication with the characterisation and formulation of bio-binders. The resulting strategies will be explored in architectural-scale demonstrators. Job description You will develop a robotic fabrication process for biocementation, including adapting existing deposition hardware, and the computational workflow linking design intent to material placement You will use it to produce architectural components, investigating through making how graded biocementation can inform structure, surface, and assembly You will assess the environmental footprint of the process and use it to guide fabrication and design choices You will conduct research in close collaboration with project partners at ETH and EPFL and, where applicable, industry partners. You will work closely with the Soil Mechanics Laboratory at EPFL, whose characterisation of the material will inform the development of the process You will write scientific articles for publication in peer-reviewed journals, present at international conferences, and contribute to teaching through the supervision of semester and master's projects Profile A Master's degree in architecture or a closely related discipline, with a demonstrated body of work in digital fabrication Competence in building and modifying fabrication equipment; experience with robotics, electronics, or control software is a strong asset Fluency in computational design and experience moving between digital models and physical results Interest in biological or material processes; experience in a wet lab is welcome but not required. Interest in circular and low-impact construction; familiarity with life cycle assessment is an advantage Excellent written and spoken English; conversational German is an advantage Strong communication skills and a collaborative disposition, as the project spans disciplines and research groups Workplace Workplace We offer The Chair for Digital Building Technologies within the Institute of Technology in Architecture conducts research at the intersection of computational design, materials, and construction-scale fabrication. Over more than a decade, the group has developed and operated powder-bed and extrusion-based printing systems at architectural scale, with built results including the tallest 3D-printed structures in the world. In-house expertise in materials, mechanical design, electronics, and software, together with complete workshop and prototyping infrastructure, allows research ideas to move directly from concept to machine to printed artifact, and doctoral researchers are given considerable latitude in shaping that trajectory. Our highly diverse and international group offers extensive networks within ETH and internationally. We are committed to diversity by offering flexible working hours, home office options, and other measures to ensure team members can perform their roles effectively. chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.title: Two Doctoral Positions in the SNSF Research Project "From Homes to Habitat – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition"
jobs.description:
Two Doctoral Positions in the SNSF Research Project "From Homes to Habitat – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition" Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Two Doctoral Positions in the SNSF Research Project "From Homes to Habitat – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition" 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken ETH Wohnforum – ETH CASE (Centre for Research on Architecture, Society & the Built Environment) at the Department of Architecture, ETH Zurich, is seeking two doctoral researchers (100%, four years) to join the SNSF-funded research project “From Homes to Habitats – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition,” starting on 1 June 2027 or upon agreement. The PhD will last from 2027-2031 (4 years). Project background How can housing support a shift towards more sustainable ways of living? The overall research project investigates the potential of housing cooperatives in Switzerland as agents of socio-ecological transition. Moving beyond their established role in providing affordable housing, the project examines how housing cooperatives develop innovative social, spatial, and ecological practices across diverse territorial contexts. While existing research has predominantly focused on housing cooperatives in major cities, the project investigates housing cooperatives in metropolitan, peri-urban, rural, peripheral, and Alpine territories, examining how different urbanisation processes shape cooperative housing practices and their potential for socio-ecological transformation. The project is hosted at ETH Wohnforum – ETH CASE, Department of Architecture, ETH Zurich, under the responsibility of Prof. Dr. Elli Mosayebi , Professor of Architecture and Design. The doctoral researchers will work within an interdisciplinary research team bringing together expertise in architecture, housing, urban and territorial studies, and socio-ecological transformation. In addition, you will benefit from being associated to the Doctoral Programme at the ETH Zurich Department of Architecture’s Institute of Landscape and Urban Studies (LUS). ETH Wohnforum – ETH CASE (Centre for Research on Architecture, Society & the Built Environment) is an interdisciplinary institute for research, consulting and education in the field of housing, architecture, and urban development at the department of architecture at ETH Zurich. Job description We are seeking two motivated doctoral researchers to join our interdisciplinary research team and contribute to the investigation of housing cooperatives as agents of socio-ecological transition across Switzerland. Your responsibilities and tasks will include: Contribute to the development of the project's conceptual and methodological framework. Participate in the mapping and typology building of housing cooperatives across Switzerland. Design and conduct qualitative case studies within the respective territorial focus. Undertake fieldwork, including site visits, interviews, participant observation, and spatial documentation. Analyse architectural, spatial, social, and ecological practices through qualitative and visual research methods. Participate in the organisation of workshops with researchers, housing cooperatives, and relevant stakeholders. Profile Master's degree in architecture, urban studies, sociology, or a related discipline, with a strong interest in housing, territorial transformation, and socio-ecological questions. Strong interest in interdisciplinary research at the intersection of architecture, society, and ecology. Knowledge of and/or experience with qualitative research methods, including interviews, participant observation, and case study research. Interest in architectural and spatial analysis, mapping, and visual research methods. Experience with architectural drawing, GIS, or cartographic tools is an advantage. Ability to work independently and collaboratively within an interdisciplinary research team. Strong analytical, communication, and academic writing skills. Excellent command of written and spoken English. Knowledge of German, French, and/or Italian is highly desirable, particularly for conducting fieldwork in Switzerland. Workplace Workplace We offer ETH Zurich is a family-friendly employer with excellent working conditions. You can look forward to an exciting working environment, cultural diversity and attractive offers and benefits. The positions offer the opportunity to pursue doctoral research within an interdisciplinary and collaborative research environment at ETH Zurich, engaging with contemporary debates on housing, architecture, urbanisation, and socio-ecological transition.The doctoral researchers will benefit from close collaboration with the ETH Wohnforum research team and an international network of academic and practice-based partners. The general area of the laboratory covers the study of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in the context of Engineering Design problems in domains such as healthcare, power generation, aerospace, and robotics. jobs.title: Doctoral Student in Quantum Error Correction
jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Quantum Error Correction Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Quantum Error Correction 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We invite applications for a doctoral position in the theory of quantum error correction at ETH Zurich, supervised by Joseph M. Renes and co-supervised by Renato Renner. Quantum computers promise capabilities far beyond today's computers, but only if we can reliably protect quantum information from errors. Quantum error correction (QEC) is therefore one of the central challenges on the path toward large-scale quantum computing. In this Doctoral project, you will investigate the fundamental limits of quantum error correction. The position is part of QuBriC , the first European Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network (MSCDN) dedicated entirely to QEC, and includes secondments to Politecnico di Milano and Quantinuum in Cambridge, England. The PhD position is fully funded for 3 years. The expected starting date is early/mid 2027, but a later start is also possible. Job description Your main responsibility will be to conduct high-quality research within the project and progressively develop your own research ideas The exact direction of the project can be shaped according to your background and research interests You will perform numerical experiments and theoretical analysis, develop algorithms and software, and communicate your results through publications and presentations at leading international conferences and journals You will collaborate extensively with researchers within QuBriC and participate in the network's research, training, and dissemination activities. The position also includes teaching at the undergraduate and Master's level and other departmental duties, corresponding to up to 20% full time The position is a fixed-term appointment of three years, with a starting salary of 61’400.00 CHF per annum. Profile To qualify as a Doctoral student, you must have a Master's degree (or equivalent) in physics, mathematics, electrical engineering, computer science, or a closely related field. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position: 3D scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for digital twins of stone-built heritage Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position: 3D scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for digital twins of stone-built heritage 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Geosensors and Engineering Geodesy at ETH Zurich is looking for a Doctoral candidate to work on 3D mapping, scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for information-rich digital twins of heritage buildings. The position is part of the collaborative project “HC3 – Heritage Conservation Collaboration Copilots”. HC3 aims to establish information-rich 3D digital twins of stone-built monuments that are interoperable through eXtended Reality (XR), together with the sensing and monitoring methods that provide the data they are built on. These will help us model and understand how stone-built heritage deteriorates, and predict how this deterioration will evolve under climate change. Within the project, you would collaborate with two other Doctoral students employed by the Chair of Physical Chemistry of Building Materials at ETH Zurich and a postdoctoral researcher working on the interface of both Chairs. The HC3 project is lead by Prof. Robert Flatt at Chair of Physical Chemistry of Building Materials and by dr. Tomislav Medic at Chair of Geosensors and Engineering Geodesy (Tomislav would be your direct supervisor). Job description Reality capture at scale: Plan and carry out multi-sensor mapping campaigns of monuments (including LiDAR and imaging technologies using ground-based and UAV platforms) Multi-modal data fusion and 3D scene reconstruction: Calibrate, register and fuse point clouds and imagery into unified, data-rich 3D representations (point clouds, meshes, neural radiance fields, 3D Gaussian splatting) 3D scene parsing: Develop deep learning enabled methods that segment the scene into individual building elements (stone blocks) for automated digital twin (HBIM) generation Inference of material properties: Develop machine learning methods that infer building material properties (stone deterioration type and severity) per element from multi-modal data and time series Collaborate on integrating this data into digital twins and extended reality, validate your methods against conservation expert assessments and physical chemistry laboratory experiments; publish in leading journals and conferences; contribute to teaching (upon agreement) Profile MSc degree (completed or about to be completed) in geomatics, remote sensing, computer vision, robotics, computer science or a related field Solid background in 2D/3D perception (point cloud and image processing, photogrammetry, 3D reconstruction) and in parameter estimation, incl. machine and deep learning; good programming skills (Python or C++) Hands-on experience with laser scanning (LiDAR) or imaging systems is an advantage, and willingness to do fieldwork on monuments is a must Further requirements: Interest in interdisciplinary work with material scientists and conservation practitioners; excellent English; French or German is an advantage Workplace Workplace We offer A fully funded four-year doctoral position in an international, dynamic team of highly motivated and supportive colleagues, state-of-the-art sensing equipment, and work on a project with a potential to evolve beyond the initial scope. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Magnetic Resonance Applications in Porous Media Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Magnetic Resonance Applications in Porous Media 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The ETH Zurich Geothermal Energy & Geofluids ( GEG.ethz.ch ) Group in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences investigates subsurface reactive fluid and geothermal energy transfer, developing and employing computer simulations, laboratory experiments, and field analyses. Our aim is to gain fundamental insights and develop sustainable technologies to address societal needs. The position is 100% with a competitive salary according to ETH Zurich standards. The position is for one year with the potential for annual extensions based on project needs and employee performance. The position start date is 1st of February 2027 or as soon as possible thereafter. Project background We are excited to announce a PhD opportunity focused on developing and applying multi-modal magnetic resonance techniques for studying chemical and physical processes in porous media (e.g., natural rock formations). The group is implementing state-of-the-art nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMR/MRI), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)-MRI, and dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) instrumentation. Fundamental processes will be probed in porous media including multicomponent fluid flow (e.g., H2O, and CO2), H2O-quartz-radical reactions, mineral precipitation, microbial methanogenesis, and crystalline hydration. Job description The PhD project will explore: Developing new methods and techniques in NMR/MRI, pulsed-EPR-MRI, and DNP Characterization of radical centers in natural rock samples with EPR spectroscopy and imaging Understanding DNP in porous media both with exogenous and endogenous radical sources Studying selected applied chemical and physical processes in porous media possibly including: Multicomponent fluid flow and temperature encoding Mechanochemical radical generation during rock fracturing and its role in water splitting to form hydrogen gas, oxygen gas, and reactive oxygen species Quantification of 13C-enriched CO2, bicarbonate, and/or CH4 in porous media through different phases and geochemical reactions Tracking mineral precipitation via 23Na and/or 7Li isotope handles The work will include method development of various magnetic resonance techniques with a focus on porous and fractured media. Applied projects will combine experimental stimulations (e.g., high-pressure fracture experiments), magnetic-resonance-based characterization, geochemical analysis, microbial ecology approaches, alongside modeling fluid migration and storage potential. Profile We seek a highly motivated and self-organized individual with: Background in chemistry, physics, engineering, or similar Strong interest in interdisciplinary research bridging chemistry, physics, geochemistry, geomechanics, microbiology, and energy science Experience with liquid- or solid-state NMR, MRI, or EPR Familiarity with analytical tools such as X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray computed tomography (XRCT) Experience in designing and performing high-temperature and high-pressure in-situ experiments is advantageous Fluency in English (both written and spoken) Workplace Workplace We offer We provide a dynamic and exciting work environment with cutting-edge computational and laboratory infrastructure at ETH Zurich in general and in the GEG group in particular. The GEG Group’s laboratory includes both low-field (~ 50 mT) and high-field (5.6 T) multinuclear NMR/MRI, pulsed-EPR-MRI, and DNP instruments. Further capabilities include an XRCT, laser Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), and Laser-Induced Fluorescence (LIF). These are used to monitor reactive experiments, quantify, and visualize a wide range of components over varied temperatures and pressures in up to three spatial dimensions. jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Magnetic Resonance for the Study of Granular Systems Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Magnetic Resonance for the Study of Granular Systems 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken ETH Zurich is one of the leading universities worldwide and renowned for its excellence in education, fundamental and applied research, and technology transfer. At the Institute for Biomedical Engineering, one research focus is on nuclear magnetic resonance. The team of Prof. Klaas Prüssmann drives innovation in magnetic resonance from physical and mathematical principles all the way to novel imaging, sensing, and tracking technology. In close collaboration with academic and industrial partners, we pursue applications in the biomedical realm, process engineering, and materials science. One recent focus of interest is on the use of magnetic resonance for particle tracking in granular systems. We are looking for a Physicist or Engineer to join us on this frontier as a Doctoral Student. Project background Granular systems are ubiquitous in nature and of fundamental importance to industry, from food and pharma to material conversion. However, despite their widespread occurence and use, many important phenomena such as the transition between flowing and solid states, mixing, segregation, or surface instabilities, are poorly understood. Magnetic resonance has proven a powerful means of studying granular physics, permitting both dynamic imaging and, newly, the tracking of particle swarms. The focus is now on further expanding the tracking strategies and, in the applied realm, on exploring the role of the shape of particles and how granular dynamics change when particles are soft and deform upon stress. The project is a shared effort with ETH colleagues in process engineering and encompasses two Doctoral Student positions, one each at the Institute for Biomedical Engineering (Prof. Prüssmann) and the Laboratory of Energy Science and Engineering (Prof. Müller). The two Doctoral Researchers will benefit from immersion in both environments and are foreseen to collaborate closely. Job description The objective of the Doctoral Student hired by the Institute for Biomedical Engineering is to advance magnetic resonance technology and methods towards the study of granular systems made up of arbitrarily shaped and soft particles. This will include work on principles of particle tracking and imaging, creation of new methods, implementation on magnetic resonance equipment, all the way to  experimental exploration and use in granular systems. The collaborative effort with the partner Doctoral Student will particularly target the fabrication of tailored and soft particles, applied studies in granular systems science, and the creation of experimental setups to this end. Profile Applicants for this position are expected to have a Master’s degree in Physics, Electrical Engineering, or Mechanical Engineering, or from another program with substantial coverage of Physics and Mathematics. The position also requires a good command of English, both oral and written. We highly value: Analytical strength Intellectual rigor Creativity Passion for both abstract thought and practical implementation Intrinsic motivation Team orientation Previous experience with magnetic resonance or granular systems is a benefit but not a requirement. jobs.description:
Doctoral Positions in Exoplanet Atmosphere Characterisation and the Search for Life Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Positions in Exoplanet Atmosphere Characterisation and the Search for Life 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for one or two Doctoral Students to work on the atmospheric characterisation of temperate terrestrial exoplanets and the search for life within the Exoplanets and Habitability Group led by Prof. Sascha P. Quanz at ETH Zurich. The positions is closely connected to the ETH-led LIFE space mission . LIFE is a space-based mid-infrared nulling interferometer to directly detect and spectroscopically characterise dozens of temperate terrestrial exoplanets around nearby stars. The successful candidates will join the LIFE Science Team and work closely with researchers and students at ETH Zurich and across the wider LIFE collaboration. Project background A central goal of LIFE is to characterise the atmospheres of temperate terrestrial exoplanets and ultimately assess their habitability and possible signs of life. Understanding which atmospheric properties can be robustly inferred from mid-infrared observations is also essential for translating LIFE's science goals into science requirements and corresponding instrument-performance requirements. Our group has developed the atmospheric retrieval framework pyRetLIFE and has so far investigated mainly Earth-like planets and classical atmospheric biosignature gases. An important next step is to broaden this work towards the diversity of potentially habitable and inhabited worlds: different atmospheric compositions and climates, non-Earth-like biospheres, non-standard biosignatures, and the abiotic scenarios against which potential signs of life need to be interpreted. Possible research directions for the successful Doctoral students include The modelling and characterisation of non-Earth-like atmospheres and biospheres, using physically motivated atmospheric models and retrievals to understand which properties and potential biosignatures future missions like LIFE can robustly constrain The exploration of alternative inference approaches, including machine learning and AI, for atmospheric characterisation and the interpretation of potential signs of life, this could include investigating where such methods provide additional information compared with conventional retrievals, and assessing their robustness, interpretability and sensitivity to modelling assumptions Job description Develop and pursue research on the characterisation of temperate terrestrial exoplanet atmospheres and the search for signs of life in the context of the LIFE mission Investigate atmospheric scenarios beyond modern Earth analogues; this may include non-Earth-like biospheres, non-standard biosignatures and/or relevant abiotic alternatives Use and further develop atmospheric retrieval and/or complementary modelling and inference approaches Explore, where relevant, ML/AI approaches for atmospheric inference and interpretation Investigate the robustness and limitations of atmospheric characterisation methods and compare complementary approaches where scientifically useful In close collaboration with the LIFE Science Team and LIFE Instrument Science Team, translate atmospheric characterisation results into science requirements and related instrument-performance requirements for LIFE Contribute new scientific ideas to the development of the LIFE science case and interact with the broader LIFE collaboration Profile Master's degree (or equivalent degree) in astrophysics, planetary science, atmospheric science, physics or a closely related field, completed by the start date Strong interest in exoplanet science, atmospheres, habitability, biosignatures and the search for life Experience in one or more of the following is welcome, but not required: atmospheric modelling, atmospheric retrievals, radiative transfer, photochemical or climate modelling, statistical inference, machine-learning/AI methods, or related numerical approaches Strong scientific programming skills, preferably in Python; jobs.title: Doctoral Position: Development of an Organ-on-chip platform
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position: Development of an Organ-on-chip platform Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position: Development of an Organ-on-chip platform 100%, Basel, fixed-term print Drucken The Bioanalytics Group at ETH Zürich in Basel (Switzerland) is developing so-called lab-on-chip technology (or microfluidic technology) for applications across the life sciences and biomedicine. Our interdisciplinary approach includes the design and manufacturing of miniaturized platforms and their optimization for biochemical assays and analytical procedures. To strengthen our team, we are offering a Doctoral Position for developing an organ-on-chip model system. Project background Organ-on-chip systems, also known as microphysiological systems, are promising platforms for investigating disease development and evaluating potential treatments. Their miniaturized design enables the reproducible and controlled formation of human tissues with specific functions, as well as the parallelized study of biological processes. In the Bioanalytics Group, we are developing vascularized tissue models to investigate how cells, cell-secreted molecules, and drugs cross the endothelial barrier to reach surrounding tissues and how compounds translocate from tissue into the blood stream. As part of a project focused on understanding the mechanisms underlying cancer metastasis, we are looking for a motivated Doctoral student interested in experimental research at the interface of engineering and biology. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Groundwater Microbial and Viral Ecology and Environmental Bioinformatics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Groundwater Microbial and Viral Ecology and Environmental Bioinformatics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Geomitigation of Greenhouse Gases group at ETH Zürich is actively recruiting a highly motivated and curious Doctoral candidate with a strong interest in environmental microbiology, biogeochemical cycling, and bioinformatics. The position is part of a newly funded SNSF interdisciplinary project investigating how microbial and viral communities influence carbon cycling in groundwater systems. The project brings together microbial and viral ecology, environmental genomics, and hydrogeochemistry to better understand how biological processes influence the fate of carbon in the subsurface. Project background Groundwater represents an important but poorly understood component of the global carbon cycle. While water-rock interactions strongly influence groundwater chemistry, microbial communities actively transform carbon through diverse metabolic pathways, and viruses may further regulate these processes through infection and metabolic reprogramming. However, how microbial and viral communities respond to changes in groundwater age and geochemistry, and how these interactions influence carbon cycling, remains largely unknown. In this project, you will investigate microbial and viral diversity, metabolic activity, and evolutionary adaptation across groundwater age gradients. By combining metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and viral metagenomics with hydrogeochemical measurements, you will explore how microbial metabolism and virus-host interactions influence carbon cycling in the subsurface. Job description Analyze large-scale environmental metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and viral sequencing datasets to investigate microbial and viral diversity, activity, and function in groundwater systems Characterize microbial metabolic potential and activity, with a particular focus on pathways involved in carbon cycling and their responses to environmental conditions Investigate microbial and viral community dynamics, virus-host interactions, and evolutionary adaptation across groundwater age and geochemical gradients Integrate environmental multi-omics datasets with hydrogeochemical measurements to better understand the biological processes influencing subsurface carbon cycling Perform DNA and RNA extractions from environmental samples and contribute to complementary laboratory analyses, including microbial cell abundance and activity measurements using flow cytometry and microscopy Synthesize research findings into scientific manuscripts and present results at international conferences and workshops Collaborate closely with the Principal Investigator, project partner, another Doctoral student working on groundwater hydrogeochemistry, and other group members while contributing to a supportive and communicative research environment Profile We are looking for a candidate who is curious, independent, and motivated by questions at the intersection of microbial ecology, evolution, and environmental biogeochemistry. You enjoy working with large biological datasets and are excited about using computational approaches to understand how microorganisms and viruses interact with their environments. An MSc degree in microbiology, microbial ecology, bioinformatics, computational biology, geobiology, or a closely related discipline Previous hands-on experience with metagenomic data analysis or closely related environmental bioinformatics approaches Experience working in Linux/Unix command-line environments and familiarity with computational biology workflows Experience with at least one programming or scripting language, such as Python, R or Bash A strong understanding of microbial ecology, physiology, and/or metabolism Excellent analytical and problem-solving skills, including the ability to work with complex biological datasets Creativity, curiosity, and motivation to explore new research questions and computational approaches Ability to work both independently and as part of a collaborative interdisciplinary team Excellent spoken and written English Experience with genome-resolved metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, comparative genomics, or high-performance computing is particularly advantageous. Previous experience with DNA and/or RNA extraction from environmental samples is also desirable. A background in groundwater microbiology, environmental geochemistry, or biogeochemical cycling is beneficial but not required. Our group explores the fascinating world of anaerobic microbiology from the global to the microscopic scale. This project investigates the physiology and bioenergetics of alkaliphilic methanogenic archaea. Project background The National Centre of Competence in Research NCCR Genesis is a research infrastructure project funded by SNSF focussing on exploring the emergence of life in the Universe. This interdisciplinary research infrastructure brings together physicists, earth and planetary scientists, chemists and biologists to understand the conditions and the mechanisms that enable life to emerge. Developing reliable methods to detect reliable traces of life (biosignatures) – whether through remote sensing or direct onsite measurements – requires significant innovation. These challenges demand close collaboration across physics, biology, chemistry and the earth sciences. NCCR Genesis does not aim to provide answers in all fields, but to drive innovative research and achieve decisive progress. Details on NCCR Genesis are available on its website . NCCR Genesis is deeply committed to equality, diversity and inclusion. Our aim is to cultivate a respectful and fair work culture with equal access to professional development and support for all. We strongly encourage applications from under-represented groups. Job description Alkaline environments such as soda lakes and serpentinising vents are candidate sites for the emergence of life on Earth and potential habitats on ocean worlds like Enceladus Methanogenic archaea are the main biological source of the greenhouse gas methane Some methanogenic archaea can thrive under alkaliphilic conditions where conventional energy conservation reaches its limits This Doctoral project seeks to investigate what limits the growth of alkaliphilic methanogens, how they conserve energy and acquire carbon at high pH, and which signatures distinguish their methane from abiotic methane The work combines anaerobic cultivation, physiology and biochemistry Profile MSc (or equivalent) in microbiology, environmental sciences or a related field Experience in anaerobic cultivation and/or protein biochemistry is an advantage Curiosity about fundamental questions and enthusiasm for experimental work and excellent communication skills in English Workplace Workplace We offer Opportunities to engage in cutting-edge research with the potential for high impact in the field of environmental microbiology Encouraging and collaborative research environment A Doctoral Position in a national, interdisciplinary network linking microbiology with geochemistry, planetary science and origin-of-life research Training in anaerobic microbiology, bioenergetics, and omics A fundamental research question with direct relevance to astrobiology and the methane cycle Support for career goals through conference travel and workshops Exciting working environment, cultural diversity and attractive offers and benefits chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.description:
Three Doctoral Positions in History and Theory of Urban Design and Architecture Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Three Doctoral Positions in History and Theory of Urban Design and Architecture 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of the History and Theory of Urban Design (Prof. Dr. Tom Avermaete) at the Institute for the History and Theory of Architecture (gta), ETH Zürich, is looking for three doctoral candidates within the ERC Advanced Grant Project “Co-opolis: Another Architectural History of the European City (1890–1990).” The positions are expected to start in March 2027 and are fully funded for four years. Project background The ERC Project explores how third-sector actors, such as cooperatives, mutual aid societies, associations, and other collective institutions, co-produced the city following precise values and collectivist agendas centred on the shared provision, usage, and maintenance of built resources, resulting in housing and civic structures (e.g., people’s palaces, cultural centres) that complemented and shaped the urban spaces produced by the state and the market. To this end, the project compares selected examples from Sweden, France, and Switzerland from 1890 to 1990 to examine how the ideologies and practices of third-sector actors influenced the built environment within the evolving frameworks of European welfare states. The project seeks to demonstrate the contribution of collective initiatives to the making of contemporary European cities and to assess the lessons they can offer for current challenges such as affordable housing, social inclusion, and sustainable urban development. Job description The three PhD candidates within the “Co-opolis” project will investigate the conditions of emergence, spatial characteristics, and endurance of architectural and urban projects at the intersection of welfare regimes and third-sector collective actors in France, Sweden, and Switzerland over the project’s timeframe. Each candidate will focus on one of these countries, examining how housing projects and civic infrastructures developed through the initiatives of third-sector actors within different welfare regimes. Specifically, the candidates will: Focus on the line of enquiry previously described, producing research on the case studies as well as bringing their own original ideas to the topic. For this reason, we ask potential candidates to include a short description of a possible research direction with the application documents. Complete the PhD dissertation within the given timeframe (March 2027–March 2031). Contribute to the activities and outputs of the overall ERC project, such as workshops, seminars, authoring articles, presenting their research at international conferences, and contributing to the project’s website. Actively engage with the courses and seminars of the PhD programme at the gta Institute, as well as in the academic activities of the Chair of the History and Theory of Urban Design, including participation in research discussions and occasional contributions to teaching activities, such as critiques, reviews, and examinations. Profile We are looking for passionate candidates with an MSc degree in Architecture, History of Art, Social History, or closely related fields in the humanities, to be completed by the start of the position. Previous experience in publishing, as well as archival and historical research, is welcome. The working language is English. Candidates must also be proficient in the language relevant to their selected case-study country: French (France), German plus French and/or Italian (Switzerland), or Swedish (Sweden) Workplace Workplace We offer The successful candidates will join a stimulating and international research environment at the Chair of the History and Theory of Urban Design and Institute for the History and Theory of Architecture (gta), benefiting from close collaboration, structured mentoring, and opportunities to strengthen academic networks through conference participation, training, and teaching activities. jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Environmental Bioengineering Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Environmental Bioengineering 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Environmental Microfluidics Group of Prof. Roman Stocker in the Institute of Environmental Engineering is seeking a dynamic and motivated doctoral student with an engineering background for a project on how bacterial chemotaxis accelerates plasmid transfer, including the spread of antibiotic resistance. The position is funded by a recently awarded SNSF grant, and the project is a joint effort with Prof. Jonasz Slomka at the University of Warsaw. This position will be based in the laboratory of Prof. Roman Stocker. Project background Bacterial conjugation, the contact-dependent transfer of plasmids between cells, speeds up bacterial evolution and is a major route for the spread of antibiotic resistance in the environment, which in turn poses a global health threat. Aquatic environments are full of microscale chemical hotspots, such as the nutrient-rich 'phycosphere' around phytoplankton and sinking marine particles, and chemotactic bacteria are known to find and accumulate rapidly at these locations. This project will test the hypothesis that this accumulation enhances plasmid spreading in the environment, contributing to a cutting-edge view of the role of antibiotic resistance in nature. The project seeks to study when, where and how strongly this enhancement operates across different chemical hotspots, fluid flows and bacterial strains, and what it means for the spread of antibiotic resistance among aquatic bacteria. Job description This is a primarily experimental PhD at the interface of engineering and microbiology. The student will: Design, build and characterize new instrumentation to couple existing chemotaxis assays to controlled shear systems. This includes mechanical design, 3D printing, control systems and integration with a fluorescence microscope. Run chemotaxis and conjugation experiments with bacterial donors and recipients of plasmids and a range of chemoattractants, with the opportunity to learn and use advanced techniques such as flow cytometry and plate-reader-based plasmid transfer quantification. Image and track fluorescently labeled bacteria and chemical plumes in shear flow, and analyze the data with quantitative image- and data-analysis pipelines. Test clinically relevant bacteria and freshwater (e.g. lake) bacteria, to assess the potential for chemotaxis-driven spread of resistance in the environment. Contribute data to mathematical models of plasmid spread. Profile We are looking for a hands-on, skilled and curious engineer who loves to build new tools and is interested in using them to answer fundamental scientific questions. Ideal candidates hold an MSc degree in bioengineering, mechanical engineering, mechatronics, electrical engineering, environmental engineering, physics or a related discipline, and have some (not necessarily all) of the following skills: Practical experience in prototyping and manufacturing, for example CAD, 3D printing, machining (strongly preferred). Experience with control systems and instrumentation, for example motor control, sensors, microcontrollers, and automation or data-acquisition code (Python, MATLAB, LabVIEW or similar) (preferred). Openness to gain experience in the microbiology laboratory: bacterial cultures, sterile technique, plate readers and flow cytometry. Familiarity with microscopy, image analysis, fluid mechanics or microfluidics (beneficial but not necessary). Fluency in English (oral and written), enthusiasm for working in an interdisciplinary and international team, and the drive to pursue scientific excellence (required). You will be guided by Prof. Roman Stocker and by members of his lab with extensive experience in microbiology, experimental techniques and environmental processes. You will have the opportunity to work in a cutting-edge, fast-paced research environment, interact with researchers from many different disciplines (engineers, physicists, microbiologists, oceanographers, chemists, mathematicians), gain technical experience across diverse research approaches and interact with world-class collaborators. Doctoral Students in Quantum Networking with Superconducting Circuits Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Students in Quantum Networking with Superconducting Circuits 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Quantum Device Lab is looking for highly motivated Doctoral Students for the development of a superconducting qubit quantum network and research in quantum networking applications. A team of researchers led by Andreas Wallraff from the Quantum Device Lab , at the Department of Physics of ETH Zurich has developed a unique superconducting qubit system consisting of two dilution refrigerators equipped with superconducting qubit chips, separated by 30 meters, and connected through a cryogenic link. By exchanging microwave photons across the link, this system can generate remote entanglement between the separated chips as a resource for quantum information experiments and applications. The platform has already enabled demonstrations including loophole-free Bell tests and randomness amplification . We are now expanding the platform through advances in chip fabrication, packaging, networking protocols, and distributed control systems. These developments will enable research into further potential application areas of quantum networks, including loss-tolerant photonic state transfer, distributed quantum computing and quantum error correction, blind quantum computing, and non-local sensing. To ensure this project's success and fast progress, we are looking for highly motivated Doctoral Students in quantum networking with superconducting circuits. Job description You will become part of our team developing and running a two-node quantum network You will be working closely with the rest of the Quantum Device Lab, a well-established research group with a strong background in quantum computing with superconducting qubits, and be able to both benefit from the expertise developed there and contribute to its progress You will perform collaborative research towards the realization of quantum networking technologies You will get to contribute to diverse aspects of the experimental effort, both technical (design of electronics and mechanical components, building of microwave setups, fabrication of superconducting circuit chips) and conceptual (design of experiments, exploring quantum networking applications, planning of future research strategies) In the lab, you will pursue the development of the platform by enabling and implementing quantum networking protocols on a network of multi-qubit superconducting circuit chips Profile You have a strong interest in experimental realizations of quantum information processing systems, with a focus on remote and non-local applications You are dedicated to pursuing a successful career in research, development, or education, either in academia or industry You have experience and a proven record in one or more of the following: Quantum information processing and its implementations (e.g. with superconducting circuits, quantum dots, ion traps, NMR) Experimental quantum optics and atomic physics (cavity quantum electrodynamics) Micro and nano-electronic devices and their fabrication (lithography and deposition techniques) Quantum networking and remote entanglement generation Mesoscopic solid state physics Low temperature physics Microwave electronics Digital electronics FPGAs Instrumentation, drivers, and software development Workplace Workplace We offer Your project is embedded into the Swiss Quantum Science and Technology network, the Quantum Center at Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken Our research group, based at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), explores new technologies for future accelerator facilities. Through the development of new technologies and techniques, we develop high intensity particle sources, high gradient particle accelerators and beam diagnostics systems that measure beam qualities down to the sub-femtosecond regime. Our research combines beam/plasma physics, unique RF technologies and high-power lasers to realise the accelerators that exist within the Paul Scherrer Institute and reaching beyond with contributions to CERN’s future circular collider (FCC). This Doctoral Position will be based at PSI Villigen but with teaching assistant duties at ETH Zurich. Project background The project involves developing electron sources for future accelerator facilities at PSI and the institute’s contributions to the FCC. A central shared challenge is shaping the electron beam as it is generated or shortly afterward. For the FCC, precise control of the laser profile in the RF photogun enables the flexible filling schemes needed for top-up operation. For X-ray free-electron lasers, like SwissFEL, transverse laser shaping and early RF compression are key to producing brighter electron beams. This PhD project will advance beam-shaping techniques for both applications. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Infrastructure Management, led by Professor Dr. Bryan T. Adey within the Institute of Construction and Infrastructure Management of the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering, has an opening for a doctoral student. This position focuses risk-based inspection and maintenance planning for tunnels, including probabilistic risk updating, Value of Information analysis, and intervention program optimisation. This position is part of an interdisciplinary SNSF project in collaboration with the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, the Hagerbach Test Gallery, and the EuroTube Foundation. The preferred starting date is 1 February 2027, although other dates are negotiable. Project background Tunnels are critical links in transport networks, and many Swiss road and rail tunnels are ageing while being subject to increasing traffic loads, climate-related stressors, and evolving safety requirements. Their maintenance involves two interdependent asset domains, namely structural elements, such as lining, portals, and drainage, and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems, such as ventilation, lighting, and fire detection. In current practice, these domains are managed largely in isolation, inspections remain heavily manual, and evidence from different campaigns, sensors, and specialists is fragmented across separate reports and databases. Interventions are therefore often planned using disjointed evidence and conservative heuristics, even where substantial data exist. The project Predictive, Resilient, Integrated Systems for Management of Tunnel (PRISM-T), funded by the SNSF, addresses this challenge through an integrated digital twin workflow for tunnel maintenance decision support. Heterogeneous inspection and monitoring evidence is transformed into uncertainty-aware condition indicators, which are used to update risk, to assess whether additional information is worth collecting, and to derive executable intervention programs. Extended reality (XR) is used to validate decisions and to guide inspection and maintenance work on site. The workflow is developed and validated in the Tunnel Digitalisation Centre of the Hagerbach Test Gallery in Flums, and its transferability is tested at the DemoTube facility of the EuroTube Foundation in Dübendorf. Regular field work at both sites and close collaboration with the partner team in Bolzano form an integral part of the doctoral research. Within this project, the doctoral position addresses the decision layer of the workflow, in which maintenance decision processes are formalised and uncertainty-aware condition indicators, developed in a companion doctoral position, are used to update risk and to optimise intervention programs under realistic tunnel constraints. Job description The successful candidate will map and formalise current tunnel maintenance decision processes for the structural and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing domains through workshops and interviews with practitioners. On this basis, risk and consequence models based on Bayesian networks will be formulated, and incremental risk updating methods will be developed. A computationally tractable Value of Information analysis will be developed using approximation strategies, such as surrogate models and scenario reduction. Intervention program optimisation models accounting for sequencing, bundling, access windows, and resource constraints will be formulated and solved, with outputs traceable to the underlying evidence. The candidate will contribute to validation campaigns at the Hagerbach Test Gallery and the EuroTube Foundation. Profile A Master’s degree in civil engineering, operations research, industrial engineering, applied mathematics, or a related field A strong background in probabilistic modelling, reliability and risk analysis, and mathematical optimisation Very good programming skills, preferably in Python, and experience with optimisation solvers Familiarity with infrastructure asset management, Bayesian networks, decision analysis, Value of Information analysis, or business process modelling would be considered an advantage Willingness to carry out field work in underground environments and to collaborate within an interdisciplinary and international team Proficiency in written and spoken English is required, and knowledge of German is regarded as an asset Workplace Workplace We offer ETH Zurich is one of the world’s leading universities specialising in science and technology. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Uncertainty-Aware Condition Assessment of Tunnels
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Uncertainty-Aware Condition Assessment of Tunnels Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Uncertainty-Aware Condition Assessment of Tunnels 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Infrastructure Management, led by Professor Dr. Bryan T. Adey within the Institute of Construction and Infrastructure Management of the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering, has an opening for a doctoral student. This position focuses on transforming heterogeneous inspection and monitoring evidence into uncertainty-aware condition indicators for tunnel structures and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems within a digital twin. This position is part of an interdisciplinary SNSF project in collaboration with the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, the Hagerbach Test Gallery, and the EuroTube Foundation. The preferred starting date is 1 February 2027, although other dates are negotiable. Project background Tunnels are critical links in transport networks, and many Swiss road and rail tunnels are ageing while being subject to increasing traffic loads, climate-related stressors, and evolving safety requirements. Their maintenance involves two interdependent asset domains, namely structural elements, such as lining, portals, and drainage, and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems, such as ventilation, lighting, and fire detection. In current practice, these domains are managed largely in isolation, inspections remain heavily manual, and evidence from different campaigns, sensors, and specialists is fragmented across separate reports and databases. Interventions are therefore often planned using disjointed evidence and conservative heuristics, even where substantial data exist. The project Predictive, Resilient, Integrated Systems for Management of Tunnel (PRISM-T), funded by the SNSF, addresses this challenge through an integrated digital twin workflow for tunnel maintenance decision support. Heterogeneous inspection and monitoring evidence is transformed into uncertainty-aware condition indicators, which are used to update risk, to assess whether additional information is worth collecting, and to derive executable intervention programs. Extended reality (XR) is used to validate decisions and to guide inspection and maintenance work on site. The workflow is developed and validated in the Tunnel Digitalisation Centre of the Hagerbach Test Gallery in Flums, and its transferability is tested at the DemoTube facility of the EuroTube Foundation in Dübendorf. Regular field work at both sites and close collaboration with the partner team in Bolzano form an integral part of the doctoral research. Within this project, the doctoral position addresses the evidence layer of the workflow, in which inspection images, 3D laser scans, and sensor data are transformed into condition indicators that form the basis for the risk updating and intervention planning carried out in a companion doctoral position. Job description The successful candidate will develop methods to extract defect and deterioration indicators from inspection images, video, sensor data, and periodic 3D laser scans, including domain adaptation for tunnel environments and time-lapse change detection. Evidence from multiple sources will be fused into asset-level condition indicators using a hierarchical Bayesian framework, and uncertainty models and evidence quality flags will be developed for each source. The candidate will contribute to defining the condition indicator types in the digital asset model, to integrating the indicators into the digital twin prototype, and to inspection and validation campaigns at the Hagerbach Test Gallery and the EuroTube Foundation. Profile A Master’s degree in civil engineering, geomatics, computer science, or a related field A strong background in machine learning, computer vision, or 3D point cloud processing, as well as in probabilistic modelling and Bayesian inference Very good programming skills, preferably in Python Familiarity with digital twins, building information modelling (BIM) and IFC, sensor data processing, or tunnel inspection would be considered an advantage Willingness to carry out field work in underground environments and to collaborate within an interdisciplinary and international team Proficiency in written and spoken English is required, and knowledge of German is regarded as an asset Workplace Workplace We offer ETH Zurich is one of the world’s leading universities specialising in science and technology. Doctoral Researcher in Pulse Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Researcher in Pulse Electron Paramagnetic Resonance 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Spin Dynamics and Hyperpolarisation group is looking for a doctoral researcher, fully funded by a Starting Grant from the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF). The group explores ways to enhance the sensitivity of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR, also known as electron spin resonance, ESR) by orders of magnitude. The project lies at the interface between method development and applied chemical spectroscopy. Starting date: by mutual agreement. There is no deadline and the position will remain open until suitable candidates are found. Applications are considered as long as this advertisement is online. Job description The position involves working with a state-of-the-art pulse EPR spectrometer with arbitrary phase and amplitude control. The aim is to develop new pulse sequences with improved sensitivity and higher information content, and to apply them to challenging systems from inorganic chemistry and catalysis, as well as to organic radicals. Our group is also developing a new method based on optical hyperpolarisation, which will eventually be applied to the same systems. The work will focus on the spectroscopic aspects, including experiments and spin-dynamics simulations. Depending on the candidate's background, it can also include chemical synthesis and catalysis, as well as quantum-chemical calculations. The working language of the group is English. Profile The candidate must hold a Master's degree in (physical) chemistry or a related field by the start of the position. Interest in spin dynamics, magnetic resonance, and their applications to (in)organic chemistry is essential. Research experience in an advanced magnetic resonance technique (EPR, solid-state NMR, or similar) is required. A good understanding of the physics underlying magnetic resonance is expected. In addition, the candidate should have: the drive to take ownership of their project and push it forward openness to collaborating with people from different backgrounds Workplace Workplace We offer An exciting project at the forefront of magnetic resonance method development A position in a new research group with close collaboration and structured mentoring Considerable freedom to pursue your own ideas and to develop both academically and personally World-class infrastructure Opportunities to initiate your own collaborations chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.description:
RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027 Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken RobotX, the Center for Robotics at ETH Zurich, is looking for outstanding doctoral students who want to build robots that work in the real world. With the RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027, you apply once and are considered by several RobotX research groups across ETH Zurich. You choose up to three professors you would like to work with, and they review your application. Application deadline: 27 November 2026. Job description The research groups of RobotX cover a broad spectrum of robotics, including but not limited to: Soft and Musculoskeletal Robotics: bioinspired robots built from compliant materials, artificial muscles, and tendons, for safe and adaptive interaction with an unstructured world. Robotic Locomotion and Manipulation: legged robots, robot arms, and hands that move and act reliably in complex terrain and contact-rich tasks. Biohybrid Robots: robots built from living cells, engineered tissue, and synthetic materials, actuated by muscle and powered by chemical energy. Perception and Computer Vision: 3D reconstruction, object recognition, and scene understanding that give robots reliable perception of their surroundings. Human-Robot Interaction: sensory-motor interaction between humans and machines for assistive, rehabilitative, and cooperative tasks. Computational Design and Fabrication: simulation, optimization, and learned surrogate models to design and fabricate efficient, bioinspired robots. Reinforcement Learning and Machine Learning: data-driven methods that let robots learn new skills and adapt to new tasks and environments. Humanoid Robotics and Tactile Sensing for Manipulation: humanoid loco-manipulation, whole-body control, and tactile sensing that let robots reason across touch and vision to handle objects dexterously. Motion Planning and Control: algorithms for navigation, control, and decision-making in dynamic environments. Safety-Critical Robotic Systems: robots that perform reliably under uncertainty, in particular when they work alongside humans. You define your doctoral project together with your supervisor during your first months. Project background Digital twins of living systems are a hard computational problem: nonlinear, high-dimensional models with uncertain parameters that must be fitted to noisy data, and simulations so expensive that fitting them demands new algorithms and scalable software. We apply this to real questions, from how tissues self-organise during embryonic development to digital twins that support IVF treatment planning. You will build the algorithmic infrastructure that makes this possible, working with modellers, experimentalists and clinicians, and building on our open-source simulation tools. Job description The PhD position focuses on developing the algorithmic infrastructure behind our digital twins. You will: develop and benchmark methods for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, from classical optimisation and Bayesian inference to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and other machine-learning approaches build and extend our simulation environment, with a focus on performance, scalability and reproducibility apply your methods to real models and data, from imaging-based models of tissue development to our digital twin of the hormonal cycle and IVF treatment, together with the modellers, experimentalists and clinical collaborators in the group publish your results and present them at international conferences contribute to the group's open-source software and to teaching Profile We are looking for a self-motivated candidate who is enthusiastic about developing algorithms and software for data-based modelling of biological systems. The position suits someone with training in computer science, scientific computing or a related quantitative field, and an interest in applying it to biology and biomedicine. You should have: a Master's degree in Computer Science, Computational Science and Engineering, Applied Mathematics, Physics or a related field strong programming skills, e.g. in Python, Julia or C++, and experience in writing clean, well-tested code experience in numerical methods, optimisation, statistical inference or machine learning, gained through coursework, a thesis or a project an interest in biology and biomedicine and the willingness to learn the biological background of the project; prior knowledge of biology is not required good written and spoken English Experience with PDE-based simulations, finite element methods, high-performance computing or deep-learning frameworks (e.g. PyTorch, JAX) is an advantage. jobs.title: PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics
jobs.description:
PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a highly motivated PhD student to join our nonlinear dynamics team. Do you have a broad interest in physics and technology? Do you like the prospect of working in an experimental project in close collaboration with theory? Are you creative, persevering, independent, and a good team player? You can expect a cutting-edge research project that is very challenging due to the many aspects of science that are involved. For the same reason, it is a highly rewarding experience if you enjoy expanding your knowledge beyond textbook physics. We look forward to meeting you! Project background Is it possible to build artificial neural networks from driven nonlinear resonators? This question builds on the ideas of Hopfield and Hinton, but takes them out of equilibrium: in our resonators, a balance of continuous drive and dissipation sustains stable oscillation states. This gives us access to phenomena that are absent in equilibrium physics. For example, this may allow us to investigate how a physical network turns stored memories into dynamical patterns. In our lab, each node is an electrical circuit or a micro-electromechanical (MEMS) resonator implementing a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO): a driven, dissipative resonator with two stable oscillation states that act like a bit of memory. We couple several such KPOs, reading out every oscillator simultaneously and in real time. This gives us complete access to the dynamical many-body phase space. With it, we reconstruct the attractor landscape of the network, track how noise drives switching between collective states, and measure probability currents that appear when detailed balance is broken. The central question is whether these currents organize into stable, reproducible temporal patterns and coexisting limit cycles. Networks like these bridge nonequilibrium statistical physics and neuromorphic computing, and could provide a physical route to Ising and Boltzmann machines that operate on dynamical rather than static states. Job description Build and operate a programmable network of coupled KPOs with up to eight nodes, including control and readout electronics and measurement software. Map attractor landscapes, switching statistics and probability currents from measured trajectories. Compare experiment with simulations and analytical models in close contact with our theory partners (Prof. O. Zilberberg at the University of Konstanz) and publish and present your results internationally. Profile You hold (or are about to complete) an MSc in physics, electrical engineering or a related field, with a solid background in nanomechanics, nonlinear dynamics, or statistical physics. You enjoy hands-on experimental work (electronics, signal processing, Python) and are not afraid of a bit of analytical theory. Experience with MEMS, lock-in detection, or FPGAs is a plus. You communicate well in English. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken At the Professorship of Solid Mechanics (SMEC) in the Institute for Building Materials at ETH Zurich, we aim to understand how materials deform, degrade, break, and ultimately fail. Our research is driven by curiosity about the physical mechanisms that underlie failure and by the ambition to translate this understanding into more reliable and resilient materials and structures. By combining numerical modeling, laboratory experiments, and theoretical analyses, we seek to link microscopic processes with the macroscopic behavior of both engineering and natural systems and develop predictive tools for mechanical failure. Our team is highly interdisciplinary and international, bringing together researchers with backgrounds in materials science, mechanics, and applied physics. We work across a broad range of topics, including the mechanics of particle systems (colloidal and granular), architected and topologically interlocked materials, the mechanics of fragility in collagen, the mechanics of earthquakes, fracture of soft materials, and modeling failure in multiphysical processes such as corrosion-driven degradation of concrete. What unites these efforts is a shared curiosity about why complex materials fail and a commitment to developing new concepts, experiments, and models that advance our understanding of failure mechanics. We are seeking a motivated and innovative doctoral student with a strong interest in solid mechanics, interface mechanics, and computational modeling to investigate how local contact interactions in architected materials shape their macroscopic interface response. The project will explore how architecture influences collective contact behavior, aiming to develop design principles. The work will combine physics-based numerical modeling, theoretical reasoning, and concepts from rough-surface and multiscale mechanics. Job description You will conduct a computational and theoretical investigation of how local contact interactions in architected materials collectively determine their macroscopic interface response. The work will connect cell-scale mechanics with concepts from multiscale/rough-surface contact mechanics to develop effective descriptions of architected interfaces. You will develop and use numerical models of lattice materials to investigate the underlying principles of contact behavior of architected materials. You will analyze how architectural features, material properties, and characteristic length scales influence quantities such as contact area, pressure distributions, interface stiffness, and load transmission. Building on these results, you will seek statistical or homogenized descriptions that connect the mechanics of individual contacting cells to the effective behavior of large architected interfaces. The position provides a stimulating environment for scientific growth and collaboration. Profile You hold an MSc degree in mechanics, physics, (civil, mechanical, aerospace, or bio-) engineering, material science, computational science, or a related discipline. You have a background in mechanics, applied physics, computational mechanics, scientific computing, or a related field. A foundation in areas such as solid mechanics, contact mechanics, or multiscale modeling is particularly relevant. You have experience implementing scientific code and assessing computational results through validation, verification, and quantitative comparison with reference data. You have prior programming experience in Python and have used version control. You are curious, self-motivated, and interested in using modeling and quantitative reasoning to answer mechanics and physics questions. Experience with architected materials, rough-surface contact mechanics, homogenization, statistical mechanics, or multiscale methods is an advantage but is not required; the project-specific methods and concepts can be learned during the doctoral studies.
