jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Single Ion Capture and Imaging to Determine the Majorana Nature of the Neutrino
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: All year round
Research theme: High energy physics

This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

Is the neutrino its own antiparticle? Answering this could explain why the Universe is made of matter rather than nothing, and would reveal physics at energy scales far beyond the reach of any collider. This project develops a new way to ask the question: searching for neutrinoless double electron capture at the single ion level. In this ultra-rare nuclear process, ³⁶Ar transmutes into sulphur (or ⁷⁸Kr into selenium), and the decay leaves behind just one chemically distinct ion in the gas. Our concept, CODECS, aims to capture that single ion, identify it and image it. This would make an effectively background-free search possible, with sensitivity an order of magnitude beyond current limits. It could also produce the first observation of the standard-model two-neutrino mode in argon.

The project involves development of one of the key technologies at the heart of this scheme: moving single ions over surfaces through dense gas and watching them arrive, one by one. Ions will be swept across microfabricated radiofrequency “carpets”, which are fine-pitch electrode arrays. These use travelling-wave RF fields to levitate ions and carry them to a millimetre-scale collection point. There they meet a monolayer of molecular sensors that light up when they capture the target ion. Working with the National Graphene Institute, we will design and produce photonic integrated chips containing nanofabricated 5×5 cm carpets and integrated microscopy systems, and characterise their transport efficiency at pressures up to 5 bar. This will then be combined with a single ion source, to show that individual ions created in the gas can be delivered, captured and imaged, enabling a powerful new technology in neutrino physics.

The project sits where particle physics, ion trapping, microfabrication and optical microscopy meet. It builds on our group’s demonstration of imaging individual ions in high-pressure xenon, and you will work closely with synthetic chemists and international collaborators. We welcome applicants with a background in physics, engineering or physical chemistry who want to build instruments at the interdisciplinary frontier of particle and nuclear physics, and quantum sensing.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor Dr Benjamin Jones. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Nanoquakes for Pressure Sensing
jobs.description_html:
The aim of this project is to investigate the feasibility of creating a new generation of pressure sensors based on one important kind of elastic wave, surface acoustic waves (SAWs), which propagate on the surface of a solid. Although SAWs occur over many length scales, for example as earthquakes, research into devices that utilise SAWs with micron scale wavelengths [1], and nanometre amplitudes, has been a vibrant and active area since the invention of the interdigital transducer in the 1960s. SAW based devices are key components, for example, in mobile phones and televisions, and in such a device a radio frequency signal is applied to an interdigital transducer, on a piezoelectric substrate to launch a SAW pulse, with an identical transducer used for detection.

As the majority of the energy of the wave is confined within one wavelength of the surface, the propagation of the SAW can be dramatically affected by its interaction with the environment. SAWs are therefore also widely used in sensing applications [1] and are particularly attractive for operation in harsh environments due to their robustness and potential for wireless connection. One of the simplest SAW sensing mechanisms is via mass loading, where a mass on the surface damps the SAW propagation, which includes attenuation by a gas. 

Over the last few years, we have been investigating whether it is possible to increase the sensitivity of a SAW sensor to changes in pressure by patterning the surface of a SAW device into a metamaterial. Metamaterials are artificial materials that can be designed to have properties that don’t exist in nature, and preliminary measurements in Exeter have shown that one type of metamaterial [2, 3], made up of an array of resonators, is extremely promising for use as a SAW pressure sensor, with greatly enhanced sensitivity. 

The project will involve a mixture of simulations, experiments and computational analysis, and can be tailored to the interests of the successful applicant. Simulations will make use of the finite-element modelling package Comsol, and measurements will make use of a state-of-the-art laser Doppler vibrometry system that can map out the propagating waves, even though they only have nanoscale amplitudes. There is also potential to incorporate machine learning approaches into the design of the metamaterial.  

[1] D. S. Ballantine, R. M. White, S. J. Martin, A. J. Ricco, E. T. Zellers, G. C. Frye, H. Wohltjen, Acoustic wave sensors: Theory, Design, and Physico-Chemical Applications (Academic Press, San Diego, 1997).

[2] B. J. Ash, S. R. Worsfold, P. Vukusic, and G. R. Nash, “A highly attenuating and frequency tailorable annular hole phononic crystal for surface acoustic waves”, Nat. Commun. 8, 174 (2017).

[3] C. Pouya and G. R. Nash, “Sub- and supersonic elastic waves in an annular hole phononic metamaterial”, Commun. Mater. 2, 55 (2021).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Open Quantum Batteries via Time-Fractional Dynamics
jobs.description_html:
Quantum batteries are nanoscale energy storage devices that leverage quantum phenomena—such as coherence and entanglement—to achieve charging powers that scale superlinearly with the number of operational cells. However, standard modelling frameworks rely on ordinary, time-local quantum master equations. These models frequently fail to capture the complex, non-Markovian memory effects and anomalous diffusion inherent to structured solid-state or many-body quantum environments. 

This project proposes using the time-fractional Schrödinger equation to model, simulate, and optimize the charging profiles, capacity, and work extraction capabilities of quantum batteries operating in complex open environments.  Methodology & Key Transitions The research will replace the standard first-order temporal derivative in the Schrödinger and Lindblad master equations with a Caputo or Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative of order alpha. 

By varying the fractional parameter alpha, the project will map how non-local temporal memory structures alter the ergotropy (the maximum extractable work from a quantum system) and charging efficiency of the battery. 

The project will progress through three core phases:

  • Analytical Foundations: Derive exact solutions for single-cell and multi-cell Dicke quantum batteries under fractional time evolution.
  • Memory Optimization: Quantify how memory effects can be engineered to suppress quantum decoherence and aging, effectively locking stored energy in the battery.
  • Many-Body Enhancements: Simulate collective charging protocols under fractional dynamics to evaluate how anomalous diffusion influences the quantum advantage in charging power.  

Expected Impact:

This work will bridge fractional calculus and quantum thermodynamics. By establishing a rigorous fractional framework, the project aims to deliver actionable design blueprints for high-efficiency, low-leakage quantum batteries. These insights will prove vital for powering next-generation quantum processors and nanoscale energy harvesters.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Decoding Charge Dynamics in Triboelectric Nanogenerators with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
jobs.description_html:
Every mechanical contact between two dissimilar materials initiates a complex, microscopic migration of charge such as a transient of electrons and ions governed by local surface states, overlapping wavefunctions, and local potential barriers. Despite the rapid development of triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), i.e. devices able to harvest charge transfer occurring at the contact/separation of materials, mapping this interface dynamics in real-time remains a formidable boundary in applied physics.

The complex convolution of environmental parameters, material degradation, and multi-axial mechanical strain yields highly non-linear displacement currents that elude standard analytical formulas. This proposal introduces a novel methodology to map these hidden interface physics by utilizing deep neural networks as universal function approximators. By treating the neural network not just as a statistical black box, but as a framework bound by the fundamental conservation laws of electrostatics and quantum charge trap states with characteristic energies and relaxation, this research will decode the micro-scale charge transfer and relaxation mechanisms that ultimately dictate macro-scale energy harvesting performance. 

The doctoral researcher will fabricate TENGs using films derived from Ghanaian agricultural residues and investigate the effects of surface functionalisation. They will vary contact force and relative humidity independently while controlling approach and separation speeds. Independent measurements of charge transfer and decay will provide reference data for testing a compact neural network that incorporates the physics of charge evolution and electrical readout. The researcher will compare the network with a conventional physical model on devices held out from training to determine when both quantities can be recovered reliably and when a further measurement is needed.  

Decoding these charge dynamics would provide the physical basis for multimodal sensing with a single triboelectric element. The project will test whether contact force and local humidity affect charge transfer and decay in sufficiently different ways for both quantities to be estimated from the same waveform when they vary together. This would open a route to wearables that measure mechanical and environmental conditions through a single electrical readout. The same approach could later be tested for contact speed or changes in the local chemical environment. 

The project builds on Exeter’s EPSRC-funded research in quantum materials, its work on triboelectric nanogenerators and its recent use of AI to reconstruct optical spectra from a single two-dimensional perovskite photodetector by the team of supervisors. Prof Saverio Russo (Physics) will guide device measurements and AI-based inference, Dr Steven Hepplestone (Physics) will guide physical modelling and interpretation of charge dynamics at material interfaces and Prof Monica F. Craciun (Engineering) will guide film development and controlled testing, drawing on her work on cellulose–graphene nanogenerators and textile sensor stability. The findings will inform planned ERC and EPSRC proposals on what AI can infer from experimental signals and how to design measurements that resolve ambiguities.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Accessing the Nonlinear Regime by Coupling Graphene Resonators with Superconducting Circuits
jobs.description_html:
Quantum optomechanics explores how light can control and measure the motion of tiny mechanical drums using the laws of quantum physics. In most current devices, the interaction is linear: the light changes in direct proportion to the resonator’s displacement (if the motion doubles, the effect doubles). Linear interactions are useful, but they mainly produce smooth motion. Quantum Optomechanics in the Non-Linear Regime (QON) targets the much harder-to-reach nonlinear regime, where the interaction depends on the square of the motion. In simple terms, the response is no longer proportional. 

The goal is to develop and analyse opto-mechanical device designs that can access this nonlinear quantum regime using extremely light resonators made from graphene or carbon nanotubes. Because these resonators have very low mass, even the tiny momentum carried by a photon can strongly affect their motion, making nonlinear effects more visible. A key part of the research is to overcome two major obstacles identified by theory: unwanted (parasitic) linear coupling and interference between electrical/optical modes. 

The project will establish clear, testable requirements, such as the needed electrical and mechanical quality factors and the ratio of nonlinear to linear coupling, to guide device design that experimental teams will realise in fabrication. Reaching this regime would enable genuinely quantum mechanical states of motion and open routes to quantum technologies such as improved sensing for measurements of force, mass, and displacement beyond standard limits, mechanical signal processing, and new components for quantum information processing (for example, compact memories).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Water Governance Legal Frameworks and Socio-Economic Outcomes
jobs.description_html:
College of Business and Law at the University of the West of England in Bristol invites applications for a fully funded interdisciplinary PhD studentship in Water Governance Legal Frameworks and Socio-Economic Outcomes.

Start date: 1 April 2027 

In October 2025, UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights to water and sanitation called for a ‘paradigm shift’ in global water governance away from market-driven models and towards democratic, rights-based approaches. England's privatised system, which the Rapporteur had previously criticised, shows what is at stake: with public trust at an all-time low after repeated raw sewage discharges into rivers, it faces a deepening crisis rooted in decades of policy choices and regulatory failure. Following the Independent Water Commission's final report in July 2025, the government has committed to a major overhaul of the regulatory architecture in England, including a single integrated water regulator. This moment of institutional change creates an opportunity to examine how legal and regulatory design shapes outcomes for countries, communities, and the wider stakeholders involved. 

We invite research into questions such as: whether ownership structure explains differences in investment and environmental performance; whether embedding water governance within wider statutory frameworks shapes outcomes; whether legal innovations like the recognition of rights of nature and/or participatory management models involving civil society, hold transformative potential; and how governance arrangements distribute costs and benefits across regions, communities, and stakeholders as climate pressures intensify. 

This studentship offers an opportunity to develop an interdisciplinary, social sciences-based study on water governance and public policy, jointly supervised by a team combining expertise in law and economics.

Funding details

Eligibility criteria

This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. This project aims to measure fundamental nuclear properties in exotic super-asymmetric fission fragments and atomic-nuclear processes in ultra-low lying nuclear excited states.

The project is to be based at the IGISOL facility, JYFL, Jyvaskyla, Finland and ISOLDE, CERN. The research will exploit a number of recently constructed electrostatic ConeTrap and use them, for the first time, to facilitate high efficiency laser spectroscopy of exotic short-lived nuclei (precision measurements of nuclear parameters via atomic hyperfine structure and isotope shift).

The project is based at facilities where The University of Manchester and our national and international collaborators, from the UK, Belgium, China, Finland, France and Germany, have performed successful nuclear structure (and atomic) studies for a number of years. In the new work our objective is however to achieve spectroscopic efficiencies at an order of magnitude higher than that we have previously attained. Historical efficiencies have permitted in-flight studies of short-lived radioactive ions with lifetimes as short as 10 ms and production rates as low as 10 ions per second. We now intend to supersede these efficiencies and be capable of studying the most weakly produced and highest Z systems available at our on-line isotope separators.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Animal Behaviour: How Urban Living Shapes Reproductive Decisions and Success in Gulls
jobs.description_html:
Some wild animals live and reproduce in urban environments, where they encounter novel resources and challenges. Yet we know surprisingly little about the costs and benefits of urban living, or how animals adjust their behaviour and physiology while maintaining health, welfare and reproductive success. Apparent success may reflect abundant food and nesting opportunities but could conceal nutritional, physiological or reproductive costs. Understanding why individuals differ in their responses can reveal the biological mechanisms that enable animals to adapt to rapid environmental change. 

Urban herring gulls (Larus argentatus) provide an exceptional system for addressing these questions. Individuals make different choices about where to nest, what to eat, and how to raise their offspring. Some nest at ground level, others on low roofs or high buildings, and their diets range from marine prey to human-derived foods. 

You will study approximately 100 breeding gull pairs on Swansea University’s campus, linking nest-site choice and nutritional ecology with parental behaviour, physiology, affective state and reproductive success. Across breeding seasons, you will map available and occupied nest sites and follow identifiable birds and nests using observations, fixed cameras, ringing records and drone surveys. Monitoring will quantify reproductive decisions and outcomes, including egg laying, parental care, hatching, chick growth, survival and fledging. For focal parents, GPS tracking and dietary measures will establish reliance on urban, terrestrial and marine resources, while behavioural experiments and physiological sampling (faecal and feather glucocorticoids) will assess behavioural flexibility, affective state, stress and reproductive investment. These data will reveal how nest-site and foraging decisions relate to parental phenotype and chick success, whether different indicators of health and wellbeing align, and whether apparently successful urban breeding conceals costs to parents or offspring. 

You will gain interdisciplinary training in field biology, behavioural experiments, biologging, physiology, spatial analysis and statistical modelling. The project combines Swansea expertise in behavioural ecology and endocrinology (Prof Andrew King, Dr Ines Fürtbauer) with Exeter expertise in cognition, behavioural plasticity and experimental studies of wild gulls (Dr Neeltje,  Boogert, Prof Alex Thornton) and with support from Swansea’s biodiversity staff and established ringing networks.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Environmental Planning: ESRC Welsh Graduate School for the Social Sciences (WGSSS)
jobs.description_html:
Environmental planning examines the spatial dimensions and decision-making processes for the sustainable management of the relationships within and between natural and human systems. This interdisciplinary PhD training pathway bridges social and natural environmental sciences. It focusses on key environmental challenges, and their manifestation in Wales, the UK and globally, reflecting current policy challenges for Welsh and UK governments in the environmental sector. Major concerns include but are not limited to: impacts and management of climate change; local and regional environmental quality; conservation management; and post-Brexit environmental legislation.

The Department of Geography at Swansea is a vibrant and dynamic place for interdisciplinary doctoral studies. Our academics have a long history of successfully training PhD students for careers in the public, private, and third sectors, as well as in academia. Our staff have a wide range of expertise central to this pathway including quantifying and mitigating climate change, landscape carbon dynamics, flood management, pollution, environmental hazard management, wildfire mitigation, environmental archaeology, GIS and remote sensing applications, and cultural, urban, political, and economic geography. jobs.title: PhD Studentship - What’s the Worst that can Happen? Stress-testing Coupled Meteorological - Hydrological Models for Manchester
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: All year round

This 3.5-year PhD studentship is funded by the NERC i-Risk DFA and is open to Home (UK) and overseas students. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27; subject to annual uplift), and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

This project strengthens urban resilience by improving how we simulate extreme weather and water related hazards. By coupling high resolution meteorological and hydrological models, we aim to demonstrate how cities can better prepare for integrated water risks.

Through stress testing worst case scenarios, this project will identify vulnerabilities in current understanding of flood, drought, and water quality risks, helping agencies plan for future events. We aim to provide the scientific foundation needed to build a more resilient regional planning.

Research questions

This project will address the following research questions:

  • How much improvement in water related multi-hazard estimation can be gained by driving hydrological models with dynamically modelled atmospheric precipitation over current best practice?
  • What spatial and temporal resolution of precipitation is required to produce hydrological forecasts and planning scenarios of sufficient accuracy for a range of urban catchments?
  • What kinds of extreme precipitation and hydrological events could occur across the UK, and how good are models in predicting those extremes?
  • For events producing combined sewer overflows, what meteorological and hydrological factors determine their occurrence and magnitude?
  • What aspects of model configuration most strongly control predictability of extreme hydrological events?
  • How do multi-hazard events (coexistence of heavy rain and strong wind) affect rain-gauge undercatch, and how does this propagate into hydrological uncertainty?

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, an excellent academic record (UK First-class or 2.1 honours or international equivalent depending on the funding source) in Mathematics, Engineering, Earth Sciences, Computing or another related physical science discipline (MSc, MSci or BSc).

Applicants should have a strong quantitative background in applied mathematics, physics, engineering, or a related discipline. They should be confident in python or other programming languages.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor, Prof David Schultz. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Nanoscale Electrochemistry: Electrodeposition of Crystalline Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Materials
jobs.description_html:
Supervisors: Prof. Julie V. Macpherson and Prof. Patrick Unwin (Warwick Chemistry)

Funding: Fully funded PhD studentship (48 months)

Start date: September/October 2027

Application deadline: Ongoing 

Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) are an important family of layered semiconductors with tunable bandgaps and remarkable electronic and optical properties. These materials are emerging as key candidates for next‑generation semiconductor technologies, enabling ultra‑low‑power nano‑transistors, neuromorphic computing architectures, photonic integrated circuits, and quantum devices. Traditionally TMDCs are produced using chemical vapor deposition and microscale structures achieved from the top-down using lithographic procedures. This project is aimed at using electrodeposition as a bottom-up method of TMDC formation. In particular, it is focused on unravelling the nanoscale mechanism of TMDC electrodeposition in crystalline form and the role of the electrode surface structure. Nanoscale electrochemical imaging techniques such as scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) and in-situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy (EC-AFM) will be employed. The PhD is at the interface of materials science, nanotechnology and electrochemistry. The successful candidate will have the opportunity to develop experience and skills in high resolution electrochemical imaging techniques, scanning probe microscopy and electron microscopy. 

The research will be carried out in the Warwick Electrochemistry and Interfaces Group in the Chemistry Department at the University of Warwick (UoW). It will make extensive use of state-of-the-art analytical/microscopy facilities across the University (https://warwick.ac.uk/research/rtp/), in addition to cutting edge electrochemical nanoscale instrumentation. This studentship is aligned with the new EXPRESS (Exploiting Single Source Precursors for the Electrochemical Growth of Functional 1D and 2D Metal Dichalcogenide Semiconductors) research programme jointly funded with the University of Southampton (https://warwick.ac.uk/news/pressreleases/new-10m-project-next-generation-semiconductor-materials/). The student will join the UoW/UoS ExPRESS team (which consists of eight academic research groups spread across Chemistry, Physics and Engineering at both institutions). They will benefit significantly from interdisciplinary interactions with the wider team.

Applicants must have (or expect to obtain) at least the equivalent of a UK first or upper second-class degree in Chemistry, Physics or Materials (or related subjects). The studentship will commence in October 2027 (although an earlier start is possible based on your availability) and the position is fully funded for UK applicants over a period of 48 months including tuition fees and a maintenance grant at the standard UKRI rate, which is currently £21805 p.a. Applications are also welcome from those able to support themselves. Such applications will go through the same level of academic assessment.

The University of Warwick and the Chemistry Department hold Athena SWAN Silver Awards, reflecting their commitment to equality, diversity and inclusion, and particularly to gender equality. 

If you are interested in the position, please contact Prof. Julie Macpherson (j.macpherson@warwick.ac.uk) and provide a CV. 

Further information about the research of Profs. Macpherson and Unwin FRS can be found at:  https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/chemistry/staff/juliemacpherson/ and https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/chemistry/staff/patrickunwin/. The Warwick Electrochemistry and Interfaces Group is internationally renowned, offering an excellent research environment with world class facilities dedicated to electrochemical and interfacial research, see: Warwick Electrochemistry and Interfaces Group

jobs.description_html:
The project:

Undertake a research project at the forefront of railway infrastructure safety, developing innovative ultrasonic inspection technologies to detect cracks in the foot of railway rails before they lead to failure. Despite major advances in rail inspection, many remaining rail breaks originate from fatigue cracks in the rail foot, often associated with corrosion and residual stresses. Reliable detection of these defects remains a significant engineering challenge.

This PhD will combine advanced data analytics, machine learning, and state-of-the-art ultrasonic sensing to develop new methods for identifying rail foot cracks from measurements made at the rail head. The project will investigate both enhanced analysis of data from existing inspection trains and novel ultrasonic array imaging techniques capable of detecting defects hidden from direct view.

The research will involve:

  • Developing statistical and machine learning approaches for analysing ultrasonic inspection data;
  • Working with large industrial datasets from rail inspections;
  • Designing advanced ultrasonic array imaging methods for non-line-of-sight defect detection;
  • Evaluating how new inspection technologies could be deployed within real-world rail monitoring systems.

This project offers an excellent opportunity to gain expertise in ultrasonic non-destructive evaluation (NDE), signal processing, imaging, machine learning, and infrastructure monitoring while contributing to the safety and reliability of rail networks.

The PhD will be undertaken within the Future Innovation in Non-Destructive Evaluation (FIND) centre for doctoral training. This is a multi-university collaboration with the partner universities providing optional taught specialist modules on different NDE modalities and related topics. The centre also provides cohort building and networking opportunities with the chance to attend and present at its annual conference to an industrial and academic audience. jobs.title: PhD Studenthsip: Project 3666 Exploring Bacterial G-Quadruplex Sequences as Targets for Novel Antibiotics
jobs.description_html:
The project:

https://www.swbio.ac.uk/engineering-biology-projects/ 

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global public health challenge, with infections by antibiotic-resistant bacteria estimated to be responsible for 1.3 million deaths worldwide in 2019. Developing new antibiotics effective against strains of bacteria resistant to current agents is one approach to overcoming AMR. G- quadruplexes (G4s) are non B-form nucleic acid structures formed by guanine-rich DNA and RNA sequences, and are increasingly recognised as functionally important in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. A number of small molecule ligands have been identified that bind selectively to G4s over other nucleic acid structures, and some of these have been intensively investigated as potential therapeutics for conditions such as cancer, and for infections by viruses and eukaryotic parasites. In contrast, the effects of small-molecule G4 ligands upon bacteria have been much less studied. This project aims to characterise the interactions of a series of newly-synthesised investigational small-molecule G4 ligands with acteria, seeking to assess their potential, and the potential of G4-directed approaches, to form a basis for development of novel antibiotics. This project will use bioinformatic approaches to identify candidate G4 sequences in S. aureus laboratory, against these sequences in vitro; and translating these findings into the cellular environment using reporter assays and imaging approaches. In parallel we will test activity against a panel of S. aureus knockout strains, and attempt to generate and characterise mutants that are resistant to the activity of our ligands. In combination these methods will identify likely G4-containing target genes and sequences in S. aureus; and assemble evidence linking binding to these with bacterial killing. The student will gain experience of a range of biophysical, bioinformatic and microbiological methods in a cross-disciplinary environment underpinned by the dynamic, collaborative Bristol AMR environment.

See academic criteria here: https://www.swbio.ac.uk/programme/eligibility/

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B34 Extreme climatic events in a warming world understanding limits to resilience in freshwater ecosystems
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Across the globe, extreme climatic events such as heatwaves and droughts have increased dramatically in frequency and intensity over the past 30 years, with potentially profound consequences for freshwater ecosystems. Repeated heatwave events have blighted the UK in 2026 yet very little is known about their effect on river life. Rare long-term studies suggest the impacts may be long-lasting and profound, but questions remain regarding the resistance and resilience of ecosystem to these recurrent events, especially when they occur together. During heatwaves, water temperature may approach or exceed the thermal tolerance limits of river organisms, leading to physiological stress, functional impairments and even local extinctions of sensitive species, but we do not know the tolerance limits of most British river fauna. In some regions, river flows are suffering drought and in extreme cases shifting from perennial to intermittent, modifying the ecological connectivity among habitats within the river network. Where low river flows persist, connections to riparian ecosystems are likely to be enhanced as terrestrial flora and fauna colonise the riverscape, altering biodiversity and the structure and function of food webs in unknown ways. Despite the growing prevalence of extreme climatic events, research on their effects in streams and rivers continues to lag far behind other environmental stressors (e.g. acid pulses or pesticides) and has focused on community level responses (e.g. species richness and abundances). Far less is known about impacts of interacting extremes on ecosystem functioning (e.g. production, decomposition, consumption) and food webs. Similarly, knowledge of the extent of ecosystem recovery of ecosystem to drought and heatwave pulses is poorly understood, and much research is needed to understand the vulnerability of key biological groups (e.g. invertebrates) to heatwaves in running waters across the UK.

The successful candidate will join a team undertaking research to address these research gaps and will have the opportunity to conduct field surveys of thermal tolerance of key species across the UK along with flow / temperature manipulation experiments in a new state of the art mesocosm facility at the University of Birmingham (see Fig .1 below). These experiments will be combined with sampling and analysis of long-term records of flow, temperature and biodiversity in streams monitored by the Environment Agency, our project partner, in order to assess ecological resilience using time series data.

The results of the research will reveal how river biodiversity and ecosystem processes are affected by extreme events in an era of rapid global change, and will be used to help inform and guide climate change mitigation and adaptation policy.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please click the 'Apply' button above.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B35 Go with the flow Guiding sustainable dam flow releases to simultaneously promote ecological health and water security
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
There are >3000 dams in the UK that provide >75% of national public drinking water supplies (1). These unnaturally transform river flow regimes, where typically fixed ‘compensation flows’ are released for most the year except when reservoir spillovers cause rapid downstream flushes. Excessive compensation flows can reduce water supply availability in the lead-up to and during drier month, which can trigger drought permits restricting public water use. Water supply dams also degrade river ecosystems dependent on natural flow variations where hydrological modifications can disrupt ecological processes like habitats, feeding patterns and migratory cues (2, 3, 4).

This PhD will aim to address these critical environmental and societal challenges by undertaking a multi-scaled approach across England. For this, the hydrological and ecological impacts of dams will first be assessed on a national-scale. This will then feed into regional evaluations, where the successful candidate will examine how dam flow release mechanisms are shaping water security and the ecological health in downstream environments. Optimal scenarios balancing these two demands (see 4, 5) will then be quantified across different climate change forecasts using state-of-the-art statistical analyses. Under supportive supervision, the student will become proficient in both hydrological and statistical modelling in order to achieve these goals.

While there is a national-scale, ‘big data’ focus for this PhD, the successful candidate will have the opportunity to collect field data from targeted study sites. This will not only provide additional evidence that may not be extractable from secondary datasets, but will also enhance the skills being assimilated by the student and allow them to glean greater insights into how river systems regulated by dams operate. More broadly, the successful candidate will draw on the expertise of the interdisciplinary supervisory team, who specialise translating scientific research to management solutions and work closely with water companies (2). These links to industry will help ensure that the outcomes of the PhD will translate to real-world action, where the findings will be shared with the water industry to help support dam flow release operations.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-UKCEH01 HInterMap drone-based mapping to improve monitoring and understanding of headwater and intermittent streams
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Intermittent streams (c. 50% of world rivers) and headwaters (c. 90% of rivers) are key riverine systems for hydrology, ecology and water quality, which are poorly monitored and lack data (Dugdale et al. 2022; Mainstone et al. 2018; Datry et al. 2016). Streams are often flagged as intermittent based on downstream flows, but where or how they dry is not known. Capturing the evolution of river habitat and connectivity as streams dry out is particularly important (Dugdale et al. 2022) for process hydrology, river ecology (e.g. refugia during drought, loss of physical in-channel habitat, loss of longitudinal connectivity, loss of lateral connectivity with riparian area, floodplain and wetlands), and water quality (pools are considered to favour algae blooms). Unpiloted Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), more commonly called drones, are a potential way to address these issues (Kelleher et al. 2016). River habitat monitoring can also benefit from using UAV data, which can provide fast higher resolution updates than traditional techniques. Figure 1 shows an example of mapping an intermittent chalk river in the UK. This research is relevant to other water-dependent systems faced with similar issues (e.g. wetlands) and could complement research on UAV-based water quality surveys in larger rivers. Beyond the riverine environment, the project would also explore potential to link with terrestrial UAV applications (e.g. biodiversity).

While the primary focus of this project in on headwaters and intermittent streams, the techniques and approaches developed by the student could be explored within the context of other river types or topics (e.g. thermal regime of contrasting river typologies or of groundwater-fed systems, mapping thermal refugia, longitudinal temperature change).

The successful candidate for this project would be based with the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology and would be registered at the University of Birmingham.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B33 When does snow matter Looking at the sensitivity of river flow to a warming climate
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Snow acts as a natural seasonal reservoir across many regions of the world. Water that falls as snow can be stored through winter and often released later during spring and summer, sustaining river flows, ecosystems, hydropower and water supplies. As the climate warms, however, more precipitation may fall as rain, snow melt timing may change, and seasonal snowpacks are changing in coverage. These changes are already widespread, but their consequences for rivers and water resources are surprisingly difficult to understand.

A key reason is that losing the same amount of snow does not have the same effect everywhere. In some catchments, large areas of the landscape lie close to the climatic boundaries, meaning that even modest warming can fundamentally change how water is stored and released. Elsewhere, snow occurs mainly at high elevations and may be less sensitive. Groundwater, lakes and other catchment stores can further buffer, or even amplify, the effect of changing snowmelt on river flow.

This PhD will investigate when and where changes in snow translate into important changes in river runoff and water availability. It will build on major Northern Hemisphere snow datasets and analysis framework published and developed by the supervisory team and collaborators, combining these with additional large datasets on climate, landscape, and river discharge.

The PhD students will be able to examine a large spectrum of snow observations and river catchments spanning contrasting climates and mountain environments. They will be able to directly test how landscape, temperature gradients, precipitation patterns and water-storage characteristics control the sensitivity of snow accumulation, melt timing and seasonal runoff to warming.

The broad structure of the project will be to progress from observed relationships to new conceptual frameworks and future climate experiments, with plenty of scope for incorporating individual student interests within this. This project will not rely only on complex hydrological simulations, but rather seek simple and transferable explanations for why some rivers are much more vulnerable to declining snow than others.

This project will provide an exciting opportunity for a PhD student interested in working on new frameworks for identifying the snow sensitivity of river systems and emerging water resource hotspots under climate change, with relevance from local catchment management to continental and hemispheric scale assessments of future water availability.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B21 Developing climate models to capture past warm-world rainfall change
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Computer climate models are the only way to predict future climate change and to understand the drivers of environmental change at the global scale. But these models do not always agree on regional changes, especially for monsoon regions. Part of this is because the gridcell resolution does not capture the full sub-grid dynamics of these systems and so paramerisations of for example convective storms are required (e.g. Bordoni et al 2025). It is increasingly being recognised that these parameterisations can be hugely improved through the addition of a stochastic or random component that is designed to represent small-scale features that occur in the real world but are weak or missing in gridded models (Palmer et al 2001; Wang et al 2016).

This can be partly understood by considering the famous butterfly effect – a tiny disturbance of the atmosphere in one region that has major knock-on effects elsewhere. This effect as stated cannot happen in global models because they lack the fine-scale disturbances. Stochastic parameterisations could go some way to resolving this and have already shown promise in improving the simulation characteristics of present-day rainfall (Wang et al 2016).

In this project you’ll build on these established schemes to add random (stochastic) perturbations to key parts of a climate model and use this to perform new simulations of past and future change. This work will allow us to assess the improvements relative to a standard climate model configuration and we’ll use deeper past changes (e.g. Hopcroft & Valdes, 2021) to gauge the response to a changed climate which is more relevant for testing the feedbacks that may come into play in a future warmer world.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B22 How fast is magma made in Large Igneous Provinces
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Throughout Earth's history, episodic Large Igneous Provinces (LIPs) coincide with environmental crises including mass extinction, global warming and oceanic anoxia events. We cannot explain this coincidence because we do not know how LIPs that span 10 million years can trigger environmental crises that span 10 to 100 thousand years. Consequently, short environmental crises are often attributed to climate system tipping behaviour, when slow LIP magma and greenhouse gas emissions build to some critical threshold. This project investigates the alternative proposition that LIP magma and greenhouse gas emissions occur fast enough to explain the environmental crises directly, without climate system tipping.

Growing evidence suggests that LIP activity is strongly pulsed. The Birmingham-led IMPULSE project recently presented the most compelling evidence to date for pulsing within the Icelandic mantle plume from its inception to the present (Jones et al. 2026). A strong pulse of magma generated by the same mantle convection system could explain the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum global climate change event that accompanied the North Atlantic LIP (Jones et al. 2019; Voosen 2026). In parallel, high-resolution radiometric dating of the Deccan Traps LIP shows that a pulse of volcanic eruption spanning approximately 100 thousand years occurred immediately before the end-Cretaceous mass extinction (Schoene et al. 2019).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B23 Functional morphology and ecology of the Pleistocene mammal fauna of Crete
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Islands are often described as natural laboratories for evolution. Due to their isolation and constrained size, islands are ideal model systems to study evolution and ecological processes firsthand; for example, for studying island effects (or island rules), whereby animals become smaller due to spatial and resource limitations or larger due to the absence of predators and competition compared to their mainland counterparts.

The Mediterranean Islands are famous for their Cenozoic fauna. In particular, the Greek island of Crete is a treasure trove for studying unique animal assemblages. Its Pleistocene mammal fauna features an exceptional diversity of species that have undergone an astounding morphological transformation in adaptation to the changed geographical and environmental conditions: the smallest known mammoth (ca. 1 m shoulder height), dwarf elephants and hippos, several species of dwarf deer, but also giant rodents (rats and mice five to ten times the "normal" size) and otters. These extreme examples of dwarfism and gigantism were often accompanied by a radical change in habitat.

Although Cretan fossils have been studied for over hundred years, research predominantly focussed on descriptive/ taxonomic work, whereas functional and biogeochemical studies have been neglected. This project will focus on how a diverse range of species was able to adapt to their island habitat, not just once but several times which morphological changes allowed these animals to cope with fundamentally different environments.

As one of the best documented and diverse island faunas in the Mediterranean, Crete's Pleistocene mammals provide an exceptional opportunity for a multi-disciplinary and multi-angle investigation on the adaptive evolution of the endemic island fauna from a palaeontological, biomechanical, and geochemical perspective. With over 100 recorded fossil localities and two independent phases of colonisation and adaptation events, Crete represents an ideal model system for this study.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B24 Reconstructing Plio-Pleistocene Ice-Sheet Evolution in the North Sea Basin Using Paleomagnetism and Magnetic Fabric
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
IODP Expedition 507 (GLACE-NS) running in June-July 2027 will recover a unique Plio-Pleistocene sedimentary archive from the North Sea Basin (NSB), providing an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the onset, evolution, and variability of Northern Hemisphere glaciation and its links to environmental and oceanographic change. This PhD project will exploit a large collection of approximately 2,000 to 3,000 sediment specimens that will be obtained from Expedition 507 cores by co-supervisor Dr Marco Maffione, a member of the science party, to develop high-resolution reconstructions of ice-sheet development, sediment provenance, and ocean circulation across the last ~3 million years.

The project will directly address key scientific objectives of GLACE-NS by integrating paleomagnetic, environmental magnetic, and rock magnetic proxies. A primary goal will be to establish a robust chronological framework through magnetostratigraphy and relative palaeointensity (RPI) analysis. While magnetostratigraphy will provide age constraints based on geomagnetic polarity reversals, RPI records will enable substantially higher-resolution stratigraphic correlation, particularly during the last 1.5 million years. This age model will permit detailed quantification of sedimentation-rate changes associated with glacial-interglacial cycles and major climatic transitions.

Building on this framework, the project will investigate variations in sediment source regions and transport pathways using magnetic susceptibility and magnetic grain-size sensitive parameters. These records will provide insight into changing erosion patterns, ice-sheet dynamics, and landscape evolution across northwestern Europe during periods of climatic reorganisation. The resulting provenance reconstructions will be integrated with sedimentological and geochemical datasets generated by the wider expedition science team (~25 members with a broad range of expertise).

A further objective is to reconstruct changes in bottom-current circulation and depositional processes using anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS). Magnetic fabric data will provide quantitative information on current intensity and flow directions through time, allowing assessment of how oceanographic circulation responded to ice-sheet expansion and retreat. Together, these records will generate a comprehensive reconstruction of cryospheric, environmental, and oceanographic evolution in the North Sea Basin, contributing to a broader understanding of the mechanisms linking ice sheets, ocean circulation, and climate during one of Earth's most significant long-term cooling trends.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B25 Which Floodplains are the Most Important Characterising Global Connectivity Between Rivers and Their Flood Corridors
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
When river flow is high enough to exceed the banks of its channels, it inundates the floodplain. Integrated over entire catchments, so-called river-floodplain exchange impacts a significant amount of the flow moving through river basins, carrying sediments, nutrients, and other materials. As flood regimes shift under climate change, they represent an important natural hazard that has long been the focus of flood modelling. However, flooding also has a major effect on water quality and ecosystem health through the interactions that river water (and the materials it is carrying) has with a variety of new substrates and ecological communities on the floodplain during exchange.

Only recently has a systematic, large-scale characterization of river-floodplain exchange been performed, revealing regionally-specific heterogeneities across the United States (Brinkerhoff et al. 2026). But because this work focused on only one continent and one country, we still struggle to understand these impacts across all climate regions and in countries with different approaches to flood management. This means at present, it remains challenging to describe which regions are most impacted by river-floodplain exchange, where human disturbance most alters these processes, and what are the associated impacts on downstream water quality and ecosystem health.

This PhD will investigate how and where the largest (and smallest) river-floodplain exchange events occur around the world, what exchange regimes exist across climate, topography, and disturbance gradients, and how such interactions may change under future climate conditions. It will build on recent modelling work in the United States by the supervisory team, as well as other global modelling efforts by collaborators. The student will combine these existing approaches with other large datasets of climate, river flow, and catchment characteristics covering all major river basins on Earth.

The broader structure of the project will be to move from empirical models to a global conceptual framework. Rather than rely on complicated land surface hydrological simulations, the project will develop relatively simple, globally transferable heuristics that help explain why some river basins are more sensitive to river-floodplain exchange than others, the downstream impacts of those sensitivities, and how they may change into the future given our changing climate.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B26 Thermal Sensitivity of West African Tropical Moist Forests
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Global air temperatures and the occurrence of heatwaves are increasing and set to continue over the coming century. Plant physiological processes such as photosynthesis are highly temperature sensitive and therefore there are significant potential consequences of climate change for plant function. Tropical forests are essential ecosystems for the safe operating of the planet due to their role in the carbon and water cycles and high biodiversity. Long-lived species such as trees will be exposed to extreme climatic conditions within their lifetimes. This project will assess the thermal sensitivity of tropical tree species in West Africa using an array of novel methods, to inform on the potential future functioning of tropical forest systems.

The objectives of this project are:

O1 To determine seasonal change in canopy temperature and thermal sensitivity of leaf physiology of West African moist tropical tree species, including assessing the importance of leaf and crown traits on canopy temperatures.

O2 To assess the acclimation of West African tree species to climatic change over the past decades in leaf temperature regulation traits and estimated leaf temperatures.

O3 To assess change in tree species composition of West African forests in relation to measured thermal sensitivity.

The project benefits from planned and previous data collection, including 1 year of continuous canopy temperature monitoring data from 2023 and field campaigns measuring thermal physiology and drone-based canopy temperature in two sites in autumn 2026. This PhD project will have access to and extend these datasets to assess seasonal change in thermal vulnerability. It is envisaged that the student will carry out one extended trip to Ghana, during which they will undertake field campaigns under differing seasonal conditions (dry and wet), and spend time analysing locally stored herbarium samples.

This project will offer the opportunity to develop skills in the use of environmental sensors including drones, field measurements of tree physiology, and use of historical archived plant material. The student will work with experts from a range of institutions enabling development of a broad research network and will be supported by the Birmingham Institute for Forest Research (BIFoR).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B27 Mangroves in a Changing Climate How Increasing Salinity Alters Carbon Gain and Water Use
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Climate change is accelerating sea-level rise, increasing saltwater intrusion into coastal wetlands and exposing mangrove ecosystems to increasingly saline conditions (Acosta-Motos et al., 2017; Dessu et al., 2018). Mangroves occupy the interface between terrestrial and marine environments, making them particularly vulnerable to changes in hydrology driven by rising sea levels and reduced freshwater inflows. Although most mangrove species are naturally salt-tolerant, increasing salinity can alter soil water availability and threatens the ecological functioning of these ecosystems. These changes may reduce forest productivity and impact the ecosystem services mangroves provide, including carbon sequestration, coastal protection, and nursery habitat for marine biodiversity. Thus, understanding how mangroves respond to increasing salinity is essential for predicting the resilience of coastal ecosystems.

Salinity directly affects plant water relations by reducing the osmotic potential of soil water (Parihar et al., 2015), making water uptake increasingly difficult. To maintain water transport, mangroves employ a range of physiological adaptations, including osmotic adjustment, allowing leaves to maintain turgor under saline conditions (Suárez & Sobrado, 2000). However, these adjustments often come at a physiological cost: declining leaf water potential increases the risk of hydraulic failure, which can lead stomata to close to minimise water loss and prevent embolism. In turn, stomatal closure reduces CO2 uptake, limiting growth. The balance between maintaining hydraulic function and sustaining carbon gain therefore represents a key challenge for mangroves exposed to increasing salinity.

Responses to salinity vary considerably among mangrove species, developmental stages, concentration and the duration of exposure. Seedlings are particularly vulnerable due to their limited root systems while mature trees possess more developed hydraulic systems and greater physiological plasticity. Yet, they may still experience reductions in gas exchange and carbon assimilation under prolonged salinity stress (Clough & Sim, 1989). Despite growing recognition of salinity as a major consequence of climate change, understanding how increasing salinity influences leaf-level carbon and water dynamics across different life stages of mangroves remains a critical gap. This PhD project aims to address this gap by investigating how salinity alters leaf physiology in both mangrove seedlings and mature trees, improving predictions of mangrove resilience, restoration and future carbon storage under rising sea levels.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B28 AI-Enhanced Global Hydrological Modelling for Assessing UK Water Security Threats
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Global hydrology models (GHMs) play a crucial role in understanding threats to water security. Their global remit means they can be used to assess transboundary impacts from water security crises, e.g. how flooding in East Asia might affect UK supply chains. They also help with quantifying cascading climate change risks, such as how a drought can lead to reductions in crop yields, which in turn lead to rises in food prices, and migration. The UK faces multiple environmental, economic and political threats from around the world. Water is one of these primary risks because it is associated with flooding, droughts and long-term water security, and can affect large land areas and multiple sectors of the economy, from days to years at a time.

Despite the importance of understanding the implications of global hydrological change for the UK and its security, there are only two GHMs in the UK’s environmental modelling national capability. One of these is JULES (the Joint UK Land Environment Simulator), which is a community land surface model that is used both as a standalone model and as the land surface component in the Met Office global climate model. However, whilst JULES includes complex representation of physical land surface environmental processes and feedbacks, its representation of direct human forcings on the hydrological cycle, such as dams, reservoirs, and water abstraction for different water users (e.g. agriculture, industry and domestic) is still being developed. The other model is MacPDM, which was originally developed at UKCEH and has undergone several updates over the past few decades, including several by this project’s supervisor (Gosling & Arnell, 2011; Müller Schmied & Gosling et al. 2024). However, just like JULES, MacPDM does not currently represent direct human forcings. Other national modelling infrastructure capabilities include these important aspects of the global hydrological system, such as WaterGAP (Germany) and H08 (Japan).

This project will provide an important update to the UK’s ability to simulate global hydrological risks and their impacts by using AI methods with global observation datasets to develop, test and optimise the parameterisation of direct human forcings in the MacPDM global-scale hydrological model.

Project Description

PhD studentship within the ERC-funded Anonymous Agency project, Department of Music, University of Bristol. https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101264213.

Old Hispanic chant is preserved in unpitched notation, which communicates note count, syllable underlay, and contour (but not precise intervals or pitches). The repertoire’s musical grammar is well understood, but among the thousands of extant chants can we discern chronological layers, distinct communities of practice or even individual (anonymous) authorship?

This PhD will harness machine learning approaches to explore these questions, drawing on the ca. 3000 melodies already in machine-readable format (see https://neumes.org.uk/view for published examples). The student will be trained to transcribe further chants as necessary. (S)he might focus on particular chant genres, or on specific feasts, types of feast, or liturgical seasons.

jobs.description_html:

The project:

Decision-making under uncertainty is a fundamental challenge in AI and data science, particularly in dynamic settings where observations are collected sequentially and decisions influence future outcomes. This project will develop novel machine learning and statistical methods for adaptive learning, sequential decision-making, and control, motivated by applications in public health and epidemiology.

The project will focus on methodological advances in reinforcement learning (RL), active learning, Bayesian decision theory, and stochastic optimisation for partially observed and evolving systems.

Key research directions include:

  1. adaptive data acquisition strategies that maximise information gain under resource constraints;
  2. RL-based approaches for sequential intervention and control; and
  3. robust learning methods that adapt to incomplete observations, changing environments, and distributional shifts.

The research will combine probabilistic modelling, network-based representations, and modern AI methods to enable scalable and interpretable decision-making in complex systems. Applications will include adaptive disease surveillance, outbreak monitoring, resource allocation, and intervention planning using dynamic mobility and contact networks as motivating examples. The methodological contributions have broader relevance to sequential optimisation and decision-making problems across AI and data science.

The ideal candidate will have foundational knowledge of machine learning and strong self-motivation. You will be supervised by Dr. Mengyan Zhang (https://mengyanz.github.io/), whose research focuses on sequential decision making and public health. Dr. Zhang has published in leading venues including Nature, PNAS, ICML, AAAI, etc. She collaborates widely through the Machine Learning and Global Health network, including with researchers at the University of Oxford, Imperial College London, and the National University of Singapore.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Harnessing Nature’s CO2 Catalyst to Accelerate Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal
jobs.description_html:
Could biology help us engineer a new way of removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?

Achieving carbon dioxide removal (CDR) at enormous scale is likely to be an important part of tackling climate change. The ocean naturally exchanges CO2 with the air, but because the alkalinity of that seawater buffers CO2, the amount of carbon dissolved in the ocean is vastly greater than in the atmosphere. For context, if you took all the CO2 that humanity has every emitted and stirred it into the ocean, the seawater carbon concentration would only increase by about 2%.

An extremely promising technique, known as Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement, aims to increase the buffering of CO2 by seawater. This would allow seawater to take up even more atmospheric CO2, helping us to balance the emissions from activities - such as flying and farming - that we don’t know how to decarbonise, and potentially even begin to reverse climate change.

But there is a fundamental problem.

Transferring atmospheric CO₂ into that seawater is slow. This means that CO2 uptake happens over tens to hundreds of kilometres downstream of where a carbon removal facility may be, with implications around marine ecosystem impacts, scalability, verification and cost. If this exchange could be dramatically accelerated, it could open the door to a different approach to marine carbon dioxide removal.

This PhD, part of the  CASE4CDR project which is aligned with ARIA’s Resilient Climate and Ecosystems Opportunity Space,  will explore whether  harnessing biology can allow us to overcome this problem.

Carbonic anhydrases catalyse the conversion between carbon dioxide and bicarbonate, speeding up the reaction by up to 10 million times. These enzymes are found in almost all living organisms, and we will work with you to isolate and stabilise them, utilising the same chemistry that operates in your body and in marine organisms to overcome the reaction bottleneck and rapidly convert carbon dioxide and water into ocean bicarbonate. The project will give you the opportunity to learn advanced skills in enzymology, structural work, and protein chemistry to develop these enzymes to meet the environmental challenge. It will also involve small lab-scale tests to quantify the efficacy of atmospheric CO2 absorption by alkalinity-enhanced seawater using immobilised enzymes.

You will work closely with a parallel PhD researcher working on larger-scale CO₂ exchange and measurement.

From laboratory experiments to the sea

A particularly exciting feature of this PhD is that, with the right safeguards in place, the work is intended to move beyond laboratory proof-of-concept.

Upon meeting key acceptance criteria, you will help translate fundamental measurements and engineering designs into trials using real seawater at the SeaCURE pilot facility situated on the coast near Weymouth.

This will create a unique opportunity to follow an emerging climate technology through multiple stages of development: from calculations and controlled laboratory experiments, through engineering and instrumentation, to operation in a real marine environment.

Carbon dioxide removal cannot succeed on engineering performance alone.

You will join a wider interdisciplinary project examining what would actually be required to deploy a new marine carbon removal technology responsibly. Alongside your core research, you will have opportunities to contribute to work around environmental permitting, regulation, environmental impacts, public and stakeholder engagement, and trials at the Weymouth plant.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B17 Finding the most explosive volcanoes on earth
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
While advances in volcanology have revealed much about eruption processes, research has largely concentrated on a small set of well-monitored volcanoes, geographically skewed towards continental and northern hemisphere regions. This focus has left significant gaps in our understanding of many volcanoes, especially in resource-poor regions including island arcs in Southeast Asia. These areas coincide with the world’s highest volcanic activity, yet eruption histories, geological maps, and monitoring data are incomplete or absent. Volcanoes capable of very large magnitude eruptions (M ≥ 6), with the potential to cause severe regional or global impacts, remain missing from current risk assessments.

This PhD project will address this critical knowledge gap by identifying which volcanoes are most likely to produce highly explosive, large-magnitude eruptions. The student will combine global datasets with targeted field investigations to test the attributes hypothesised to favour such eruptions. Using a training dataset of well-studied volcanoes with known large eruptions, the project will employ statistical and machine learning (ML) methods to identify the strongest predictors of eruption magnitude. These predictive models will then be applied to poorly characterised volcanoes, producing a prioritised list for further research and monitoring.

Fieldwork in Southeast Asia, in collaboration with Indonesian partners, will test and refine these predictions. The student will also help organise a joint field course (with the Global Volcano Risk Alliance charity), to train local and international students in volcanic mapping, tephra sampling, dating techniques, and the analysis of volcanic ash for health impacts. This component will strengthen scientific capacity, foster community engagement, and produce valuable new data for the project.

By integrating advanced data science with traditional field volcanology and community-based training, the project will identify hidden high-risk volcanoes and contribute directly to monitoring priorities and the next generation of volcano scientists. The outcomes will be relevant to global disaster risk reduction efforts and will support targeted investment in monitoring infrastructure where it is most urgently needed.

Applicants should be comfortable working with quantitative analytical methods (specific machine learning skills can be developed during the PhD). Willingness for fieldwork in challenging environments is essential.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B18 Modelling function in the jaws of sharks throughout their evolutionary history
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Sharks are a diverse, ecologically important, and vulnerable group of fishes with an ancient history. Although the word shark tends to conjure the image of a primeval apex predator, living elasmobranchs live in open ocean, nearshore, and freshwater habitats worldwide, with ecological roles as diverse as bottom-dwelling suction feeders, open ocean filter feeders, and flat-bodied shell-crunchers. Moreover, far from being primitive this rich biodiversity is rooted in a unique feeding system. Highly mobile jaws made from a specialised calcified cartilage and lined with ever-replacing tooth tows are linked to the skull via ligaments and a rod-like hyoid cartilage which allows them to swing outwards during feeding (Wroe et al. 2008). There is great variation in the shape of shark jaws and presumably their function.

The fossil record of isolated teeth shows that this feeding system extends back least 400 million years, and it has rich potential for understanding the relationship between ecology and evolution (López-Romero et al. 2023). However, understanding it is hindered in living sharks by the difficulty of studying anything but small, shallow-water species, and in extinct sharks by the sparse record of fossilised cartilages. Most functional studies have either focussed on specific taxa with specialised feeding mechanics (e.g. Wroe et al. 2008) or looked at the shape of individual parts of the feeding apparatus across the group (e.g. López-Romero et al. 2023, Griffin et al. 2025). Our understanding of how different jaw arrangements in both living and extinct shark relates to their function is very limited.

Recently surging use of tomographic methods has seen a huge increase in datasets on the skeletal anatomy of sharks both living and extinct (e.g. Dearden et al. 2025). This presents the opportunity to carry out quantitative, comparative functional morphological studies across the sweep of fossil and living sharks to understand their feeding apparatus as a multipart system. Using computed tomographic data on fossil and living elasmobranchs and multibody dynamics approaches (Lautenschlager 2020, Dearden et al. 2023) this project will investigate how different forms of the living shark feeding system affect its function throughout their long evolutionary history.
