jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Neuromorphic Systems for Low-latency and Efficient Multimodal Processing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Modern AI systems achieve remarkable performance on tasks ranging from language modelling to computer vision. However, their large size, and significant data requirements, make them costly to train and deploy, with AI systems set to consume 3% of global energy supply by 2030. Neuromorphic systems aim to solve this challenge, by taking inspiration from the brain, to develop algorithms and computational substrates that can achieve intelligent processing on a similar power (approx. 20W).

However, while modern AI systems have benefited from access to large volumes of high-quality and labelled data, these resources do not exist in the neuromorphic domain, limiting overall progress. The proposed supervisory team are addressing this gap and are currently collecting the world’s first phonetically rich multi-modal neuromorphic dataset, containing audio and video recordings of spoken language (ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11043887). [ieeexplore.ieee.org] The unique contribution captures data using neuromorphic sensors allowing high temporal accuracy, while simultaneously introducing sparsityto increasing overall efficiency. 

However, while neuromorphic processors can exploit these data structures, specialised algorithms are required to perform tasks such as classification and reasoning, which are severely lacking in the community.

The project is structured into 3 equally weighted research streams to deliver new fundamental knowledge through harnessing the capabilities of neuromorphic sensors to better capture and process speech (Streams 1 & 2), and generate impact through applications of this technology in society (stream 3):

Stream 1: Algorithmic exploitation of neuromorphic audio-visual speech data, to address the major computational bottlenecks in speech recognition and speech production analysis, e.g. minimising data movement using neuromorphic algorithms and chips such as Intel’s Loihi2.

Stream 2: Developing language understanding through neuromorphic representations. Speech sounds are produced using coordinated movements of articulators to achieve specific acoustic targets (e.g. fast movements of the tongue and lips). These are challenging to process using conventional techniques, as individuals can produce the same sound in multiple ways, and the same articulatory movement in different individuals can lead to different sounds.

Stream 3: Impact through real-world applications of low-power speech processing, for tasks such as lip reading for the hearing impaired, and language understanding. The goal will be to develop technology suitable for deployment at the edge, such as in mobile devices and hearing aids, and with potential for embedding in augmented reality scenarios.

Please see here for further details.

Please contact the main project supervisor, Dr. Luca Peres, to learn more about the project and discuss whether it may be suitable for you.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B03 Managing Contrasting Landscapes for Soil Carbon Sequestration, Soil Biodiversity and Tree Health
jobs.description_html:
The City of London Corporation manages a nationally significant portfolio of open spaces including Epping Forest, Burnham Beeches, Hampstead Heath, Queen's Park, West Ham Park, Copped Hall and Patmore's Field. Through its Carbon Removals Programme, the Corporation is investing in habitat restoration, meadow creation, soil improvement initiatives and woodland resilience measures to support climate mitigation, biodiversity recovery and ecosystem resilience.

Land management practices influence soil microbiology and chemistry, which in turn regulate carbon sequestration, nutrient cycling and tree resilience. By understanding these relationships, it is possible to design management interventions that simultaneously enhance carbon storage, biodiversity recovery and ecosystem resilience. However, there remains a significant evidence gap regarding which site-specific land management interventions most effectively improve soil condition, increase carbon sequestration and strengthen ecosystem resilience.

Research Aim 

To develop evidence-based land management recommendations that maximise soil carbon sequestration, enhance soil biodiversity, and improve tree resilience across a diverse network of restored meadows, urban parks, wood pasture and forest landscapes. We would like to answer following questions:

1. How do different interventions influence ecosystem resilience, tree and soil health? 

2, Which soil microbial communities and processes are most strongly associated with carbon accumulation, nutrient cycling and ecosystem recovery under various management strategies? 

3. How can monitoring evidence be translated into practical land management decisions?

jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Why does prevalence of UTIs increase so substantially during the menopause? How do the hormonal changes associated with menopause come to affect competition between bacterial species in the unique flow conditions of the bladder and urethra? We hypothesise that menopause-associated changes in hormone signalling alter the urinary tract environment, disrupting the balance of microbial communities and their interactions with the host.

We will use an interdisciplinary approach, combining mathematical modelling, microfluidic lab-on-a-chip experiments with cells, and bioinformatics and genomics to study how cell signalling affects gene expression. In particular, we want to capture how microbial competition is communicated -how cells sense and respond to biochemical and mechanical signals from the same and other microbial species and those from the host environment. A further goalis to understand our role as scientists and sensors: how should microfluidic devices best be designed and deployed as sensors and emulators of disease?

Overview

Contact events, including player collisions and static exertions, define rugby union and set it apart from other field-based team sports. Despite their importance, practitioners have limited ability to accurately quantify contact training load and understand how it affects recovery, adaptation and injury risk. This creates significant challenges to those responsible for optimising performance, safeguarding player health and adhering to governing body training regulations in elite environments. This PhD project aims to advance our understanding of contact training load and its effects in professional rugby union.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in the Stefan Cross Centre for Women, Equality & Law
jobs.description_html:
Southampton University Law School invites applicants for a fully funded PhD studentship within the Stefan Cross Centre for Women, Equality and Law, commencing in September 2027.

The studentship runs for a period of three years and includes a stipend in line with UKRI levels (£21,805 in 2026/27, uprated annually) and tuition fees (UK/Overseas).

Southampton Law School is a global Law School, firmly rooted in the UK with a mission to respond to the greatest global challenges that humanity faces. We have a robust internationalisation agenda and as a Law School in a Russell Group University we are committed to research-driven legal education as well as engaged, innovative and impactful scholarship. Southampton Law School was ranked 15th in the U.K. according to the Complete University Guide 2027. It also came 16th in the UK in REF2021 for outputs. This places us in the top 25% of Law Schools in the UK, with 81% of all outputs submitted considered to be “world-leading” or “internationally excellent”. Our triple helix approach (people, education, research and enterprise) accentuates the value of our people and exemplifies our constant pursuit of solidarity and social cohesion among staff members, who comprise a diverse international cohort of renowned leading as well as early career researchers.

The Stefan Cross Centre for Women, Equality and Law is one of eight research centres which together serve as essential clusters for the achievement of our objectives. The centre was launched in 2018 with a generous donation from Southampton Law School alumnus, Mr Stefan Cross KC. The goal of the centre is to increase understanding and awareness of discrimination against women and girls, investigate the causes of this discrimination and seek effective solutions to gendered inequalities.

Successful applicants will be assigned two supervisors and will join the Stefan Cross Centre contributing to its objectives and continued success. They will be part of and help develop our vibrant PhD community.

We are keen to foster the Equality Law scholars of the next generation and are interested in proposals to work on legal topics related to women and equality in the broadest sense. We particularly welcome research proposals that address intersections of women’s equality and the law with the following areas:

  • employment
  • AI/new technologies
  • human rights
  • sustainability
  • criminal justice
  • equal pay

For an initial conversation regarding the Stefan Cross Studentship, please contact the Centre Manager; Susanne Berger, at: sb24@soton.ac.uk

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - The Role of Adaptive Evolution in the Microbial Sensing of Anthropogenic Molecules
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Introduction. There is now a realisation both in the public and scientific communities that discarded plastic materials present a growing hazard to the natural environment and human health across the globe. Here, a major concern is the release of molecular breakdown products that alter the biochemistry of the exposed organisms. Since microbial life is abundant in the natural environment, it is hypothesised that they will be the most significantly impacted by any such effects. However, it remains unclear as to how microbes sense the presence of such molecules, and whether they could be adapting their behaviour or evolving to enable the detection of these compounds.

Aims, Objectives and Methods. This project aims to investigate the biochemical and genetic changes that occur to these microbes upon exposure to various small molecule degradants of plastics. The technical objectives are thus the: (1) culturing of microbes in the presence of these compounds and the profiling of their growth behaviour; (2) transcriptomic analysis to identify which genes have been expressed; (3) proteomic DNA-binding analysis (e.g. reverse-ChIP) to identify the proteins that bind to the regulatory regions of differentially expressed genes (i.e. the transcription factors that are performing the molecular sensing of these compounds); and (4) validation of transcription factor function in a model microbe (E. coli).

Before you apply: Please contact the main project supervisor, Dr Wong, to learn more about the project and discuss whether it may be suitable for you.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B11 Learning the Changing Extremes of European Precipitation in a Warming Climate
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
One of the major challenges for the current and future climate diagnostics is the occurrence of very rare, but extreme intense precipitation events. Those record-shattering events lead to the Valencia-Flood in October 2024 in Spain or the Ahr-floods in July 2021 in Germany with billions of Euro of financial losses and unfortunately significant numbers of fatalities (cf. e.g., Leckebusch & McCarthy (2026) and references therein).

While the principal underlying physical mechanism of precipitation formation and the principal mechanisms of necessary precursor conditions are well understood, the exact amount of extreme precipitation and when and where those events may occur are less well understood. The same holds true for the principal rate of occurrence, which is difficult to estimate as those events may occur only once or twice per century in the current climate. Even more difficult is an assessment of those events for future climate conditions, altered by human activities. We can already diagnose that those events are more likely to occur under the influence of a warming climate, but the exact changes in those statistics of their occurrence remains a challenge. One of the reasons for this is the inability of current climate models to fully simulate those rare and extreme precipitation events in their full characteristics, from very local scale processes to the wider statistical occurrences for e.g., 30-years climatic time spans.

This project will develop and test a novel approach to estimate those rare events. It will investigate whether a combination of AI- and Extreme Value Theory (EVT)-approaches can produce reliable estimates for future climate states. Thus, can AI–EVT models trained on reanalyses and large hindcast ensembles estimate regional extreme-rainfall distributions that remain reliable when transferred between global warming levels and circulation regimes?

This project would best suit a student with a Computer Science background, or otherwise a numerical background for example Meteorology, Physics, or Maths, with experience coding in Python or similar (e.g. R, Matlab), and preferably with some experience in AI approaches.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Radicals and Reactive Intermediates in Heavy Main-Group Chemistry
jobs.description_html:
This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is October 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

A fully funded PhD studentship is available for a highly motivated, outstanding chemist with a passion for inorganic synthesis and spectroscopy.

Heavy pnictogen compounds have received considerable attention in recent years as competent reagents for two-electron redox chemistry and the activation of small molecules. In comparison, the area of heavy main-group radical compounds remains relatively underdeveloped. Their electronic structures are typically affected by strong spin-orbit coupling effects, leading to fascinating spectroscopic features and reactivities. The capability of heavy main-group elements to stabilise open-shell fragments in their vicinity remains equally underexplored but holds great promise for the development of atom-transfer reactions with small molecules.

In this PhD project, we aim to access open-shell main-group species either by redox reactions (authentic main-group radicals) or via the formation of open-shell fragments (carbenes, nitrenes and higher homologues) in their direct vicinity. The electronic structures of the synthesised compounds will be elucidated by spectroscopy, and reactivity studies towards small molecules will be conducted. This will require the appointed student to undertake inorganic synthesis (Schlenk and glovebox techniques), followed by characterisation using a range of spectroscopic and analytical techniques (NMR, IR, UV/vis, EPR, SQUID, XAS and scXRD). The focus at the start of the project will be on bismuth chemistry, but extension towards other heavy elements, e.g., antimony, tin, lead, indium or thallium, will be targeted based on the results obtained.

In addition to training in the above techniques, the student will receive training in scientific writing, oral and poster presentations, lab management, lab safety and other transferable skills. The student will benefit from co-supervision by experts in inorganic synthesis and magnetism. The project offers opportunities for publication in leading international journals, presentation of results at national and international conferences, and collaboration with researchers across the UK and Europe.
This project is expected to start in late September / early October 2027.

Eligibility

Applicants should hold, or expect to obtain, a First Class or high Upper Second Class degree in Chemistry or a closely related discipline. Prior experience with synthetic chemistry under inert conditions is essential, while experience in spectroscopy of paramagnetic compounds is advantageous but not required.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor, Dr. Josh Abbenseth. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B13 Health Risks from Individual and Synergistic Heat and Air Pollution under Climate Change
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Extreme heat and air pollution are among the leading environmental threats to human health. They frequently occur together, yet their health impacts are still commonly assessed independently. This is important because simultaneous exposure may produce health effects greater than expected from either hazard alone. As climate change intensifies heat extremes and alters patterns of PM2.5 and ozone, understanding these interacting risks is increasingly important for climate adaptation, air-quality management and public-health protection.

Our recent analysis across England and Wales provides compelling evidence of this interaction. In London, when temperature and PM2.5 simultaneously exceeded their 97.5th percentiles, the relative risk of all-cause mortality reached 1.51, with a relative excess risk due to interaction of 0.33. Synergistic effects were particularly strong for respiratory mortality, while older adults and females showed greater susceptibility (Fig. 1). Importantly, applying London’s higher absolute PM2.5 thresholds to other regions revealed similar synergistic effects where sufficient co-exposure occurred, suggesting that interactions may become especially important once pollution exceeds critical concentrations.

These findings raise an urgent wider question: how important are synergistic heat–air-pollution health risks globally, and how will they change as the climate warms? Existing studies have examined historical interactions or projected future compound events, but a globally consistent framework linking observed synergistic mortality effects with future climate and air-pollution change is currently missing.

This studentship will address this gap through four linked objectives:

  • Establish how heat, PM2.5 and ozone have individually and synergistically affected mortality across different regions and vulnerable populations.
  • Determine how the frequency, intensity and geographical distribution of compound heat–air-pollution events will change under future climate and emission scenarios.
  • Quantify future mortality attributable specifically to synergistic exposure and determine where conventional single-hazard assessments underestimate health risks.
  • Evaluate the health benefits and economic implications of alternative climate and air-quality mitigation strategies.

By connecting observed health responses with emerging CMIP7 projections, the project will provide a global assessment of compound heat–air-pollution risks from the past through the twenty-first century. It will identify emerging hotspots and vulnerable populations and establish where integrated climate and air-quality interventions can deliver the greatest public-health benefits.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B01 Can a Tree Remember a Drought? Understanding the Mechanisms of Tree Memory
jobs.description_html:
Trees are long living, sessile organisms that represent a fundamental component of most of earth ecosystems. Being immobile during their life, trees need to efficiently adapt to changes of environment and to stresses, in order to reach maturity and reproduction.

Recent advanced in genomics studies are always more convincingly showing that environmental information can be recorded at molecular level on DNA through epigenetic marks. Epigenetics studies molecular changes of DNA (mostly DNA methylation) in response to developmental or environmental stimuli, which does not involve a change of the DNA sequence itself. These changes can be inherited during cell division and are particular stable in plants, where they represent the base of an epigenetic “memory”, which remains encoded in biological tissues and can be transmitted to progenies.

In trees, wood is produced by plant cells that lignified and die to provide physical functions such as of mechanical support, storage and water conduction. However, part of their DNA is preserved unaltered, and retains the epigenetic information encoded in the cells in the moment they died. In temperate zones, most trees produce in their wood one growth-ring each year, so that the entire period of a tree’s life remain impressed in its wood material. As wood growth is affected by environmental conditions, trees have marks of past interactions with the environment recorded into their wood as they grow, at both physical and molecular level. However, while physical propriety of tree rings is well investigated, the possible epigenetic changes associated to the residual DNA in different rings re.

This project aims to understand how trees use environmental information to adapt to a changing condition. This will be done by extracting DNA from different parts of tree rings and compare their epigenetic profiles. The PhD researcher will compare the DNA methylation from different tree rings and associate epigenetic changes to historical and ecological record of drought. This will allow to connect tree molecular and physical responses to the environment in in tree rings, creating for the first time a direct connection among dendrochronology, ecology and epigenetic data in trees.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B05 Novel Ways to Deal with the Complexities of Detecting Selection for Antimicrobial Resistance under Realistic Natural Conditions
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major public health threat. The environment plays an important role as resistant microorganisms are transmitted between people and animals through the environment; they also survive or thrive there and exchange genes.

One of the big debates is whether the low concentrations of antibiotics in the environment are selecting for resistance.

One approach to experimentally test this is to compete a ‘special pair’ of sensitive and resistant bacteria at a range of antibiotic concentrations in the lab, where their only difference is resistance so they share the same ecological niche. This is an accurate and sensitive method, but the conditions in the lab do not mimic the environment.

An alternative approach is to bring a complex sample from the environment into the lab and measure whether resistance genes are increasing at different antibiotic concentrations. This would seem to mimic the environment as a diverse community of bacteria is used, but the inevitable shifts in microbial community composition when incubating in rich media can result in increased resistance levels in the absence of selection.

We have a different idea, to use mathematical models based on results from simple lab experiments and then create the complexity in the model by including the effects of diversity, predation, low substrate concentrations etc, ultimately predicting at which concentration selection happens in the environment and also understanding the effects of the complications. This will be coupled with experiments under natural conditions to test and validate the model, in flume mesocosms that can mimic river conditions in the lab at UKCEH Wallingford and also in situ in rivers. For this, we will put the special pair in ‘cages’ (dialysis bags) so they cannot escape but are immersed in the environment and experience the same nutrient concentrations etc. as the other bacteria in the surrounding environment.

Such a validated mathematical model that can predict the risk of selection under environmental conditions is hugely important because it is impossible to expose thousands of different pathogenic and environmental bacteria with various (combinations) of resistances to many levels of hundreds of potentially selective antibiotics and other compounds under a variety of relevant environmental conditions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B04 Microbial Degradation of Trace Gases in Post-wildfire Soils
jobs.description_html:
Background

Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity in many regions as a consequence of climate change1. In addition to releasing large quantities of carbon dioxide, wildfires generate atmospheric trace gases including carbon monoxide (CO), methane (CH₄) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs)2,3. The fate of these gases after deposition to soils is poorly understood, despite the potential importance of microbial trace-gas oxidation for atmospheric chemistry, soil carbon cycling and ecosystem recovery.

Wildfire substantially alters soil physicochemical properties and microbial communities through the loss and transformation of organic matter, formation of pyrogenic carbon, changes in pH and nutrient availability, and alterations in soil moisture and structure. These changes may strongly influence the capacity of soil microbial communities to consume atmospheric trace gases. Early studies have shown that organic amendments can increase soil atmospheric methane uptake in agricultural soils4. However, we lack a mechanistic understanding of how wildfire severity and post-fire recovery affect microbial trace-gas oxidation.

This PhD will investigate how wildfire alters the capacity of soils to act as microbial sinks for atmospheric trace gases and whether this function can be enhanced during ecosystem recovery. It will examine interactions between fire severity, soil properties, pyrogenic carbon and trace-gas-oxidising microbial communities.

The research will employ a combination of gas measurements, soil mesocosm, and cutting-edge molecular techniques. DNA sequencing and metagenomic analyses will identify functional genes responsible for trace gas oxidation. Mesocosm experiments will test the effects of organic amendments on microbial activity and trace gas consumption, providing critical data on soil recovery and greenhouse gas mitigation.

Overall outputs:

The project will establish how wildfire affects soil trace-gas consumption and identify the microbial and environmental mechanisms underpinning this process. It will generate datasets linking fire severity, soil properties, microbial community composition and trace-gas oxidation, and provide a platform for future research on microbial ecosystem services and restoration of soil biogeochemical functions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B02 Microbial Lipid Cycling in the Oceans: An Integrated ‘Omics’ Approach
jobs.description_html:
Lipids, containing carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur, are a major component of all living cells and are constantly released into the oceans due to programmed cell death, viral infections and zooplankton grazing. Current estimates suggest that lipids can account for 10% of total dissolved organic matter (DOC) in the oceans. However, our knowledge on microbial lipid transformation in the oceans is very limited. Neither the identities of the microbes involved, nor the mechanisms by which lipids are degraded, have been well understood.

A major hurdle in understanding the microbial lipid cycle lies in the difficulty in characterizing and quantifying numerous lipid classes in marine samples. Commonly observed lipids in marine ecosystems include phospholipids, glycolipids and amino acid-containing lipids. Recent advances in technologies such as liquid chromatography electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS) has enabled high throughput identification and quantification of thousands of cellular lipid molecular species (Shevchenko, 2010), which now enables lipid characterization both qualitatively and quantitatively. Indeed, lipidomics is starting to complement the rapid progress made in genomics, metagenomics, transcriptomics and proteomics.

Here in this project, we will combine laboratory and filed based methodologies to fully uncover the lipid cycle in marine waters. The aim of this project is thus twofold:

Firstly, we aim to establish a high throughput workflow for simultaneous determination of common lipids species in marine surface waters using our in house HPLC MS platform. This will involve examining samples from the Western English Channel, collected via the Marine Biological Association research vessel, Sepia.

Secondly, we aim to determine the identity and activity of key microbial populations in the recycling of representative lipids in marine surface waters and coastal marine sediment using integrated omics approach, e.g. high throughput sequencing of 16S/18S rRNA, metagenomics, metagenomics and lipidomics.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship Engineering - Chemical Probes to Sense Dynamic Molecular Neighbourhoods in Living Cells
jobs.description_html:

The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

How can we measure the fleeting molecular neighbourhoods that control signalling inside living cells?

Proximity-labelling methods provide a powerful way to address this problem by converting spatial proximity into a permanent chemical tag that can subsequently be detected by imaging or proteomics. However, current approaches face an important trade-off: the reactive chemistry needed to generate a measurable signal can perturb sensitive biological systems, while the spatial reach of labelling is difficult to control. This project will develop a new generation of chemically engineered proximity probes that act as tuneable molecular sensors of local cellular environments.

The student will design and synthesise new probe molecules whose chemical and physical properties are systematically varied to control their behaviour during proximity labelling. Combining synthetic chemistry with biochemical and cellular experiments, the project will establish how molecular structure determines key sensing properties including labelling efficiency, biological compatibility and spatial precision. Preliminary work from the supervisory team supports the feasibility of this concept while leaving substantial scope for fundamental discovery and technology development.

The project will progress through three linked stages. First, the student will create and characterise a focused library of new proximity-labelling probes and establish relationships between chemical structure and probe behaviour. Second, promising probes will be evaluated in living cells using biochemical assays, advanced fluorescence imaging and super-resolution microscopy to determine how accurately and efficiently they report local molecular neighbourhoods. Finally, selected probes will be applied to biologically challenging systems in which conventional proximity labelling can itself perturb the processesbeing studied. Proteomic analysis will be used selectively to identify the molecular networks revealed by the new sensing platform.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Mechanochromic Molecules for Cellular Forces Sensing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Tensile forces influence a variety of important cellular processes including cell division, stem cell differentiation and gene expression.

  1. At the tissue level these forces play a crucial role in morphogenesis, wound healing, the immune response and in pathological processes such as cancer metastasis. However, our understanding of how force influences cell function is very limited due to a lack of techniques to measure force within live tissue. To date, genetically encoded tension sensors have been developed, but their use in whole tissues has so far been limited. One reason for this limited use is the low sensitivity of current in vivo tension sensors. At the molecular level, the unique ability of mechanical force to distort, bend and stretch chemical bonds has led to the development of mechanochromic molecules acting as spatially sensitive molecular probes or micro-crack sensors in synthetic materials.
  2. Chemical mechanosensors offer a potentially powerful solution to this problem but have yet to be translated into biological systems. Here we will take a multidisciplinary approach to bridge this gap and aim to develop and test novel chemical force sensors suitable for measuring tensile forces at cellular/tissue level.

The goals of this project are:

  • The creation of new mechanochromophores that can be used as force sensors in a biological context
  • Determine how physicochemical parameters influence mechanochromophore activation and fluorescence.
  • Demonstrate the performance of selected mechanochromophores using human cells as a biological model system.

The postgraduate researcher (PGR) will be trained by means of a training-through-research model by:

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Treatment Planning of FLASH Delivery of Cancer Therapy with Focussed Very High Energy Electron Beams
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. The global burden of cancer continues to increase, with more than 500,000 new cases predicted annually in the UK by 2040. Radiotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment, but irradiation of healthy tissue surrounding or traversed by the tumour remains a significant limitation. Very High Energy Electron (VHEE) radiotherapy offers substantial penetration and may complement existing photon and particle therapies. Combining VHEE with ultra-high dose-rate (UHDR) delivery, including FLASH dose rates, could further exploit physical and biological advantages.

This project will investigate treatment planning and focused VHEE delivery in the FLASH regime. Methods will include Monte Carlo modelling of beam transport and dose deposition, treatment-plan optimisation, analysis of dose distributions, and evaluation of parameters influencing healthy-tissue sparing and target coverage. Computational results will, where appropriate, be compared with experimental dosimetry and existing radiotherapy data. Outcomes will include improved understanding of VHEE dose deposition and assessment of focused FLASH-VHEE delivery for future clinical translation.

The student will receive interdisciplinary supervision from the Faculty of Science and Engineering and School of Medical Sciences, with training in Monte Carlo methods, radiation transport, treatment planning, optimisation, dosimetry, data analysis and scientific computing, supported by cross-faculty expertise and wider postgraduate research training.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Phase-optimised PUFA Production in Oleaginous Yeast via Transcriptomics-Guided Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Modelling
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

We hypothesise that defining empirical reaction-specific translational efficiency operators (TE = [E]/mRNA) within phase-specific ecGSMMs will enable resource-balanced cassette design and allow inference of enzyme abundances from RNA-seq data alone in subsequent iterations. Combined with genomic information and genome-scale modelling, this framework will predict production efficiency and identify phase-optimised targets.

The project will:

  • Estimate the mRNA expression levels required to achieve desired increases in reaction capacity.
  • Categorise transcriptionally versus translationally bottlenecked genes under nitrogen limitation.
  • Deliver predictive models of PUFA production efficiency across selected oleaginous yeasts.

Methodology (DBTL)

Design & Build

Round 1: Curate a library of native phase-responsive promoters from selected oleaginous yeasts (examples include Yarrowia lipolytica, Rhodotorula toruloides or Lipomyces starkeyi). Characterise promoter kinetics using RNA light-up aptamers. Subsequent rounds will design phase-specific expression cassettes informed by modelling outputs and assemble them using modular cloning toolkits appropriate to the chosen host(s).

Test

Perform controlled fermentations under exponential and nitrogen-limited conditions. Measure process kinetics, lipid titres (GC-MS), phase-resolved RNA-seq and LC-MS proteomics to calibrate TE operators. Later rounds will rely primarily on RNA-seq and process data. Genomic data (genome sequences, annotations and comparative analyses) will support model construction and strain selection.

Learn

Apply enzyme-constrained flux scanning based on enforced objective flux (ecFSEOF) and kinetic flux control coefficient analysis on protein-constrained GSMMs to identify systemic pathway demands and kinetic bottlenecks. Verify protein headroom for overexpression. In subsequent iterations, infer enzyme states from TE operators and new RNA-seq data, rank rate-limiting constraints via dual variables, and update models to guide further engineering. Genome-scale models will explicitly predict production efficiency (titre, yield and rate) under different genetic and process scenarios

Focussing on the international flower trade, where temperature and spatial control are essential to preserving flower quality across borders, we will assess how proposed future autonomous systems alter the social perception and material footprint of this complicated delivery process.

The focus of this PhD studentship will begin with road haulage, examining the transition from traditional cold chain trucks to new autonomous long-haul provisions. Wholesalers, truckers, grocery stores, and high street florists form a set of interviewees to explore the unintended consequences, with the goal to both understand the social cost of proposed transitions and the unintended consequences of proposed efficiencies.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Terahertz Photons for Quantum Control and Topological Quantum Information
jobs.department: Physics and Astronomy, Mathematical and Physical Sciences (MAPS)
jobs.description_html:
Principal supervisor name: Arijeet Pal

Principal supervisor UCL profile website: https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/66876-arijeet-pal 

Funding: Maintenance stipend at UELA enhanced rate - rises each year (For 2026/27, the total stipend is expected to be £26,022, i.e. £1,500 above the UKRI London-weighted rate of £24,522)

Project summary

Terahertz (THz) frequencies occupy a largely unexplored regime for quantum technologies, bridging conventional microwave quantum circuits and optical platforms. The energy of a THz photon naturally matches important excitations in quantum materials, including cyclotron transitions, collective modes and Landau-level excitations. This PhD project will investigate how quantum states of THz radiation can be used to manipulate matter at the single- and few-photon level and, ultimately, to engineer robust qubits based on topological quantum states.

A central direction will be the strong and ultrastrong coupling of confined THz photons to two-dimensional electron systems in high magnetic fields. In the quantum Hall regime, coupling cyclotron and collective electronic excitations to THz cavity modes produces hybrid light–matter states known as Landau polaritons. The project will develop theoretical models for controlling these states using shaped THz pulses, cavity engineering and nonlinear interactions. We will investigate whether individual polaritonic excitations can constitute effective two-level systems and determine how their coherence, interactions and readout could be optimised.

A more ambitious objective is to explore whether THz cavities can manipulate or mediate interactions between topological excitations in integer and fractional quantum Hall states. In particular, the project will investigate cavity induced interactions, photon-mediated coupling between spatially separated edge or bulk excitations, and protocols for creating and controlling entangled states. An important question will be whether coupling to THz photons can provide new routes towards protected quantum information processing, including manipulation of fractionalised excitations and candidate topological qubits.

The research will combine quantum optics, condensed-matter theory and numerical modelling of driven open quantum systems, with close connections to experimentally achievable THz cavities and quantum materials. It will establish the opportunities †and fundamental limits- of THz photons as a new resource for quantum control and topological quantum technologies.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Mineral–Fluid–Rock Interactions for Sustainable Subsurface Energy Technologies
jobs.description_html:
Subsurface geological formations play a vital role in supporting the energy transition, including geothermal energy extraction, geological CO₂ storage and underground energy storage. The performance and long-term integrity of these systems are strongly influenced by interactions between fluids, minerals and fractured rocks. Understanding these coupled processes is therefore essential for developing safe, efficient and sustainable subsurface energy technologies.

This interdisciplinary PhD project will investigate fundamental mineral–fluid–rock interactions, with particular emphasis on mineral crystallisation, interfacial processes and their relationships with the hydraulic and mechanical behaviour of fractured rocks. The research will integrate environmental geochemistry and mineral–water interface science with experimental rock mechanics and fracture characterisation. Depending on the expertise and background of the successful candidate, specific investigations may include mineral nucleation and crystal growth, mineral–surface interactions, geochemical reactions in confined environments, and the evolution of fracture properties under coupled chemical and physical processes.

The project is jointly supervised by researchers at The University of Manchester and Peking University, bringing together complementary expertise in environmental geochemistry, mineral crystallisation, rock mechanics and subsurface engineering. The successful candidate will receive interdisciplinary research training and gain access to complementary experimental and analytical capabilities at both institutions.

The PhD follows a 1+2+1 structure, with Years 1 and 4 based at The University of Manchester and Years 2-3 at Peking University. Applications are welcomed from candidates with backgrounds in environmental engineering, geoscience, geochemistry, chemical engineering, civil engineering or related disciplines.

Manchester entry is open to UK and international students. Chinese nationals from Mainland China, Taiwan, Macau and Hong Kong, including dual nationals, should apply through Peking.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Developing Density Functional Approximations for Accurate Modelling of Magnetic Organic Conjugated Systems
jobs.description_html:
Density functional theory (DFT) has become the most widely employed approach for electronic structure calculations, with broad applications spanning chemistry, physics, biology, materials science, and related fields. The accuracy of DFT predictions is however limited by the approximations inherent in existing density functional approximations (DFAs), that can lead to deviations from experimental observations or even erroneous interpretations. These limitations are particularly pronounced in the study of organic conjugated systems displaying magnetism. In this project, we aim to develop an advanced DFA with enhanced accuracy for such challenging systems. The newly developed DFA will be applied to investigate how spin can be used to control light emission or electric conductance.

Manchester entry is open to UK and international students. Chinese nationals from Mainland China, Taiwan, Macau and Hong Kong, including dual nationals, should apply through Peking.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Mapping the nanoscale architecture of T cell sensing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Immune cells continuously patrol the body to maintain health. Central to this process is their ability to sense environmental cues and respond appropriately. When T cells engage antigen-presenting cells (APCs), they simultaneously encounter numerous stimulatory, co-stimulatory, inhibitory, and adhesive signals at specialised contact sites known as immune synapses. Growing evidence suggests that the nanoscale spatial organisation of these molecular cues plays a critical role in determining how T cells interpret and integrate information.

The nanoscale architecture of the immune synapse, including how receptors and their ligands cluster, segregate, and reorganise in space and time, varies substantially depending on the combination of signals present. Because signalling output appears to depend as much on this spatial organisation as on ligand identity itself, the same receptor may generate distinct downstream responses depending on the nanoscale context in which it is engaged. Understanding immune signalling therefore requires not only identifying the molecular components involved but also determining how these components are wired into functional signalling circuits.

This project will directly address this challenge by combining a synthetic antigen-presenting cell platform with state-of-the-art nanoscale molecular mapping technologies. Engineered APCs displaying bioorthogonal click-biology handles will be used to present precisely defined combinations of peptide-MHC complexes, co-stimulatory receptors, co-inhibitory receptors, and integrin ligands at controlled surface densities. These programmable cells will provide an unprecedented ability to manipulate the composition and organisation of immune synapses. Using a combination of super-resolution imaging and photocatalytic proximity-labelling approaches, the student will generate detailed molecular maps of synapse architecture and determine how distinct combinations of extracellular cues are translated into intracellular signalling outcomes.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: PhD Studentships in Engineering Solutions for Antimicrobial Resistance (Fully funded/ Four-Year)
jobs.description_html:
Fully funded four-year PhD studentships in Engineering Solutions for Antimicrobial Resistance at UCL.

Applications are now open for four-year PhD studentships at the EPSRC and BBSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Engineering Solutions for Antimicrobial Resistance at University College London, starting in October 2027.

About the programme

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a complex challenge that must be tackled on multiple fronts. It requires people who can work across government, industry and research disciplines—from microbiology and antimicrobial chemistry to building engineering.

Our interdisciplinary programme trains the next generation of academic, industry and public-sector leaders to develop and coordinate engineering solutions to AMR

Alongside your PhD research, you will join a bespoke cohort training programme covering the AMR context, research translation, entrepreneurship, science communication, research integrity and more. Our external partners range from innovative SMEs to government agencies and global industry leaders. Explore our training programme and partner network.

Explore our research projects

We offer PhD projects across our three research themes:

  • Preventing Infections
  • Diagnostics and Surveillance
  • Novel Therapies

Explore the available projects for 2027 entry. You will indicate your project preferences when applying, and successful applicants will be matched with a suitable project before an offer is made.

Who can apply

You should hold, or expect to obtain, a UK Master’s degree with Merit or a minimum upper second-class UK Bachelor’s degree in a relevant discipline, or an overseas qualification of an equivalent standard.

Relevant work experience may be considered. Relevant subjects include physics, chemistry, engineering, biology, mathematics and related sciences.

Funding

UKRI-funded studentships are open to UK (home) and international applicants. The number of places available to international applicants is limited. Offers to international applicants are conditional on a tuition-fee waiver being agreed by the university hosting the project.

Meet the CDT

Join one of our virtual open days in October or November to learn about the programme and ask questions about the application and interview process.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Interdisciplinary Methods for Liquid Crystal-Based Biosensing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Liquid crystals (LCs) are exceptionally versatile and functional mesophases that combine fluidity with the ordering of solids. LCs have tremendous potential as low-cost and non-invasive bio-sensors and have been used to sense glucose, proteins, enzymes, cells, micromolecules etc. In this project, we will use mathematical modelling, ex-vivo (laboratory) and in-silico experiments to quantify the fundamental interactions between LCs and prototype cells. This will address open questions on - (i) how interfacial LC- cell interactions induce reorientation and structural changes in LCs and (ii) how these changes can be used to produce quantifiable signals. These signals can be used for sensing different types of cells, for detecting infected cells and for targeted drug delivery. The project has four core objectives incorporated into work packages (WP) at the interface of mathematical modelling, mechanics, machine learning and laboratory experiments, as listed below.

[1] WP I: Develop novel mathematical models for LC interactions with soft flexible surfaces, representative of human tissue;

[2] WP II: perform benchmark experiments on how LCs interact with epithelial tissue and cells;

[3] WPIII: validate and refine models with experimental data and

[4] WPIII: develop neural networks/machine learning tools for translation of LC outputs to sensing applications, e.g. in digital diagnostics and healthcare.

These WPs will set up a paradigmatic framework for the design of LC biosensors with bespoke properties.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Uranium and Thorium in Arene-Trigonal-Donor Environments
jobs.description_html:
Metal-ligand multiple bonding is a burgeoning area for making chemically novel structural motifs, probing chemical bonding, and being applied to catalysis, some of which defines the state-of-the-art in element bond forming reactions. Most metal-ligand multiple bonds involve transition metals, but in recent years we have advanced f-element, and in particular actinide, metal-ligand multiple bonding by realising unprecedented bonding combinations (e.g. Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 7136; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 137, e202419987; Nat. Chem. 2024, 16, 780-790; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2024, 146, 4098-4111; Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 4657; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 21766-21784; Nat. Chem. 2022, 14, 342-349; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 9764-9774; Nat. Commun. 2021, 12, 5649; Nat. Commun. 2021, 12, 4832; Nat. Commun. 2020, 11, 337). Nevertheless, there are still many actinide-ligand multiple bonds whose synthesis and in-depth characterisation would represent major milestones.

Building on recent preliminary results confirming the utility of a new ligand class in f-element chemistry, this PhD will target the synthesis of unprecedented actinide-ligand multiple bonds and explore their characterisation through in-depth experimental (reactivity, spectroscopic, magnetic) and computational (single- and multi-reference methods) characterisation.

The successful applicant will be a highly motivated, outstanding chemist ready to undertake research in the field of actinide synthesis, structural, spectroscopic, magnetic, and computational characterisation.

In addition to the wide range of transferable skills developed during a PhD, the appointed researcher will learn and use: (i) Schlenk and glove box techniques; (ii) characterisation methods, e.g. crystallography, NMR, IR, Raman, UV/Vis/NIR, and EPR spectroscopies, magnetometry, XAS/XANES/RIXS, and quantum chemical calculations; (iii) reactivity studies supported by analytical characterisation and modelling methods.

You will benefit from a joint supervisory team that comprises Prof. Liddle (Manchester, synthesis), Dr Baker (Manchester, XAS/XANES/RIXS), Prof. Jiang (Peking, computational), and Prof. Huang (Peking, synthesis), and also experience the diverse cultures and opportunities that come from living in the two vibrant cities that are Manchester and Beijing.

Manchester entry is open to UK and international students. Chinese nationals from Mainland China, Taiwan, Macau and Hong Kong, including dual nationals, should apply through Peking.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Sensing Urban Heat: Integrating Bicycle-Based Measurements, Local Climate Modelling and Spatial Optimisation
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Sound is fundamental to how people sense, interpret and respond to the world. Yet hearing needs vary between individuals because ear-canal geometry, hearing ability and the sounds that are most important for communication vary from person to person. This PhD will develop a new type of 3D-printed metal structure, i.e. the next generation of additively manufactured metallic acoustic metamaterials, that can shape and amplify specific sounds, particularly those important for human communication. The aim is not to build a complete hearing aid but to create a key functional component that could improve future hearing technologies.

The project will establish a human-informed inverse-design framework. Information about ear-canal geometry and speech-relevant sounds will be used as design inputs. Mathematical and computational models will then optimise metallic metamaterial architectures for targeted wave compression and pressure amplification. The resulting structures will be manufactured by additive manufacturing (AM) or 3D printing, enabling compact, geometrically complex metallic components that cannot be produced using conventional methods. Dimensional metrology, materials characterisation and acoustic testing will quantify manufacturing accuracy and functional performance. The measured data will be fed back into the models to understand how AM-induced deviations affect acoustic response and to improve subsequent designs. Artificial-ear models and acoustic sensors will be used to quantify performance and determine how manufacturing deviations affect acoustic responses.

The project brings together expertise from engineering, applied mathematics, acoustics and hearing science. The student will receive training in acoustic-wave modelling, numerical optimisation, metamaterial design, AM, process monitoring, metrology, materials characterisation, acoustic measurement, psychoacoustic experimental design, research ethics and data analysis. The project will operate through an iterative human-input, design, make, measure and perceive cycle, providing the student with an unusually broad and integrated research skill set.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Metal-Organic Framework Materials for Gas Adsorption and Catalysis
jobs.description_html:
There is increasing concern over global air quality, with high concentrations of smog posing significant health risks and environmental problems worldwide. SO2 and NOx are important components in smog causing significant respiratory disease. There is therefore an ever-increasing demand for sorbent materials that can capture SO2 and NOx in order to mitigate emissions. However, this is a very challenging target since SO2 and NO2 are highly corrosive and reactive and most materials are not sufficiently stable. Despite their widespread and successful use in separations of gases such as N2, CO2, CH4 and other small molecules, MOF materials that reversibly bind SO2 and NO2 are extremely rare. Recently, our project team has discovered a number of porous Cu-, Al- and Zn-based MOFs that exhibit unprecedented performance for SO2 and NO2 capture, demonstrating record high SO2 and NO2 selectivity, uptake capacity and storage density. Part of our research results have been recently published (Nature Materials, 2018, 17, 691-696; Nature Materials, 2019, 18, 1358-1366; Nature Chemistry, 2019, 11, 1085-1090; Nature Review Chemistry, 2019, 3, 108-118; Figure 1) and highlighted in CNN News as a breakthrough technology for a clean air. This represents a unique and very timely opportunity to study SO2 and NOx chemistry within MOF materials. The PhD project aims to support the systematic investigation of the adsorption, binding, phase behaviour, electronic structure, release, and separation of gases in a series of stable MOFs with robust framework structures and decorated pore environments. Our extensive experience in handling corrosive gases in MOFs will (i) enable their evaluation as emerging sorbents for adsorptive removal of air pollutants; (ii) afford key insights into the design of new MOFs with improved stability and gas binding properties. The project will provide an excellent training environment for the PhD student at National Facilities Worldwide. Of particular interest will be the capture of SO2 and NOx at low partial pressures using narrow pored, microporous materials, reflecting the relatively low concentration of these gases in flue emissions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Advanced Energy Materials for Bright and Efficient Optoelectronic Devices
jobs.description_html:
How to apply: 

About 20% of the world’s electricity production is used for lighting and powering our displays, which account for 6% of the world’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Organic Light-Emitting Diodes (OLEDs) have a major role as energy-saving technology with applications in displays, solid-state lighting panels, wearable electronics, sensors, and virtual/mixed-reality displays. New advanced materials discoveries are highly required on multiple fronts to increase OLED devices' colour purity, device lifetime, and light output and reduce energy consumption.

The successful candidate will be supervised by Dr Alexander Romanov and Prof. Michael Turner at the University of Manchester (2 years) and Prof Zhiwei Liu at the College of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering Peking University (2 years). The project is part of a comprehensive programme exploring a new family of strongly photo-emissive coinage metal complexes based on carbene-metal-amide (or acetylides) and the doublet state-luminophores based on Ce(III) or Eu(II) complexes. These materials recently demonstrated excellent photoluminescent properties and are capable of producing OLEDs with high efficiency and operating stability (Advanced Materials, 2024, 36, 2306249; Advanced Materials, 2024, 36, 2404357; Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2408118; Adv. Func. Mat., 2025, e05661). The successful applicant will become a part of the established team at the University of Manchester and will work in collaboration with Peking University (Prof Zhiwei Liu). The post will involve substantial collaboration and would suit an ambitious, highly motivated and practical researcher with some experience in synthetic inorganic chemistry and/or organic materials chemistry. There will also be the opportunity to develop complementary skills in the photophysical characterisation and OLED device fabrications, therefore, an additional interest in materials science would be desirable. jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Synthetic Polymers to Stabilise Sensing Proteins into Membrane Nanodiscs
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Membrane proteins are essential components of cells, allowing them to sense and communicate across their outermost barrier. Ion channels translate chemical an physical signals into cellular responses and are consequently major therapeutic targets and candidates for incorporation into synthetic cells. However, studying membrane proteins is challenging because their structure and function depend on the surrounding lipid membrane. Conventional detergent-based extraction can disrupt this native environment, resulting in loss of protein activity or structure.

Amphiphilic polymers can directly excise nanoscale sections of cell membranes to form soluble “nanodiscs”, retaining membrane proteins together with their surrounding lipids. Styrene-maleic acid (SMA) polymers are widely used for this purpose but have significant limitations, including pH and ion sensitivity, low protein extraction efficiency and limited tunability for different transmembrane proteins.

This interdisciplinary PhD project will develop a new generation of chemically defined polymers for extracting and studying membrane proteins in native-like nanodiscs. The central objective is to determine how polymer structure controls membrane insertion, lipid extraction and nanodisc formation, and use these relationships to create materials that outperform conventional SMA polymers. Particular emphasis will be placed on extracting ion channels to understand how cells sense signals across their membranes.

The student will synthesise libraries of amphiphilic polymers in the Gibson group, using automated polymer synthesis to vary composition, hydrophobicity, charge and molecular weight. Polymers will be characterised using NMR spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and complementary analytical methods, then screened for membrane interaction, lipid extraction and stable nanodisc formation. Resulting structure–activity relationships will guide subsequent polymer design.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Sensing Soil Health: Linking Biological Indicators and Human Perceptions
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. Healthy soils underpin food production, biodiversity, climate resilience and ecosystem restoration[1]. Yet the biological processes that maintain soil health occur largely out of sight, making them difficult to monitor, interpret and communicate. Soil organisms such as earthworms and microorganisms respond rapidly to environmental change and are widely used as indicators of soil condition[2]. At the same time, gardeners, land managers and communities make decisions based on their own observations and experiences of soil[3]. Emerging environmental sensing technologies offer further opportunities to detect belowground processes that are otherwise hidden. However, little is known about how these different systems of sensing align, what aspects of soil condition they capture, and how they influence environmental decision-making. This project addresses the Sensing the World theme by investigating how biological , technological and human systems sense, interpret and respond to soil condition across urban environments.

Aim. To understand how different biological, technological and human sensing systems detect and interpret soil condition, and how these perspectives can be integrated to improve soil management, stewardship and public engagement.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Process Industries: Net Zero CDT: Energy and Resource Recovery from Spent Filters
jobs.description_html:
Overview

This PhD project is part of the EPSRC Process Industries: Net Zero (PINZ) Centre for Doctoral Training and is supported by PPT Filtercycle Ltd. The project aims to develop circular approaches to maximise the energy and resource value of spent filters, reduce material disposal, and minimise the environmental footprint of filtration processes. Its approach is to develop methodologies which can be usefully and quickly converted from pilot scale to operational for SME sites who otherwise may utilise broad waste management streams. This approach will consider bespoke solutions maximising the opportunity for reuse and recycle.

The project will consider the fuel capacity of combustible spent filters as a source of energy to safely separate other filter components for reuse. This will involve characterising different waste filter materials, investigating their composition, thermal properties and energy potential. Combustion behaviour, process safety and operational risks will be investigated to establish whether different filter materials can be safely incinerated, considering emissions and residue formation.

This primary investigation will facilitate the opportunity to investigate and develop the reuse and repurposing of spent filters to extend their useful life and reduce reliance on landfill for un-separated filter composite plus residue. All methodologies will be considered including cleaning and regeneration approaches.

The project will also investigate the recovery and utilisation of valuable inorganic components, particularly calcium-rich compounds, from filtration residues. These residues will be explored as potential feedstocks for CO2 capture through mineral carbonation. This will involve investigating material composition, recovery, carbonation kinetics, CO2 uptake, and the application of resulting carbonated products.

By transforming spent filters into energy and valuable materials, this project could help make industrial filtration more sustainable. The project will appeal to applicants in chemistry, chemical engineering, or materials science who are passionate to address real-world sustainability challenges.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: High-Performance Lanthanide Single-Molecule Magnets with Monodentate Ligands
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: 18/12/2026
Research theme: Synthetic molecular inorganic chemistry

This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded by the School of Natural Sciences; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is October 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

A University of Manchester-sponsored PhD studentship is available for an outstanding and ambitious chemist to undertake research in the field of synthetic inorganic chemistry in a collaborative project at Manchester Chemistry.

In this project we target molecular lanthanide single-molecule magnets (Ln SMMs). Recently at Manchester we have developed synthetic methodologies to prepare near-linear dysprosium SMMs bound by either one or two monodentate ligands (e.g. Nature 2025, 643, 125. DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09138-0; Nature Commun. 2026, 17, 10212. DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-77104-z). These compounds show the highest effective energy barriers to magnetic reversal and magnetic hysteresis temperatures of any SMM reported to date, with magnetic memory effects shown up to 100 Kelvin. Here we propose to extend this work by targeting dysprosium compounds with geometries closer to linearity and shorter metal-ligand distances, which are expected to show improved SMM properties.

The successful candidate, based in the laboratory of Prof. David Mills and co-supervised by Dr Michael Baker, will synthesise and fully characterise a novel, exciting series of highly air- and moisture-sensitive Ln compounds, and will deposit them on surfaces using a spin-coater. These compounds will be studied by a wide variety of techniques including single crystal and powder XRD, SQUID magnetometry, X-ray magnetocircular dichroism, and infrared, UV-visible absorption/emission, nuclear magnetic resonance, electron paramagnetic resonance and X-ray absorption spectroscopy, benchmarked by density functional theory and ab initio calculations. We will determine the relaxation times of Ln SMMs in different matrices as the necessary first step towards their application in devices.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor, Prof. David Mills. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Soft Robotics and Embodied Intelligence
jobs.department: Biomedical Science and Biomedical Engineering, School of Biological Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Project title: Emergence of embodied intelligence through bioelectrical learning in soft brain-body

Supervisors: Dr Yoshikatsu Hayashi (principal supervisor)

Project Overview

How can intelligence emerge when a brain and body interact, rather than being designed separately?

A new Leverhulme Trust-funded project at the University of Reading, led by Dr Yoshikatsu Hayashi, will explore how intelligence could emerge from interactions between soft materials, a robotic body and its environment.

In living organisms, the brain and body develop together through continuous sensory feedback, a principle known as embodiment. Neural communication fundamentally relies on the movement of charged particles called ions. Interestingly, ions also flow through water-rich hydrogels, where polymer networks can guide their movement. Could this provide a primitive form of electrical communication without neurons?

Previous research demonstrated that electroactive gels could improve their performance in the computer game Pong through feedback, suggesting that materials can exhibit adaptive behaviour without living neurons (https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-02704-y). Building on this discovery, the project will connect hydrogel networks to a soft robotic body, investigating whether ionic communication, rhythmic movement and sensory feedback can collectively generate adaptive behaviour.

By exploring how brain-like control and bodily movement might emerge together from physical matter, the research aims to uncover fundamental principles of Physical AI and inspire future generations of intelligent soft robots.

Training and development

You will develop skills in hydrogel fabrication, bioelectrical measurements, soft robotics, AI and feedback control, experimental design and data analysis. Working across materials science and biomedical engineering, you will gain experience connecting physical experiments with AI (Artificial Neural Networks) platform. You will benefit from the University’s bioengineering and movement laboratory facilities and the Reading Researcher Development Programme for doctoral and transferable skills training. The project will also provide opportunities to exchange ideas with international collaborators and develop scientific communication skills through presentations and outreach. 

Eligibility

  • Applicants should hold, or expect to gain, at least a UK 2:1 honours degree (or equivalent) in physical chemistry, robotics, mechanical/electronic engineering, physics, or a closely related discipline.
  • Interest in soft matter and soft robotics, control systems and interdisciplinary research is essential. Programming, experimental design/methods and data analysis experience are desirable.
  • Due to the nature of the funding this studentship is open candidates who qualify for Home/UK/Republic of Ireland fees.

Funding Details
