jobs.title: PhD Studentship: 3.5 Year PhD Studentship in Artificial Intelligence for Eliciting Patient Histories
jobs.description_html:
A 3.5 year PhD studentship in Artificial Intelligence for Eliciting Patient Histories, funded by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) UCLH Biomedical Research Centre, is available within the Institute of Health Informatics. The studentship will commence from 1 February 2027 under the supervisor of Professor Paul Taylor.

The PhD Project

Project Title: AI for Eliciting Patient Histories

The aim of this project is to understand how AI tools can be integrated into patient consultations to improve the quality of interaction between clinicians and patients. The consultation is the defining event in almost all episodes of care and remains one of the most important encounters in medical practice.

In recent years, consultations have begun to be transformed by the adoption of two distinct forms of technology. The first, AI scribes, aims to make consultations more patient-centred by automating administrative tasks. These tools record consultation audio, transcribe conversations, and generate summaries for clinicians to review before adding information to the patient record. The second technology, conversational agents or chatbots, provides a low-cost alternative to aspects of clinical consultations by eliciting information directly from patients.

The successful candidate will identify insights and frameworks from the literature on conventional clinical encounters, history-taking, and shared decision-making that are most relevant to the design of conversational agents.

The project will also develop and test AI-based approaches for analysing and assessing transcribed consultations. This work will provide an additional source of evidence on the characteristics of consultations and will enable testing of insights from the literature and exploration of more refined hypotheses, including the impact of factors such as age and gender.

Why Apply?

This PhD offers a unique collaboration between an AI start-up delivering cutting-edge technology, experienced AI researchers working in healthcare, and practising clinicians responsible for teaching communication skills to future doctors.

Applicants will be expected to contribute to teaching within the Institute of Health Informatics. The commitment is equivalent to approximately six months of teaching across the duration of the PhD.

This studentship provides an excellent opportunity to undertake supervised research at a world-leading institute, contribute to the development of AI technologies that enhance patient-centred care, and become part of a vibrant research community.

This award includes a starting stipend of £28,212 per annum and covers tuition fees at the UK (Home) rate. 

Personal Specification

Applicants should hold, or expect to obtain, an upper second-class Bachelor’s degree and a Master’s degree (or equivalent work experience) in a relevant discipline or possess an overseas qualification of an equivalent standard.

Eligibility

The studentship covers tuition fees at the UK (Home) rate. Applicants from outside the UK are welcome to apply but will be required to fund the difference between the UK (Home) and overseas tuition fee rates if they are not eligible for Home fee status.

Important: Applicants will be asked about their likely fee status during the interview process. Those unsure of their eligibility should seek advice from the UCL Graduate Admissions Office. Further information on fee status assessment is available through UCL and UKCISA guidance .

How to Apply

  2. A one-page A4 cover letter.

Applications should be sent to Professor Paul Taylor at p.taylor@ucl.ac.uk.

This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This PhD will contribute to an ongoing programme of work using quantum sensing to investigate the interaction between biological cells and electric fields. The underlying hypothesis is that precisely controlled electric fields may be able to modulate intracellular trafficking, and as a result improve the delivery of therapeutic agents into cells. This will allow “Electro-Therapeutics”, and potentially ultimately wearable units that monitor health related parameters and modulate electric fields to help direct therapeutics in a closed loop manner. This PhD will focus on creating electronics platforms to support the work and to enable in-vitro and in-vivo testing of proposed approaches.

Research will focus on electronic circuit design at the discrete component and embedded microcontroller levels for DC–1 GHz operation. This includes PCB design, fabrication, and testing. Suitable training in these techniques will be provided as required. Ideally, we aim for miniaturised, physically flexible electronic circuits. Fabrication will explore commercial Kapton substrates before potentially moving on to printed electronics approaches. The ideal applicant will have a background in electronic circuit design, and an interest performing their own printing to manufacture designs.

This is a cross-disciplinary project, and the PhD student will work closely with researchers in pharmacy to define system needs and to test different approaches. There will be the opportunity to be involved with both in-vitro and in-vivo testing of the developed electronics. The student will be exposed to state of the art approaches in quantum sensing, and will be responsible for providing essential supporting electronics for this sensing.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Sensing Below, Cooling Above: Harnessing Urban Aquifers for Climate-resilient Geothermal Cooling (Sub-cool)
jobs.department: Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

“Sub-cool” brings together expertise in hydrogeology, climate change, and social sciences to explore how aquifers beneath urban areas can become reliable and sustainable cooling resources. This work is timely as successive European heatwaves have pushed cooling to the frontline of climate adaptation and exposed growing heath consequences, with approximately 2,877 [gov.uk] heat-related deaths in the UK, reinforcing the need for low-carbon cooling to ensure resilient to future climate conditions.

Nevertheless, how aquifer thermal and hydrological conditions will evolve under intensified climate change is uncertain. In the UK, warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers may alter groundwater levels, flow and heat transport. This may lead to very different thermal footprints despite the same cooling demand, while also affecting groundwater and connected surface-water quality and supply. Past technology rollouts [nature.com] show the necessity to understand how the public weigh cooling benefits against perceived risks, costs and environmental trade-offs, making the integration of these perspectives with hydrogeological modelling essential for informing climate-resilient system deployment.

“Sub-cool” therefore asks, if changing aquifer conditions, cooling needs and public perceptions jointly shape where, and how climate-resilient urban aquifer cooling can be deployed, via the following research questions (RQ):

RQ1: How do aquifer cooling opportunities align with place-based cooling needs, and how do residents and professionals understand their benefits, risks and trade-offs? Walking interviews could provide a valuable approach to connect lived experiences of overheating and cooling access with perceptions of the subsurface resource in a selected European case alongside GM. These findings would inform the spatial priorities, scenarios and constraints examined in RQ2.

RQ2: How might climate change alter aquifer cooling capacity and capability? GM will provide the base case, supported by existing geological and borehole datasets, groundwater monitoring and UK climate projections. [metoffice.gov.uk] The comparative site selected through the work in RQ1 will be incorporated into geo-referenced GIS-based groundwater-flow and heat-transport modelling to examine how hydrogeology, climate and existing use shape spatial patterns of cooling capacity and thermal response. Modelled opportunities will then be assessed against the findings from RQ1 to shape the deployment is technically suitable, and socially and environmentally appropriate.

Before you apply: Please contact the main project supervisor, Prof Hollis, to learn more about the project and discuss whether it may be suitable for you.

To be considered for this project you must submit a formal application through our online application portal by following the instructions provided here. The Method for Observing pHysical Activity and Wellbeing (MOHAWk) is a validated systematic observation tool for assessing physical activity, social interaction and other health-related behaviours in public spaces. Although MOWAWk can be applied reliable to video footage, it currently depends on manual activity, with in labour-intensive and difficult to implement at scale. Advances in computer vision, including multimodal large language models and pre-trained video foundation models have the potential to automate this process.

This interdisciplinary PhD will develop and validate an automated version of MOHAWk. The objectives are to:

  • Develop an AI-enabled system for identifying MOHAWk behaviours in video footage;
  • Validate its outputs against expert manual coding;
  • Assess its robustness, generalisability and potential biases across different urban and observational contexts; -
  • Demonstrate its value through the evaluation of a real-world environmental intervention.

Potential outcomes:

  • An open-source framework and software for scalable behavioural observation;
  • Evidence about the accuracy, robustness and limitations of foundation-model approaches to analysing behaviour in public spaces
  • A platform for future applications across public health, urban planning, transport and environmental research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B10 A Multi-Scale Quantitative Investigation of Micro- and Nanoplastic Disruptions in Algal Physiology, Trophic Dynamics, and Carbon Sequestration
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Plastic pollution has introduced vast quantities of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) into aquatic ecosystems, raising urgent questions about their impacts on biodiversity and global biogeochemical cycles. Among the most critical but poorly understood aspects is how MNPs interact with plankton communities, which form the foundation of food webs and drive the oceans biological carbon pump-a key regulator of atmospheric CO₂.

Emerging studies show that MNPs can impair nutrient uptake, photosynthesis, and growth in algae, while also reshaping community composition by favouring opportunistic species. These changes cascade through ecosystems: plastics can alter carbon export by binding with algal cells into fast-sinking aggregates or, conversely, reducing sinking when attached to buoyant particles. Moreover, predators often ingest MNPs indirectly through contaminated prey, with transfer efficiencies up to an order of magnitude higher than direct uptake. Yet despite these findings, our understanding of how MNPs affect plankton-driven processes and carbon cycling remains fragmented, with few quantitative datasets under realistic ecological conditions.

This PhD project will bridge that gap by combining field surveys, laboratory experiments, and advanced analytical tools. Water and plankton samples from UK coastal waters will be analysed to quantify MNP types, sizes, and concentrations, correlated with plankton community metrics. Using innovative labelling and state-of-the-art techniques, the student will investigate species-specific uptake across representative algae, linking particle properties to cellular physiology and nutrient assimilation. Controlled feeding experiments will trace trophic transfer into zooplankton and higher consumers, generating quantitative coefficients for ecological risk models. Finally, the project will integrate these data into a predictive framework to assess how MNPs disrupt plankton community dynamics and the efficiency of the biological carbon pump.

The research will provide fundamental insights into the ecological and climate implications of plastic pollution, with outcomes directly relevant to environmental agencies, fisheries managers, and international policy. Training will be highly interdisciplinary, spanning environmental nanoscience, plankton ecology, analytical chemistry, and ecological modelling, equipping the student with cutting-edge skills and an outstanding platform for career development in environmental science.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please visit https://centa.ac.uk/studentship/2027-b10-a-multi-scale-quantitative-investigation-of-micro-and-nanoplastic-disruptions-in-algal-physiology-trophic-dynamics-and-carbon-sequestration/

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Light at the Atomic Scale: A PhD in Single-Molecule Nanophotonics
jobs.description_html:
We are looking for a PhD student to work in the area of nanophotonics and plasmonics. In this experimental project, metallic nanocavities, metasurfaces and/or 2D materials will be used to confine light and enhance light-matter coupling at the nanoscale, with the aim of detecting mid-infrared (MIR) signatures of single molecules [1-5]. The project is part of a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship.

Detecting MIR light, where molecular vibrations act as chemical fingerprints, normally requires cooled detectors to suppress thermal noise. We take a different route: molecular frequency upconversion. Molecules placed in a nanocavity that confines both MIR and visible light absorb MIR photons through their vibrations and emit visible photons, which can be detected with single-photon sensitivity at room temperature [1,4]. This allows both the detection and the spectroscopy of individual molecules, with wide applications in sensing, chemical analysis and biological imaging.

The applicant should have completed (or be close to completing) an undergraduate degree in Physics, Materials Science, Physical Chemistry or a related physical science, preferably with first-class honours or equivalent. Strong analytical and experimental skills are desired. Details of the project will be agreed with the successful candidate to tailor the research to their interests.

The student will work on understanding how MIR and visible light are simultaneously confined in nanometre-scale gaps, and how this dual confinement controls the efficiency of upconversion and detection. They will build and develop optical microscopy and spectroscopy setups to probe these nanocavities, spanning the visible to the mid-infrared, and will study how the response changes as a function of temperature. This will give insight into the role of molecular vibrations, thermal population and noise in the detection process. The work also involves fabricating and self-assembling plasmonic nanocavities, and exploring chiral and other tailored nanostructures [3].

The project will take place in the research group of Dr Rohit Chikkaraddy (https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/staff/profiles/physics/chikkaraddy-rohit.aspx), which is part of the Metamaterials and Nanophotonics Research Centre (https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/research/activity/physics/quantum/metamaterials/index.aspx) in the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, UK. The thesis is strongly multidisciplinary, and candidates from physics, materials science and chemistry are welcome. You will join an active, international research group and will be supported in developing a personal vision and an autonomous scientific profile, as well as industrial links and scientific collaborations.

The University actively supports equality, diversity and inclusion and encourages applicants from all sections of society. In line with the Department’s Athena SWAN programme, we particularly encourage female candidates to apply.

Funding: Funding is available for UK nationals. For details of the funding, advice on making your application or any other informal enquiries, please contact Dr Rohit Chikkaraddy at r.chikkaraddy@bham.ac.uk.

You can apply by clicking the 'Apply' button above, clearly stating the title of the project, the name of the supervisor (Dr Rohit Chikkaraddy) and the Metamaterials and Nanophotonics Research Centre.

References

[1] Chikkaraddy, et al. “Single-molecule mid-infrared spectroscopy and detection through vibrationally assisted luminescence”, Nature Photonics, 17, 865 (2023).
[2] Chikkaraddy. “Single molecule ready to couple”, Nature Physics, 20, 694 (2024).
[3] Hou et al. “Extreme optical chirality from plasmonic nanocrystals on a mirror”, Nano Letters, 25, 1158 (2025).
[4] Xomalis et al. “Detecting mid-infrared light by molecular frequency upconversion in dual-wavelength nanoantennas”, Science, 374, 1268 (2021).
[5] Chikkaraddy et al. “Single-molecule strong coupling at room temperature in plasmonic nanocavities”, Nature, 535, 127 (2016).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Non-equilibrium quantum many-body dynamics
jobs.description_html:
Macroscopic matter is composed of a huge number of quantum particles whose dynamics are typically dominated by interactions. In spite of this immense complexity, when a macroscopic object is in (or close to) an equilibrium state its gross properties are efficiently described by a rather simple set of macroscopic equations: the glorious laws of thermodynamics. One of the greatest challenges of theoretical physics is to devise a quantitative description of matter when, instead, it is far from any equilibrium state.

This project aims to study the out-of-equilibrium regime of quantum matter, which has become accessible experimentally only about twenty years ago, and is now used to realise the first noisy quantum computers. In particular, the main goals are to understand: (i) the non-equilibrium dynamics of interacting quantum matter; (ii) how thermodynamics emerges from it. The project will involve analytical and numerical approaches. The PhD work will involve techniques from quantum many-body physics, quantum information, quantum integrability, and quantum many-body chaos.

The project will be supervised by Dr Bruno Bertini.

Funding notes:

The project is directly funded by a research grant.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Predicting Attention and Action in the Developing Brain with Wearable Neuroimaging and Modelling
jobs.description_html:
Why can we respond quickly and accurately one moment, then hesitate or make an impulsive mistake the next? Attention and action fluctuate even when a task stays the same. These fluctuations matter for learning and everyday behaviour, yet response times alone cannot reveal whether their source lies in visual attention, readiness to act, or interactions between brain systems.

This project asks how the developing brain turns sensory information into reliable action. Which brain signals predict a response before it happens? Do visual attention and motor preparation make distinct or shared contributions? How does their balance change from childhood to adolescence?

You will combine wearable magnetoencephalography using optically pumped magnetometers (OPM-MEG) with visual frequency tagging. Children and adolescents aged 8-16 and adults aged 18-30 will complete a task requiring frequent button presses and occasional withholding of responses. Central and peripheral stimuli will flicker continuously at different frequencies, allowing pre-cue visual responses to be tracked alongside motor beta rhythms. Adult and child pilots will establish reliable measurements, supported by eye tracking and attention and movement localisers.

Using multilevel statistical models, you will test competing accounts of behavioural variability, quantify the unique and shared contributions of visual and motor signals to response times and errors, and ask how these change with age. Models will be tested on held-out data, including unseen participants. Working directly with children and adults, you will gain skills in neuroimaging, scientific programming and quantitative analysis. Few laboratories can record OPM-MEG in children.

Following validation, the framework could extend to neurodiverse populations, including people with ADHD, to investigate how variation in these brain mechanisms shapes attention and action.

The project will be supervised by Dr Kyungmin An and Dr Carmel Mevorach.

Before applying for the studentship, please email me (k.m.an@bham.ac.uk) with your CV, academic transcript, and a published research paper.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Mechanistic Modelling of Biofilm-Induced Host-Cell Damage
jobs.description_html:
Biofilm-associated infections can cause persistent damage to surrounding tissues, but the mechanisms linking biofilm development to host-cell injury remain poorly quantified. Biofilm growth, nutrient availability, bacterial toxins, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signalling evolve together and may contribute differently to DNA damage, repair failure, and cell death. Experiments can measure many of these responses, but they cannot easily determine which mechanisms are dominant or how they interact across space and time. This project will therefore develop a mechanistic mathematical framework that integrates experimental observations, identifies the processes driving host-cell damage, and quantifies the uncertainty in those conclusions.

The PhD will pursue four integrated aims:

1. Mechanistic modelling: develop a mathematical model linking biofilm growth and structure with nutrient transport, bacterial toxins, reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signalling, DNA damage, repair and host-cell viability.
2. Computational simulation: develop efficient numerical methods to simulate how these interacting processes evolve across space and time, including changing biofilm structure and local biochemical gradients.
3. Parameter inference and mechanism identification: use experimental data to estimate hidden biological parameters, quantify uncertainty, and determine which mechanisms are supported by the observations.
4. Prediction and experimental guidance: use the calibrated model to identify informative measurements and sampling conditions, distinguish competing damage pathways, and predict responses to selected therapeutic interventions. These predictions will be tested using independent experiments.

The project will deliver an experimentally validated framework for explaining how biofilms generate host-cell injury and for identifying which biological mechanisms should be targeted to reduce damage while maintaining effective bacterial control.

All details regarding the sources of funding and eligibility criteria can be found at this link.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: : High-Fidelity Electromagnetic-Thermal Modelling of Litz Windings for Next-Generation Cryogenic Machines
jobs.description_html:
This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is flexible but we are looking for someone to start as soon as possible.

Transport electrification is central to energy security and net zero. Electrical machines lie at its heart, providing propulsion across road, rail and maritime transport. In mass- and volume-constrained applications such as aerospace, these machines must become substantially more power-dense and efficient, a leap that calls for innovative technologies rather than incremental refinement.

Cryogenically cooled machines offer one of the most promising routes. At extremely low temperatures (around 20 K), the electrical resistance of high-purity aluminium and copper falls by up to a hundredfold, allowing windings to carry far higher currents with drastically reduced DC losses. Built from readily available materials, these “hyperconducting” windings offer a practical path to step-change performance.

However, this benefit comes at a cost. The same reduction in resistance strongly amplifies induced eddy currents, making AC losses a major concern. Litz windings, with thousands of fine, 3D-transposed strands, can mitigate these losses, but at cryogenic temperatures the losses become highly sensitive to temperature. Conductor resistance can change several-fold over a few tens of kelvin, while low heat capacity means even small losses cause significant temperature rises. Losses and temperature are therefore tightly coupled, making accurate loss prediction and assessment of thermal stability both critical and highly challenging.

This PhD project will tackle this challenge by developing high-fidelity, computationally efficient electromagnetic–thermal models of Litz windings at cryogenic temperatures, and using them to derive design guidelines for next-generation power-dense cryogenic machines with ultra-high-efficiencies.

You will:

  • extend established in-house analytical electromagnetic models to practical Litz windings, using reduced-order and data-driven AI methods for rapid, accurate loss prediction, verified against finite element simulations;
  • integrate these models with an existing thermal solver into a two-way coupled electromagnetic–thermal framework;
  • validate the framework through simulation and experiments on Litz winding samples, using an existing cryogenic test facility;
  • use the validated framework to understand the coupled behaviour, identify key design factors and optimise winding designs.

You will join the Energy Conversion group in the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, with weekly supervision from a team with complementary electromagnetic and thermal expertise. You will have access to established models, dedicated simulation software and cryogenic test facilities, so you will build on a solid foundation rather than starting from scratch. Training will cover electrical machine fundamentals, analytical and finite element modelling, data-driven methods, programming and cryogenic testing, alongside the University’s doctoral skills training.

This project suits a motivated candidate with a background in electrical, electronic or mechanical engineering, physics or a related discipline, who enjoys combining theory, simulation and experiments. Experience in electrical machine design, electromagnetic fields, finite element analysis, thermal management or programming (e.g. MATLAB, Python) is desirable but not essential.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Reductive Dearomatisation through New-to-Nature Biocatalysis
jobs.description_html:

Research theme: Biocatalysis and enzyme engineering

This 4-year PhD project is fully funded by the School of Natural Sciences; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The Buller group have co-pioneered the development of a new cofactor that substitutes the central iron atom on haem for cobalt, CoPPIX.1,2 Recently, we have reported that this new cofactor can perform enantioselective metal-hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) catalysis, a reaction of superb synthetic utility in organic synthesis.

We are working to expand the scope of transformations possible via MHAT. For this project, we will focus on a new mode of reductive dearomatization discovered originally on highly electron-deficient anisoles.3 The project will use directed evolution to increase activity on increasingly inert substrates, with the ambitious goal of achieving activity on mono-substituted benzenes and substituted heteroaromatic systems. Success will yield both a new suite of catalysts for MHAT transformations and access to chemical building blocks for use in materials and medicinal chemistry research. Engineered enzymes themselves serve as tools to study how mutations can tune CoPPIX reactivity. This project may use AI tools to model sequence-activity relationships and offers comprehensive training in laboratory enzyme engineering research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B09 Greener MOF Nanogels for Water Remediation and Critical Mineral Recovery
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Persistent organic pollutants, toxic metals and dyes threaten water quality, while discarded products and industrial residues contain valuable critical minerals. Sorbents can lose performance or release their own components as water chemistry changes. This project will develop greener metal–organic framework (MOF) nanogels and determine how their transformations govern remediation, resource recovery and environmental safety.

MOFs are porous solids with tunable binding sites. We will test whether confinement within hydrated biopolymer networks limits framework release while preserving accessible binding sites. You will prepare a small set of formulations using aqueous or reduced-solvent routes, then examine capture under different pH, dissolved organic matter and competing-ion conditions. Screening will cover persistent PFAS, represented by PFOA/PFOS, heavy metals and dyes. Detailed studies will focus on the most promising combinations. A separate pathway will test recovery of rare-earth elements, including neodymium and dysprosium, from secondary aqueous resources.

Building on our MOF remediation and transformation research, the project will connect structural and chemical changes to performance throughout synthesis, gelation, capture, regeneration and end-of-life ageing. Metal and linker release measurements, combined with pollutant mass balances, will identify potential secondary contamination. Mineral recovery will be assessed through desorption yield and product purity.

Safe and sustainable by design (SSbD) will guide material selection. You will compare treatment performance, aquatic effects, chemical and energy inputs, waste generation and reuse against relevant commercial sorbents. The outcome will be experimentally supported design rules for water treatment and resource recovery, identifying conditions that preserve useful performance while limiting environmental harm.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please visit centa.ac.uk/studentship/2027-b09-greener-mof-nanogels-for-water-remediation-and-critical-mineral-recovery

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Studying the Langlands Program via Formalisation and AI
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Christopher Birkbeck

This fully funded PhD project, based at our Norwich campus, offers an opportunity to work at the intersection of number theory, artificial intelligence and formal mathematics. You will investigate how AI can help us formalise and deepen our understanding of the Langlands program, with the aim of producing new mathematical insights, proving new results and strengthening existing ones. 

A concrete starting point will be the local Langlands correspondence for GL2(F) where F is a non-Archimedean local field. This correspondence provides a deep bridge between harmonic analysis and number theory, relating irreducible admissible representations of GL2(F) to two-dimensional Weil–Deligne representations. Using AI tools alongside the Lean 4 proof assistant, you will work towards formalising this correspondence, developing computer-verified definitions and theorems on both sides and progressing towards its construction and proof. 

You will have access to leading AI tools to support both formalisation and mathematical exploration. You will investigate how these tools can help you understand difficult arguments, work through examples, formulate conjectures, explore proof strategies and develop formally verified proofs. A central theme will be the interaction between mathematical understanding and formalisation: using the process of making definitions and arguments precise to clarify existing mathematics and motivate new research questions. 

The project is not limited to verifying known results. Alongside the formalisation effort, you will use AI to explore questions within the wider Langlands programme, seeking opportunities to establish new theorems and insights, extend or sharpen existing results, and find simpler or more conceptual proofs. These investigations will develop together with the formal work, with insights from each helping to guide the other. 

The ambition is to produce both reusable, computer-verified mathematics and original contributions to number theory, while developing effective ways to combine AI-assisted exploration with rigorous mathematical proof.

Entry requirements: The minimum entry requirement is 2:1 in Mathematics.

Mode of study: Full-Time

Start date: 1 October 2027

Additional funding information

This four-year funded studentship, starting in October 2027, comprises tuition fees at Home fee rate, an annual tax-free stipend at the UEA rate (£20,409 in 2026/27, subject to any agreed inflationary uplift for 2027/28), and a Research Training Support Grant of £3,000 per annum. It is open to applicants eligible for Home fee status.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B08 Less Emission, more Aerosol How Elevated CO2 Changes Organic Gas Emissions from Forests and their Capacity to Form Particles
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Forests emit large amounts of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). In the atmosphere these are oxidised to form large, oxygenated gases which then form secondary organic aerosol (SOA): tiny particles that scatter sunlight and form cloud droplets. The effect of aerosol on clouds is the largest single source of uncertainty in how much humans have changed the climate. Forest emissions therefore feed back on climate, but we do not know how this feedback will change as atmospheric CO2 rises.

Trees respond to high CO2 by changing both how much they emit and what they emit. Isoprene is the most abundant VOC emitted by plants, and its emission from many species, including oak, falls under elevated CO₂, while monoterpene and sesquiterpene responses are more variable. These compounds differ enormously in how well they make particles. Isoprene makes little SOA itself, and it actively suppresses particle formation from monoterpenes by interfering with the chemistry that builds oxygenated gases. A forest that emits less isoprene but similar or more monoterpene could therefore make more aerosol, even though its total emissions have fallen (Figure 1).

This project will test that idea in a real forest. The Birmingham Institute of Forest Research (BIFoR) FACE facility has exposed a mature oak woodland to CO2 150 ppm above ambient since 2017, alongside control plots at current CO2. It is one of very few places in the world where the emissions of a future forest can be measured directly.

The doctoral researcher (DR) will measure the VOC mixtures emitted under current and elevated CO₂, recreate those mixtures in the laboratory to measure how much aerosol they form, and use a chemical box model to work out which compounds cause any difference. Part of the laboratory work will take place at the University of Eastern Finland (UEF) with Dr Angela Buchholz, within the ACE-Forest Centre of Excellence, a leading group in aerosol formation from real plant emissions.

The outcome will be the first direct, mechanistic estimate of how CO2 fertilisation changes the aerosol-forming potential of a mature temperate forest, something climate models currently have to assume.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please visit centa.ac.uk/studentship/2027-b08-less-emission-more-aerosol-how-elevated-co2-changes-organic-gas-emissions-from-forests-and-their-capacity-to-form-particles

Hidradenitis suppurativa, one of dermatology’s most painful conditions, affects around one in 130 UK residents, causing recurrent boils, abscesses and scarring in the armpits, groin and under the breasts. Oral antibiotics are a mainstay of treatment, often taken for months or years, but their impact on future antibiotic effectiveness is unknown.

This PhD will answer that question using electronic health records. You will work with the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum, linked to hospital admission and mortality data. You will: map how antibiotics are prescribed for hidradenitis suppurativa across the UK and how this has changed; use machine learning to uncover distinct patterns of treatment over time and test whether they predict disease flares; and estimate whether prolonged antibiotic exposure is followed by antibiotic treatment failure when patients are later treated for chest or urine infections.

You will be trained in epidemiological study design, causal inference, survival analysis, machine learning and statistical programming, and in the governance of large health datasets. Supervision spans dermatology, pharmacoepidemiology and health informatics. You will join the Dermatology and Pharmaco-epidemiology Research Group in Manchester, within a dermatology centre that is a standalone theme of the NIHR Manchester Biomedical Research Centre. You will be supported to work with patients in shaping research.

Antimicrobial resistance is a national priority, yet dermatology evidence is scarce. Findings aim to inform clinical guidelines and stewardship policy, with all analysis code shared openly.

jobs.title: 2 PhD Positions in Business Administration, Entrepreneurship
jobs.description_html:
Lund University was founded in 1666 and is repeatedly ranked among the world's top 100 universities. The University has around 46 000 students and 8 500 staff based in Lund, Helsingborg and Malmö. We are united in our efforts to understand, explain and improve our world and the human condition. 

Lund University School of Economics and Management is one of eight faculties within Lund University. More than 4 000 students and 450 researchers, teachers and other staff are engaged here in training and research in business administration, economic history, business law, informatics, economics, statistics and research policy. 

The doctoral thesis projects will be conducted under the auspices of the Sten K. Johnson Centre for Entrepreneurship. The Centre (SKJCE) is an active, internationally recognized arena for high-impact entrepreneurship education and research. SKJCE conducts research in areas such as entrepreneurial learning and education, academic entrepreneurship, entrepreneurial ownership and finance, social entrepreneurship and immigrant entrepreneurship. 

We announce two four-year, full-time PhD candidate positions in entrepreneurship at the Department of Business Administration, Lund University School of Economics and Management, Lund. The PhD students will receive a scholarship for the first year and be employed at the department the remaining three years. 

The PhD students will start in spring 2027, date to be agreed. 

Subject area 

We are looking for two PhD students in Entrepreneurship. Both positions are anchored in entrepreneurship research, and each is connected to one of the two projects described below. 

The first position is connected to the project “AI and entrepreneurial learning”. In this project, we take a particular interest in how entrepreneurs’ use of generative AI shapes the ways they learn from experience as they develop their ventures. Research on entrepreneurial learning has largely treated the transformation of experience into knowledge as a process taking place within the entrepreneur, who reflects, interprets feedback and decides how to act. Generative AI unsettles this assumption, as parts of reflection and sense-making are increasingly performed together with, or delegated to, a machine. This may broaden and accelerate learning, but it may also substitute speed for understanding. The project builds on and seeks to extend research on entrepreneurial learning and cognition, and aims to identify the mechanisms through which AI enables, constrains or reshapes how entrepreneurs transform experience into knowledge. Questions relevant to the project include, for example: How does AI change the ways entrepreneurs reflect on and make sense of their experiences? Under what conditions does acting on AI-generated input and feedback deepen entrepreneurs’ understanding, and when does it merely speed up action? What tensions arise when parts of the learning process are delegated to AI, and how do they challenge established theories of entrepreneurial learning? 

The second position is connected to the project “Under the radar: AI-driven ventures and the changing organisation of innovation in the life sciences”. In this project, we take a particular interest in AI-driven ventures in the life sciences that emerge and develop largely out of public view before they challenge much larger established firms. Such ventures are more than a technical or commercial phenomenon. They raise questions about how entrepreneurs pursue opportunities in knowledge-intensive and highly regulated settings, what established firms can and cannot see, and where new knowledge is created and who controls it. The project builds on and seeks to extend research on new venture emergence, science- and technology-based entrepreneurship, and the dynamics between new ventures and incumbents. Questions relevant to the project include, for example: How do AI-driven ventures in the life sciences emerge, organise and build legitimacy before they become visible to established actors? How do established life-science firms detect, interpret and respond to them? How does AI change where new knowledge is created and who holds it, and what does this imply for entrepreneurial opportunities: are they genuinely novel or mainly faster variations of what already exists? How do regulation and ethical concerns shape which AI-driven ventures and innovations reach patients? 

We welcome candidates with an interest in the questions outlined above. Applicants are encouraged to develop their own research questions, theoretical perspectives and methods within these broader themes. The PhD projects can be pursued using qualitative, quantitative or mixed-methods designs. The positions are connected to ongoing research at the Department and the PhD students will be embedded in a network of researchers in Sweden and abroad. 

Work duties  

Regulations concerning appointment as a PhD student can be found in the Higher Education Ordinance Chapter 5, 1–7 §§ and SFS 1998:80. For appointment to the position, you are required to be eligible for admission to the PhD (PhD) programme in Business Administration.

The PhD programme in Business Administration at Lund University is a four-year programme consisting of two parts: a course package comprising 90 ECTS credits, and a PhD thesis comprising 150 ECTS credits. The main task is therefore to devote yourself to your research project and participation in postgraduate courses.

As a PhD student you will mainly be working with your research project, but you can also be given more general tasks at the department, e.g. teaching, research or administrative work, in accordance with the regulations in SFS 1998:80. 

Eligibility/Entry requirements 

Admission requirements for the PhD programme:

  • General admission requirements: A master’s degree, and 240 completed ECTS credits of university studies. A person may also meet the general entry requirements if he/she has acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way in Sweden or abroad.
  • Specific admission requirements: At least 90 completed ECTS credits in a subject relevant to the research studies, including a degree project relevant to the research studies, equivalent to at least 15 credits. A person may also meet the specific entry requirements if he/she has acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way in Sweden or abroad. 

Requirements for the PhD posistion:

  • Very high proficiency in English, in speech and writing.
  • Ability to work independently. 

Meritous for the PhD posistion:

  • Courses/modules in entrepreneurship. 

Basis of assessment

The applicants will be assessed on the basis of their prospects of meeting the requirements for a doctoral degree (PhD) in Business Administration. Particular emphasis will be placed on the following:

  • Academic results, particularly on the master’s level.
  • Bachelor’s and master’s theses (with special importance attached to the master’s thesis).
  • Relevance and viability of the research plan.
  • Other results and distinctions which attest to the applicant’s ability to profit from the PhD programme.
  • Other knowledge and skills relevant to the thesis work and the subject of the programme. These can be demonstrated through the attached documents and/or a possible interview. 

Decisions on admission to the PhD programme are made by the Head of department after consultation with the Director of the PhD programme and, if necessary, additional co-assessors with special expertise in the applicant’s intended thesis area. 

Application procedure 

The application is to contain the following documents:

  • A complete application form, found at: https://www.lusem.lu.se/organisation/department-business-administration/doctoral-studies-business-administration
  • Letter of introduction (max 800 words), which contains a presentation of yourself and your qualifications as well as a brief explanation of why you are interested in the PhD programme at the Department of Business Administration.
  • Curriculum Vitae (2 pages)
  • Research plan of no more than 5 pages (max 2,000 words) stating the topic to be investigated, its positioning within entrepreneurship research, and the sources of data and methodology the candidate aims to use. The topic should be specific and clearly located within one of the two projects listed in the subject area section (see above). Please indicate which project the plan addresses.
  • Degree certificates of your Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees
  • A copy of your Master’s thesis
  • An executive summary (500 words) of your Master’s thesis
  • The names and contact information of two references, preferably active in academia.
  • Copies of certificates and copies of any other documents that you wish to include in your application. 

All submitted documents must be attested as to their authenticity. 

Your application should be written in English and sent as one pdf file to: application@fek.lu.se. 

Lund University welcomes applicants with diverse backgrounds and experiences. We regard equality, equal opportunities and diversity as a strength and an asset. 

Last day for applying is: 2026-12-01 

For further information please contact: 

Diamanto Politis, Professor

Applications are invited for a three-year PhD studentship, funded by The Leverhulme Trust, in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at City St George’s, University of London. The successful candidate will be supervised by Dr Claudia Civai.

The project, Human contact as a costly premium: the consequences of new digital inequalities, investigates what happens when human contact becomes a service that only some people can afford.

As AI increasingly replaces human staff in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance, people on lower incomes may be pushed towards AI-mediated services not by preference, but by cost. Across the UK and Italy, this interdisciplinary project combines large-scale surveys, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and behavioural and physiological measures to investigate whether unequal access to human contact affects people’s satisfaction, sense of agency, and ability to retain important advice.

The successful candidate will play an active role throughout the project. In the first year, they will contribute to a large-scale survey across the UK and Italy, developing skills in experimental design, pre-registration, and advanced statistical modelling. In years two and three, they will work on laboratory studies, leading the collection of fNIRS and behavioural data at research sites in the UK and Italy. Full methodological training and travel expenses will be provided.

The project offers an excellent opportunity to develop interdisciplinary research skills at the intersection of behavioural science, social psychology, and cognitive neuroscience, within collaborations involving London South Bank University and the University of Padua.

Award Summary

Overview

Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established treatment for chronic neuropathic pain, typically considered for patients who have not responded adequately to more conservative therapies. Despite its clinical use, the mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects and the reasons for loss of efficacy over time remain poorly understood. This PhD project will investigate how different SCS paradigms influence pain processing and neuronal activity, building on our ongoing research using clinically relevant preclinical models of neuropathic pain and SCS in rats.

The project will combine behavioural, molecular and neurobiological approaches to investigate how different stimulation parameters and paradigms influence neural recruitment and the mechanisms underlying analgesia. A particular focus will be understanding why treatment efficacy may decline over time, including the role of axonal homeostasis during high-frequency stimulation. The project will also develop and validate long-term stimulation models, extending stimulation from minutes to days to better reflect clinical practice and investigate sustained neurobiological adaptations. This will provide important insights into the long-term effects of SCS and strengthen the translational relevance of preclinical research. Ultimately, the findings will advance our understanding of how SCS works, why it sometimes fails, and how stimulation protocols can be optimised to improve the durability and efficacy of treatment for patients with chronic pain.

The supervisory team brings together complementary expertise in electrophysiology, pharmacology and experimental neuroscience across multiple species, supported by successful and well-established research laboratories. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Designing Photocurable Resins for High-Resolution DLP Printing of Ultrasoft Hydrogels
jobs.description_html:
Research organisation: University of Nottingham
Application deadline: 10 December 2026
Start date: October 2027 (or as soon as possible thereafter)
Funding: Fully funded DLA PhD studentship supported by EPSRC

Project Description

Cells sense and respond to the stiffness of their surroundings. Matrix stiffness influences cell spreading, mechanotransduction and stem cell differentiation. Many soft tissues, such as brain and liver, have moduli below 10 kPa. Hydrogels that replicate this softness within precisely defined 3D architectures are therefore valuable for tissue engineering and in vitro tissue models. Digital light processing (DLP) 3D printing can fabricate complex hydrogel structures rapidly and at high resolution. Achieving such resolution with very soft hydrogels, however, remains challenging. Their dilute, loosely crosslinked networks are prone to overcuring during printing. They also swell substantially after printing, which distorts fine features and alters the final dimensions and stiffness of the construct. As a result, many DLP-printable hydrogels are considerably stiffer than the tissues they aim to mimic.

This project will develop new resin formulations that enable high-resolution DLP printing of ultrasoft hydrogels. Working at the interface of polymer chemistry and additive manufacturing, the student will design reactive crosslinkers and photocurable resins, and establish clear links between resin chemistry, swelling behaviour, print fidelity and mechanical properties. Supervision by experts in polymer chemistry and 3D printing will provide broad training in synthesis, photopolymerisation, mechanical characterisation and DLP printing. This combination offers a strong foundation for a career in biomaterials or advanced manufacturing.

Eligibility and Application Process

Applications are welcomed from candidates with a background in Chemistry, Chemical Engineering, or a closely related discipline, and with a strong interest in sustainable chemistry and pharmaceutical formulation.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to contact: Dr Vincenzo Taresco: vincenzo.taresco@nottingham.ac.uk and Dr Yinfeng He: yinfeng.he@nottingham.ac.uk. Full supervisory team: Dr Vincenzo Taresco, Dr Yinfeng He, Dr Robert Owen and Prof Ross Denton.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Programmable Matter from Entangled Architected Materials (AE0088)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Robots, software and digital memory can be reprogrammed after they are built. Materials, by contrast, have mechanical behaviour that is fixed at manufacture. This PhD will investigate whether that behaviour can be reprogrammed after fabrication.

You will study architected entangled materials: networks of curved filaments whose stiffness and toughness arise from how the filaments interweave and contact one another. Fabrics and ropes are familiar examples. In these networks, small changes in contact and friction can produce very large changes in mechanical response.

The project will exploit this sensitivity by driving a weak deformation mode, orthogonal to the deformations caused by external loads, to reprogram the network. Ordinary loading does not activate this mode, so the network remains stiff and tough in service. Driving the mode deliberately changes the contact state and releases the network.

Potential applications include spacecraft trusses that can be reconfigured after launch, and wearable braces that stiffen to protect a joint and soften to allow movement.

Key objectives:

  • Understand how contact and friction govern stiffness and toughness in each state
  • Establish how driving a deformation mode that external loads do not activate changes the contact state
  • Determine the range of loading over which this mode remains inactive
  • Identify what limits the contrast in stiffness between the two states
  • The project is approximately 50% experimental, 40% computational and 10% theoretical.

You will join the AIM Lab, a new group in the Department of Aeronautics. As one of its first members, you will help shape the group.

You will develop expertise in the mechanics of slender structures, contact and friction, and the geometry of filament networks. You will fabricate specimens using multi-material 3D printing and a robotic fabrication cell, test them mechanically, and write simulation code to model them.

You will present at international conferences, including the annual meeting of the Society of Engineering Science and the Functionality through Nonlinearity conference. Imperial’s Early Career Researcher Institute provides training in research and career skills.

Award summary

100% fees (UK Home only), a minimum tax-free annual living allowance at the 2027/28 UKRI Rate (note the 2026/7 rate is £21,805), and a research training support grant of £20,000.

Overview

Green methanol is emerging as a leading alternative fuel for deep-sea and offshore shipping, offering significant emissions reductions while utilising existing fuel infrastructure. However, current methanol fuel systems can result in substantial fuel and energy losses through venting and nitrogen blanketing, reducing both environmental and operational efficiency.

This PhD project will develop innovative solutions to improve methanol utilisation on board vessels by investigating fuel evaporation, modelling methanol vapour behaviour, and designing capture, recirculation, or combustion strategies. Building on a novel closed-system concept developed by O.S. Energy, the research aims to create a practical, scalable fuel system that improves efficiency while maintaining safety. 

Working closely with O.S. Energy's naval architects and engineers, the successful candidate will design, model and test the system with the ambition of achieving class approval and demonstrating the technology on a methanol-fuelled offshore support vessel. The project offers a unique opportunity to combine fundamental research with real-world industrial application and contribute to the decarbonisation of maritime transport.

This project is part of the EPSRC CDT in Process Industries: Net Zero. The successful PhD student will be co-supervised by academics from the Process Intensification Group at Newcastle University.

Overview

Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly central to offshore energy operations, yet their deployment remains constrained by limited endurance, energy density, and the ability to maintain station or perform interventions in harsh ocean environments. Offshore wind, subsea cables, and fixed/floating energy platforms require regular inspection and rapid-response maintenance, but current operations rely heavily on crewed vessels and ROVs-methods that are expensive, weather‑limited, carbon‑intensive, and inherently short-duration. 

This PhD project aims to develop a next‑generation endurant power and propulsion system enabling AUVs to achieve 500m+, 1000+ hours endurance and 2000+ miles operational range, unlocking persistent monitoring and immediate intervention capability for safety‑critical offshore energy infrastructure. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Powering the Future: Terahertz Technology for Next-Generation Batteries
jobs.city: Coventry, University of Warwick, Warwick Salary
jobs.description_html:
From electric vehicles to grid-scale energy storage, the future of clean energy relies on breakthroughs in battery technology. This PhD will develop cutting-edge terahertz spectroscopy methods to unlock scalable manufacturing of next-generation solid-state batteries.

The project:

Solid-state electrolytes are attracting growing interest for next-generation solid-state batteries due to their improved thermal stability, reduced flammability, enhanced durability, and potential for higher energy density. However, manufacturing high-performance electrolytes remains challenging, as their microstructures must be carefully controlled and optimised to ensure good electrochemical performance, mechanical integrity, and impermeability. This challenge is compounded by the lack of rapid inspection methods capable of assessing microstructural homogeneity, which is increasingly important for product-scale electrolytes.

The PhD candidate will join a dynamic, interdisciplinary research team working at the interface of metrology, battery materials, and ceramic processing. Building on our previous demonstrations [1], this project will begin with the fabrication and characterisation of conventional electrolyte materials using emerging terahertz spectroscopy. The work will then progress to developing the technique further for measurements on product-scale electrolytes. In the later stages of the project, thermal control will be integrated to probe intrinsic conduction behaviour and link this to longer length-scale conductions, establishing a unified framework connecting microstructure and transport mechanisms.

In close collaboration with LiNa Energy, this project offers an exciting opportunity to contribute directly to innovations in solid-state battery manufacturing, advanced metrology, and quality control for next-generation energy storage devices.

[1]https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpowsour.2024.234050

Scholarship:

The award will cover the full tuition fees, plus a tax-free stipend, currently 21,805, paidat the prevailing UKRI ratefor 3.5 years of full-time study. The award also includes a 5,000 research training support grant.

jobs.title: UKRI Funded PhD in Safe Artificial Intelligence
jobs.description_html:
Join our thriving multidisciplinary community and deliver projects focused on the safety of AI.

The Centre for Doctoral Training in Safe AI Systems (SAINTS CDT) is the UK’s first multidisciplinary PhD programme focused solely on the safety of artificial intelligence (AI).

Our vision is to train future leaders with the research expertise and skills to ensure that the benefits of AI systems are realised without introducing harm as the systems and their environments evolve.

The Centre for Doctoral Training in Safe AI Systems (SAINTS CDT) is the UK’s first multidisciplinary PhD programme focused solely on the safety of artificial intelligence (AI).

Fully funded PhD opportunity

SAINTS is part of the TechFirst pilot offering stipends of £30,000 for students eligible for home fee status. Join us and help grow the UK’s national capability in AI safety, part of the UK’s modern industrial strategy. Everyone is welcome if you are passionate about AI safety and looking to develop your research and innovation skills at doctoral level to further your career in safety-critical sectors such as transport, healthcare and national security.

As a postgraduate researcher with SAINTS CDT, you'll receive the following financial benefits:

  • A tax-free stipend £30,000* for your living costs (pro rata for part-time postgraduate researchers), which is paid to you in regular instalments. The amount of the stipend usually increases each year in line with inflation
  • Your annual tuition fees will be paid
  • Funding is available for you to attend research-related events and conferences

*You must have Home fee status to be eligible for the TechFirst stipend amount. Applicants who have International fee status are still welcome to apply but will receive the standard UKRI minimum stipend amount (£21,805 in 2026-27). The 2027-28 UKRI stipend amount will be confirmed in early 2027.

Applications are open until 12 noon GMT on Monday 11st January 2027.

The Programme

Our PhD in Safe AI takes a unique and purposeful approach. Postgraduate researchers with different backgrounds and experiences will train together.

Research will be focused on the lifelong safety assurance of increasingly autonomous AI systems in dynamic and uncertain contexts. It will build on methodologies and concepts in disciplines spanning AI, safety science, philosophy, law, sociology and health sciences.

You will also participate in a series of taught courses covering the technical, legal, ethical and societal underpinnings and implications of your research. These courses will give you the strong foundation you need for both your research and the next step in your career.

The PhD in Safe AI can be studied for four years full-time or eight years part-time.

Work directly with industry

The SAINTS CDT has an extensive network of over thirty partners, including major international companies, government organisations, regulators and charities.

Our partners will be closely involved in the research that you'll undertake throughout your PhD, and will provide you with opportunities to work in industry and gain valuable experience that will support your research development.

Some of our partners also expect to offer employment opportunities to SAINTS researchers when they graduate.

Location

You'll be based at the world's first Institute for Safe Autonomy at the University of York. It's an exciting and welcoming hub for innovation and collaboration with a modern and inclusive working environment. You'll benefit from world-class laboratories, collaboration spaces and expert colleagues working at the leading edge of their fields.

Entry requirements

Typically, you should have, or expect to obtain, one of the following combinations of academic qualification:

  • A first-class honours degree (or equivalent), OR
  • 2:1 in an honours degree and a Master’s degree (or equivalent)

We recognise that applicants may not have followed a traditional career path, and therefore relevant work experience or equivalent qualifications can be taken into account.

Your knowledge and experience should enable you to undertake doctoral research in your chosen area within the SAINTS CDT (e.g. computer science, engineering, mathematics, economics, health sciences, law, philosophy, sociology).

For more information about our entry requirements and details about how to apply, please visit the SAINTS CDT website.

Want to find out more or have a question to ask? Join us at one of our online applicant information webinars over November and December. Keep an eye out for dates and how to sign up on our website.

Contact us

If you have any questions, please email the SAINTS CDT administration team at saints-cdt-admissions@york.ac.uk

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Turbulence under Strain (AE0096)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59 on 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: Richard Feynman famously quoted ‘turbulence is the most important unsolved problem of classical physics’. Understanding and modelling turbulent flow physics will unlock a vast potential for optimising many applications of the energy and transportation sectors. While the last century has produced breakthroughs in our understanding of turbulent flows, these are confined in two extreme and polar-opposite regimes: when turbulence is highly or when it is lowly strained. Still, the physics of the in-between regime of intermediate-strain, which is critical for a wide variety of engineering and environmental applications, remains unexplored.

This project will focus on uncovering the physics of intermediate-strain turbulent wakes. Apart from being of interest from a fundamental perspective, such wake conditions are widely encountered in automotive, aeronautical and wind engineering applications among many others.

Various bluff bodies will be tested in the lab, carefully designed so that their near wakes produce average strain rates that vary from low to high levels. You will then document the failure of classical theories to describe intermediate strain regimes. The produced data-set will subsequently be utilized to develop a novel theoretical framework for intermediate strain turbulence, based on the concept of ‘simple transportation of energy’ recently proposed by the PI, and validated for the simpler case of homogenous decaying turbulence. The project will rely on laboratory experiments, conducted in the state-of-the-art wind tunnel facilities of the Aeronautics Department, and will utilize high speed particle image velocimetry to characterize 2D and 3D turbulent velocity fields.

The proposed work falls under the theme of the ERC project ONSET awarded to the PI and its successful conclusion could potentially lay the basis for the development of novel turbulence closure models for intermediate strain conditions, where current models are known to be inaccurate.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Real-time Data Assimilation for Multi-physics Flows (AE0095)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: Every model is wrong, and in engineering the errors matter. From aircraft wings to wind turbines and combustors, engineering systems are governed by fluid flows that interact with other physical processes, such as structural vibrations, acoustics and chemical reactions. On the one hand, physics-based models of these multi-physics systems are extrapolative – they provide predictions on phenomena that have not been observed. However, their parameters are uncertain, and their equations neglect part of the physics. On the other hand, measurements provide information on the true state of the system, but they are sparse and noisy. When operating conditions change rapidly, model errors grow, and forecasts lose accuracy precisely when they are needed most. Real-time data assimilation, which combines models with measurements, offers a way forward. However, most existing methods assume that the model is unbiased and they cannot cope with rapid changes in operating conditions, such as a gust hitting an aircraft wing or a sudden change in the load of a combustor. A fully-funded PhD studentship is available at the Department of Aeronautics, Imperial College London, to develop bias-aware data assimilation methods that estimate and correct model error as the dynamics evolve. The output of the project will be a model that learns from data any time that measurements are assimilated, without violating the physics. We will prototype the methods on low-order dynamical systems, and we will scale them up to higher-dimensional multi-physics problems.

You will gain experience in data assimilation and Bayesian inference, physics-constrained machine learning, and computational methods for multi-physics systems. You will employ high-performance computing facilities, present your work at international conferences, publish in peer-reviewed journals, and benefit from Imperial’s doctoral training programme and career support. These skills will prepare you for careers in academia, industry and research laboratories.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Generative Neural-Operator Surrogates for Real-Time Multiphysics Design (AE0094)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59 on 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: This PhD addresses a central bottleneck in engineering design: generating a candidate geometry is fast, but evaluating its physical performance is not. Neural operators can predict multiphysics fields in milliseconds once trained, and generative models can propose new geometries in seconds. Yet these two capabilities are rarely combined into a single, closed-loop system. Doing so would let a designer generate, evaluate and refine a component in real time, rather than waiting on costly simulation cycles. This has direct relevance to thermal management, electromagnetic components and multifunctional lightweight parts.

You will train neural-operator surrogates — Fourier Neural Operator and DeepONet-style architectures — on thermal and electromagnetic performance data, for example, from multifunctional metastructures. You will then embed these operators directly inside a conditional diffusion or transformer-based generator, so physics feedback becomes differentiable and near-instantaneous during generation, rather than computed afterwards. You will embed governing equation constraints as physics losses within the generative architecture, develop conditioning schemes letting users specify target performance directly, and validate designs computationally. You will quantify the trade-off between operator fidelity and generative design quality. You will test whether a single joint multiphysics operator (thermal and electromagnetic together) can replace two separate surrogates without losing accuracy. You will build towards an interactive design-exploration tool with sub-second feedback, benchmarking throughout against conventional solver-in-the-loop generative pipelines to prove where your closed-loop approach genuinely wins. You will work across both computational validation and, where feasible, experimental testing via 3D-printed prototypes, keeping the work tied to physically realisable structures rather than a purely theoretical exercise.

You will be supervised by Dr. Ajit Panesar and Prof. Rob Hewson, whose complementary expertise spans generative design, engineering optimisation, structural metamaterials and scientific ML, and you'll be working alongside a talented group of researchers in a dynamic, intellectually stimulating environment.
